However, many existing QSAR methods still suffer from limited applicability domains, overfitting, and instability across different datasets. To address these challenges, we present GT-QSAR , an automated machine learning workflow for structure-centric QSAR modeling that integrates heterogeneous molecular representations through ensemble learning. GT-QSAR supports both receptor- and ligand-based modeling strategies and combines diverse feature groups, including molecular descriptors, pharmacophore fingerprints, graph-based embeddings, grid-based shape and electrostatic representations, and protein–ligand interaction features. Systematic benchmarking using the Papyrus dataset demonstrates that GT-QSAR provides improved predictive accuracy, model stability, and generalizability compared with control tools. In addition, virtual screening experiments using the LIT-PCBA benchmark show that GT-QSAR substantially improves enrichment compared with conventional similarity-based and docking-based screening methods and previously reported target-specific machine learning models. These results demonstrate that GT-QSAR provides a robust and generalizable framework for QSAR modeling, enabling improved prioritization of active compounds in realistic drug discovery campaigns. The data used for QSAR modeling as part of this work is made publicly available. GT-QSAR is available online at https://gtqsar.standigm.com.

papers.title: pH-Inverted Histidine-Rich Nanochelant 5H-EAF for Electrostatic Dust Mitigation and Cation Detoxification in Lunar Regolith: Enabling Lightweight In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) for Artemis Missions
The Heisenberg Fingerprint: Physics-Informed Molecular Similarity from Neural Network Potential Hidden States
papers.abstract: Scaffold hopping, the identification of functionally equivalent molecules with different chemical scaffolds, is among the most valuable and difficult operations in medicinal chemistry. Topological fingerprints are blind to it: Morgan fingerprints assign near-random similarity (mean Tanimoto 0.20) to confirmed scaffold-hopping pairs. Here we introduce the Heisenberg fingerprint (HFP), a 256dimensional molecular embedding derived from the hidden representations of pre-trained neural network potentials (NNPs) that reliably identifies scaffold hops. Per-atom features from a DFTtrained NNP backbone are pooled via multi-head attention and trained to correlate with 3D shape overlap, electrostatic potential similarity, and pharmacophore feature matching simultaneously, using 2 million molecular pairs with computed overlap targets. On 147 known scaffold-hopping cases, HFP assigns mean cosine similarity of 0.83 to pairs that Morgan fingerprints rate at 0.20. On 24 approved drugs spanning 12 therapeutic targets, including clinically validated scaffold hops such as Imatinib/Dasatinib and Sertraline/Escitalopram, same-target pairs are separated from cross-target pairs with Cohen’s 𝑑 = 1.83 (Mann-Whitney 𝑝 < 10−6), with 100% of scaffold-hop pairs scoring above the cross-target median. HFP improves virtual screening AUROC over Morgan fingerprints on LIT-PCBA (0.524 vs 0.481, winning 10 of 15 targets) and MUV (0.596 vs 0.534, winning 14 of 17 targets, non-overlapping 95% CIs). The approach is backbone-agnostic: we validate two NNP backbones (Egret-1 and MACE-OFF23) and show both produce effective embeddings with complementary strengths. The entire pipeline was completed for under $400 on cloud infrastructure. These results establish NNP hidden states as a practical source of physics-informed molecular descriptors, with particular utility for scaffold-hopping campaigns where topological methods fail.

papers.title: When Do Models Win? A Learning Curve Benchmark for Molecular Property Prediction in Low-Data Regimes
papers.abstract: In many molecular propertIn many molecular property prediction tasks, such as drug discovery and OLED material design, labeled data are often limited to only tens to thousands of samples due to high experimental costs. Despite the rapid development of machine learning models, it remains unclear which model classes are most effective under such low-data regimes and how their performance evolves with increasing data. In this work, we present a comprehensive learning curve benchmark across traditional machine learning methods, graph neural networks (GNNs), transformer-based molecular language models, and hybrid architectures. We systematically vary the training data size from 50 to 3,000 samples and evaluate performance on QM9, ESOL, Lipophilicity, and BACE datasets using scaffold splits with repeated trials for statistical robustness. We further propose two hybrid models combining GCN and ChemBERTa with different fusion strategies—concatenation (GTCA-Cat) and cross-attention (GTCA-CA)—and analyze their data efficiency through ablation studies on both transformer layer depth (2/4/6) and fusion strategy. Our results reveal that (1) hybrid models substantially improve over single-modality GCN in low-data regimes for physicochemical property targets (e.g., 32.1% RMSE reduction on ESOL at N=50), (2) simple concatenation fusion generally outperforms or matches cross-attention due to reduced overfitting and improved stability, (3) deeper transformer layers (depth=6) consistently outperform shallower configurations across most targets and data regimes, (4) clear crossover points exist where traditional kernel-based methods outperform deep learning models depending on the task type. Importantly, we identify regime-dependent model optimality: deep learning models dominate continuous physicochemical property prediction (e.g., ESOL, Lipophilicity), while kernel-based methods can be more effective for bioactivity prediction (e.g., BACE) across most data scales. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for model selection under data scarcity and highlight the importance of learning curve analysis as a principled tool for understanding model behavior. Scientific Contribution: This study establishes a comprehensive learning curve benchmark for molecular property prediction in low-data regimes, systematically comparing eleven model families across four datasets spanning physicochemical, quantum mechanical, and biological activity properties. We identify regime-dependent model optimality and crossover points between traditional machine learning and deep learning methods, providing actionable guidelines for data-scale-aware model selection. We further demonstrate that simple concatenation-based multimodal fusion is more stable and data-efficient than cross-attention in low-data settings, offering practical design principles for hybrid molecular property prediction architectures.

papers.title: Sovereignty: A Lasso-Derived Composite Descriptor for Categorical Stability Classification of Pharmaceutical Compounds v2
papers.abstract: What changed in this version? v2: Expanded from n=294 to n=579 clinical compounds; added external validation (n=30, FDA NMEs 2020–2025, r=0.409, p=0.025); added six baseline comparisons; sensitivity analysis for weight selection; 23 references. Terminology updated from "Lasso-derived" to "Lasso-informed" for methodological clarity.

papers.title: Enzyme-Polymer stickers for assembling single and multi-analyte biosensors
Uncovering non-hydrogen bonded dormant states of perylene diimide monomer through molecular dynamics simulations and Markov state modeling
papers.abstract: Living supramolecular polymerization often involves manipulating the energy landscape of supramolecular polymerization to slow down thermodynamic processes and enhance kinetic barriers. This control allows for the precise assembly of complex supramolecular polymers. A deep understanding of the structural details and dynamic transitions of kinetically trapped intermediates is crucial for the rational design of supramolecular polymerization processes. Hydrogen bonding within the molecule is highly regarded as the primary contributor to the kinetic stability of monomeric species. The strucrual details of long-lived intermediates that delays the self-assembly are not well-understaood. In this study, we utilized molecular dynamics simulations and Markov state modeling to characterize the metastable states of perylene diimide (PDI) derivatives as a function of alkyl spacers of varying length (ethylene to pentylene chains). Our results demonstrate that these PDI derivatives become trapped in multiple metastable states, each characterized by distinct conformational pathways. All metastable states primarily exhibit intramolecular hydrogen-bonded structures regardless of alkyl spacer length. three states However, we also identied new conformation, lacking intramolecular hydrogen-bond, where the trialkoxybenzamide moiety is either parallel or slanted to the PDI π-plane. While molecules with ethylene, propylene, and pentylene spacers exhibit conformations that shield the π-surface, hindering self-assembly, molecule with butylene spacer adopt conformations that favour selfassembly. Interestingly, structural comparisons reveal similarities between molecules with ethylene and pentylene spacers, as well as between molecules with propylene and butylene spacers. We believe our work provides intruging insights into the dynamics of the kinetic trapped species, contributing to the understanding and advancement of living supramolecular polymerization.

papers.title: Predictive Modelling Enables Exploration of the Anticancer Potential of Ruthenium(II) Polypyridyl Complexes
Enantioselective Hydrogen Atom Relay via Non-covalent Catalyst Assembly
papers.abstract: Most biological functions are regulated by chiral molecules 1 that contain at least one tertiary stereogenic carbon, i.e., a carbon with one C(sp 3 )–H bond. Hydrogen Atom Transfer (HAT) 2,3 is a straightforward strategy to either edit 4 or introduce tertiary stereocenters in multiple synthetically useful transformations, 5 especially when coupled with photoredox catalysis. 6-8 However, traditional de novo designs of chiral HAT catalysts that provide sufficient enantiocontrol over short-lived open-shell intermediates, 9 have represented a major hurdle for the development of enantioselective HAT reactions. Here, we describe a distinct approach in which chiral HAT catalysts are obtained in situ by non-covalent self-assembly of privileged chiral phosphoric acids and commercial 2-mercaptopyridines. The phosphoric acid serves as a modular interchangeable chiral element that renders the achiral thiol effectively chiral, thereby allowing for a previously inaccessible combinatorial space of chiral HAT catalysts. This platform enabled the photochemical deracemization of 2-aryl pyrrolidines, a prevalent scaffold in active pharmaceutical ingredients. Optical enrichment occurs via enantioselective hydrogen atom relay, in which a single chiral assembly orchestrates hydrogen atom abstraction and delivery. This conceptual approach of relaying chiral information via non-covalent assembly paves the way for the discovery of numerous asymmetric radical transformations.

papers.title: Phospholipid Saturation Modulates Cholesterol Partitioning and Heat Transport in Lipid Bilayers under Thermal Gradients
papers.abstract: Lipid compositional asymmetry accross the two leaflets of the bilayer is a defining feature of biological membranes, critically influencing their chemical and physical properties. Understanding the factors that modulate this asymmetry is essential for elucidating the mechanisms that regulate membrane and protein function. Experimental evidence has demonstrated heat generation within cells, and localized heating strategies are increasingly used in thermal therapies for cancer. Additionally, electroporation techniques, which use electric pulses to make membranes permeable, can also create thermal gradients. These findings highlight the importance of understanding membrane behavior under nonequilibrium conditions. Here, we employ nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations with the coarse-grained MARTINI 3 force field to investigate cholesterol partitioning in lipid bilayers under thermal gradients. We explore bilayers with varying degrees of lipid saturation and cholesterol content. Our results reveal that cholesterol exhibits thermophobic behavior, preferentially accumulating in colder regions of the bilayer, a trend that aligns with previous atomistic simulations. This thermophobicity is most pronounced in bilayers composed of saturated lipids and at low cholesterol content. We further show that bilayer thermal conductivity decreases with increasing cholesterol content, while saturated phospholipid bilayers exhibit higher thermal conductivity than their unsaturated counterparts. Our findings indicate that lipid composition and cholesterol levels together modulate both mass and thermal transport in lipid membranes exposed to thermal stress.

papers.title: Proximity Binding Assay for PROTAC Ternary Complex Analysis
papers.abstract: The engineered formation of ternary complexes, in which two proteins are bridged by small molecules such as PROTACs or molecular glues, is a prerequisite for the targeted enzymatic degradation of pathogenic proteins; however, the combined analysis of these ternary interactions during the drug discovery process remains challenging. Here, we introduce a proximity binding assay for the simultaneous measurement of binary and ternary interaction kinetics on a biosensor surface. Target proteins and the substrate binding subunit of ubiquitin E3 ligase are tethered to mobile swivel arms of a Y-shaped DNA scaffold. The Y-structure induces spatial proximity between the proteins and presents them to PROTAC analytes flown across the sensor. PROTAC-induced ternary complex formation is measured by fluorescence energy transfer (FRET), while binary interactions are detected by fluorescence quenching. The assay is applied to cereblon (CRBN) and von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) as E3 ligase substrate receptors, a range of compounds including AT1, MZ1, dBETs, and ARV-825 as PROTACs, and the two bromodomains of BRD2, BRD3, BRD4, and BRDT proteins as targets. Automated workflows enable the measurement of 384 real-time sensorgrams in a single run using picomole sample quantities. The insights into proximity-mediated binding kinetics can enable the development of PROTACs and molecular glues with improved properties for targeted protein degradation.

papers.title: Benzophenone-mediated deconstructive cross-coupling of secondary alcohols with data-driven mechanistic insights
papers.abstract: We report a Ni-catalyzed deconstructive cross-coupling of secondary alcohols that enables the concurrent recovery of alcoholderived aldehyde byproducts, driven by benzophenone-mediated proton-coupled electron transfer. Machine learning-based visual analysis provided quantitative insights into the reaction system, revealing that the reaction efficiency is governed by the precise energetic matching of HOMO levels between the photocatalyst and the alcohol substrate, as well as by steric hindrance around the carbonyl group of the photocatalyst. This study demonstrates that machine learning using chemically interpretable descriptors can complement experimental approaches to rationalize complex reaction outcomes.

papers.title: How Small is Too Small? The Limits of Macrocycle Size in Active Template Cu-Mediated Alkyne-Azide Cycloaddition Reactions
papers.abstract: To maximise the effect of the mechanical bond, optimise physicochemical properties or even just to simplify the synthesis of an interlocked target, it is often beneficial for the macrocycle to be as small as possible. However, although our previous study led to the broad adoption of 26 atom bipyridine macrocycles for the active template Cu-mediated alkyne-azide cycloaddition reaction, the lower size limit for the mono- and bi-pyridine macrocycles commonly employed in this approach remains unclear. Here we study the interplay between ring size and half-axle steric demand in determining interlocking efficiency. Importantly, although 24 and 23 atom mono- and bi-pyridine macrocycles respectively mediate mechanical bond formation with less sterically demanding half-axles, 24 atom bipyridine macrocycles appear to be more generally useful.

papers.title: Single-Particle Electrochemistry Resolves Nanoconfined Ionic Polarization Dynamics in Soft Hydrogels
papers.abstract: Hydrogel iontronics offers a route toward neuromorphic computing by encoding information in field-driven ionic processes. At the level of individual hydrogel units, however, the microscopic ion transport kinetics underlying transient charge accumulation and relaxation remain experimentally inaccessible. Here we resolve ion-coupled out-of-equilibrium capacitive dynamics in cationic poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) microgels by correlating single-particle electrochemistry with optical microscopy in situ. We show that sub-millisecond, non-Faradaic charging at physiological ionic strength arises from rapid counter-ion redistribution within a nanoconfined polarization layer in the permeable hydrogel. Quantitative analysis and finite-element modelling reveal the characteristic timescale and spatial extent of this transiently polarized region, while electrolyte composition and thermally induced structural transitions provide systematic control over these responses. These results establish a mechanistic basis for capacitive writing in single hydrogel units as functional elements in iontronic and neuromorphic materials, and define key parameters linking structure, ionic dynamics and function.

papers.title: NNP/CG-MM: Embedding of All-Atom Neural Network Potentials into a Coarse-Grained Molecular Mechanics Environment
papers.abstract: Neural network potentials (NNPs), or neural network-based force fields, are gaining widespread attention for their ability to model complex chemical, materials, and biophysical systems. In NNPs, the total energy of the system can be decomposed into atom-centered components, where the energies and forces are described using a deep neural network. However, despite the flexibility and accuracy of NNPs, they are typically more computationally intensive than classical molecular dynamics. There have been recent advances in embedding NNPs into a molecular mechanics (MM)-based environment to maximize efficiency while retaining the accuracy of NNPs. In this work, we propose a method called NNP/CG-MM, in which an NN force Field is systematically embedded into a coarse-grained molecular mechanics (all-atom) environment (CG-MM). Coarse-graining (CG) involves constructing a simplified representation of a larger fine-grained (FG) system with the goal of significantly accelerating computations while maintaining the accuracy of the FG system when projected onto the CG variable distributions. The NNP-CG coupling terms are constructed using the multiscale CG force-matching (MS-CG) method. The scheme is tested on liquids and in capturing features of the hydrophobic effect, where three-body correlations in the CG solvent can play an important role.

papers.title: Nonlinear Causal Inference for Cooperative Lipid Dynamics in Molecular Dynamics Simulations
papers.abstract: When a target lipid binds to a transmembrane protein in a molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, the composition of the surrounding membrane may change. Linear causal models quantify this change as a constant shift in lipid contact counts between bound and unbound frames, but cooperative phenomena can produce a mixture of frames with and without large scale reorganization. Because a linear model averages over these distinct outcomes, the estimated effect size can vary, or even change sign, between replicates. Here, a Bayesian mixture causal model is introduced that decomposes bound state observations into two subpopulations: one with a direct binding effect only (β_direct) and one with an additional cooperative effect (β_coop), with mixing probability π estimated from the data. Automated model selection via the Watanabe Akaike information criterion classifies each lipid species as linear or cooperative. Synthetic validation achieves 100% model selection accuracy (7/7 scenarios). Application to three transmembrane receptor systems shows that model selection is fully reproducible across independent trajectory replicates. The framework extends the LIPAC causal inference toolkit for MD simulations.

papers.title: Model of the Henrys: Eyring, Frank, and the Foundations for Predicting Transport Coefficients
papers.abstract: Henry Eyring’s absolute rate theory provides a microscopic picture of liquid transport based on molecular jumps, while Henry Frank’s free volume theory relates entropy changes to an effective cage volume in condensed phases. In this work, we integrate these two frameworks to obtain the Model of the Henrys (MotH), a unified description of transport phenomena based on the (re)movement of molecules within a system. Starting from Eyring’s viscosity expression, we replace vaporization energies by residual energies, and express the free volume via Frank’s entropy–free-volume relation using residual entropy. The resulting model contains a small set of molecule-specific parameters. We demonstrate that viscosity, self-diffusion coefficient, and thermal conductivity of alkanes, alcohols, carbon dioxide, and water can be described in good agreement with experimental and molecular dynamics data over wide temperature and pressure ranges. Analysis of the fitted parameters confirms Frank’s original idea that free volume is primarily controlled by molecular size, whereas activation energies are strongly family-dependent, with associating fluids showing high activation energy. Furthermore, we show that MotH provides a theoretical foundation for empirical entropy scaling relations. Finally, we show that activation energy, free-volume, and entropy-scaling models are complementary rather than competing concepts.

papers.title: Computational Engineering of a Thermostable Enzyme for the Degradation of PET Through Manipulation of Disulfide Bonds
papers.abstract: Plastic pollution is a significant problem, accounting for approximately 12% of global solid waste [1], and plastic production and waste have more than doubled since 2000. Most plastics do not biodegrade and persist in the environment, slowly breaking down into toxic microplastics that harm ecosystems and create lasting adverse impacts. One of the most widely used plastics is polyethylene terephthalate (PET), accounting for 18% of global plastic production [2]. Currently, the most sustainable recycling method is biocatalysis, in which enzyme-catalyzed degradation of the polymer backbone generates low-molecular-weight fragments, enabling mild depolymerization. However, less than 1% of global plastic waste processing facilities use this process due to the limited thermostability of PETase enzymes, which limits the approach's general applicability and hinders its broad adoption [3]. One strategy by which nature enhances the thermal stability of enzymes is by the incorporation of disulfide bonds, a defining feature of thermophilic bacteria that thrive at elevated temperatures [4]. This study investigated whether increasing disulfide bond density could improve the thermostability of FAST-PETase by testing the hypothesis that additional disulfide bonds increase PETase thermostability. The FAST-PETase structure was mutated in PyMOL to introduce additional disulfide bonds, and the resulting mutants' thermal stability was evaluated. Engineered variants demonstrated enhanced thermal robustness compared to existing PETase benchmarks, indicating that rational disulfide bond engineering can stabilize PETase enzymes. These computational results demonstrate a novel enzyme-design approach that addresses a key bottleneck in biocatalytic plastic recycling and sets the stage for advancing enzymatic PET degradation toward global commercial viability.

papers.title: Silyl Radical Formation from Silanethiols via Sulfur Atom Transfer with Phosphinites
papers.abstract: Silanethiols facilitate H atom transfer processes in a variety of radical-mediated reactions. This work outlines how silanethiols form silyl radical intermediates via S atom transfer to phosphinites, detected by isotopically labeled H atom transfer, halogen atom transfer, and alkene hydrosilylation. This contrasts with other S atom transfer processes via selective phosphoranyl radical fragmentation, the analogous process of silanethiols is essentially thermoneutral and likely is favorable due to radical polarity matching.

papers.title: Predicting Ligand-Induced Conformational Selection: Co-Folding, Generative Docking, and the Pharmacophore Understanding Problem
papers.abstract: Many drug targets adopt distinct conformational states depending on the bound ligand, such as kinase DFG-in/out switching and nuclear receptor helix 12 repositioning, yet predicting which conformation a given ligand will induce remains an open challenge. Here we benchmark four computational paradigms, rigid docking (DiffDock, Gnina), flexible refinement (DynamicBind), co-folding (Boltz-2), and generative sequence-based docking (FlowDock), for ligand-induced conformational selection across ABL, BRAF V600E, p38α, and ERα (8 protein-ligand systems, 29 crystal H-bond targets). Boltz-2 achieves the highest interaction fidelity (86% exact crystal Hbond reproduction), followed by DynamicBind (52%), FlowDock (45%), DiffDock (45%, Type I only), and Gnina (0%). DynamicBind and FlowDock also successfully predict DFG-out from DFG-in inputs, while rigid docking fails entirely for Type II inhibitors. To test whether cofolding success reflects memorization or chemical understanding, we systematically deconstruct sorafenib into seven fragments, none of which exist in the PDB as BRAF-bound complexes. Boltz-2 maintains DFG-out through extensive modifications, including urea-to-amide substitution (S4), halogen removal, and a bare-phenyl back-pocket, switching to DFG-in only when the back-pocket tail is entirely removed (S6, S7). This topology-level tolerance indicates that the model has learned the hinge-to-back-pocket scaffold as the DFG-out determinant, rather than a narrow urea-specific pattern. At the interaction level, S4 specifically disrupts the αC-helix Glu hydrogen bond, showing that the structural requirements for DFG-out induction are learned independently from the specific H-bonds that stabilize it. FlowDock shows the same pattern with reduced tolerance, reaching the transition boundary one step earlier (S5). These results suggest that modern deep learning methods capture the chemical logic of conformational selection beyond memorized protein-ligand associations.

papers.title: Rigor and Reproducibility in Electrocatalysis: Best Practices for Operando Studies
papers.abstract: Operando measurements have rapidly expanded the scope of electrocatalysis by enabling direct observation of catalytic interfaces under working conditions and by linking structural, compositional, and spectroscopic observables to activity and selectivity. Yet the growth of operando methods has outpaced the adoption of broadly shared experimental standards, creating persistent challenges in reproducibility, interpretation, and comparison across laboratories and platforms. This Perspective synthesizes discussions from the 2025 National Science Foundation Workshop on Rigor and Reproducibility in Electrocatalysis and outlines a practical framework for the rigorous use of operando measurements in electrocatalysis. We highlight three recurring needs: careful implementation of complex methods to avoid overinterpretation; recognition that (subtle) differences in reactor architecture, hydrodynamics, and electrical boundary conditions can alter apparent kinetics and selectivity; and transparent reporting standards that enable meaningful cross-comparison without constraining measurement-specific cell innovation. Focusing on widely used techniques (including X-ray and vibrational spectroscopies, mass spectrometry, and electron microscopy) we discuss technique-specific pitfalls, cross-validation strategies, and recurring platform-agnostic considerations such as mass transport, current distribution, temporal-resolution mismatches, and catalyst evolution. This Perspective aims to strengthen the mechanistic inference and improve the reproducibility, comparability, and predictive value of operando electrocatalysis research.

papers.title: Core-Shell Perovskite Fibers Enabling Dual- Emission and Random Lasing in Various
papers.abstract: 2 ABSTRACT: Random lasing (RL) from perovskites is highly attractive for achieving specklefree imaging owing to its low spatial coherence. However, the intrinsic instability of perovskites limits their practical applications. Here, to overcome this, we encapsulate different metal-halide perovskites in a hydrophobic poly(methyl methacrylate) matrix and fabricate core-shell perovskite composite fibers via coaxial electrospinning. The composite exhibits a uniform distribution of perovskites, resulting in single- and dual-color emitting perovskite fibers. The dual-emissive fibers demonstrate remarkable water resistance, maintaining emission after 9 days. Their emission persists even under combined thermal stress (50 °C) and UV exposure in water for up to 40 min. Notably, the green-emitting core-shell fibers exhibit stable RL behavior in diverse environments, including air, water, and an acidic medium (pH=3), highlighting their robustness in extreme environments. Furthermore, RL from these fibers enables speckle-free imaging with an ultra-low speckle contrast (K = 0.008), compared to a conventional CW laser.

papers.title: Supramolecular Ir(III)/Ni(II) Photocatalyst Reveals Ni-Black Non-Innocence
papers.abstract: Dual photoredox catalysis is a powerful tool to achieve challenging bond transformations. Ir(III)/Ni(II) mediated cross-electrophile coupling is mechanistically underexplored, particularly the role of nucleated Ni(0). To exploit excited state interactions between Ir(III)* and Ni(II), we synthesized and isolated an Ir(III)/Ni(II) supramolecular photocatalyst in which the Ir(III) and Ni(II) are tethered by a bridging ligand (BL). The supramolecular Ir-Ni (Ir = [Ir(dF(CF 3 )ppy) 2 (BL)] + ; dF(CF 3 )ppy = 2-(2,4-difluorophenyl)-5-(trifluoromethyl)pyridine; BL = 1,2-Bis(4'-methyl-2,2'-bipyridin-4-yl)ethane; Ni = NiBr 2 ) and the monometallic analog Ir-BL have similar photophysical and electrochemical properties to [Ir(dF(CF 3 )ppy) 2 (dtbbpy)] + (dtbbpy = 4,4'-di-tert-butyl-2,2'bipyridine). In dual photoredox coupling with 4-bromobenzotrifluoride and bromocyclohexane, Ni(0) nucleation is observed after 24 hours. A model cross-electrophile coupling reaction with supramolecular Ir-Ni does not nucleate Ni(0) and has comparable cross-coupled product yields to dual photoredox reactions. Fresh reagent addition after 24 h resulted in continued photocatalysis in all reactions, revealing nucleated Ni(0) noninnocence.

papers.title: A flexible small-scale electrochemical flow cell
papers.abstract: Reproducible electrochemical characterization in bench-scale flow cells remains limited by variability in cell architecture, assembly practices, and operating conditions across users and laboratories. Although numerous cell designs have been reported, comprehensive guidance detailing component selection, fabrication, assembly, and testing protocols is largely absent. Here, we present a compact flow cell engineered to improve experimental rigor while maintaining architectural flexibility and cost-effectiveness. The platform incorporates interchangeable components and is amenable to a variety of testing formats, enabling adaptation to diverse electrochemical applications including redox flow batteries, electrolyzers, and fuel cells. The small-scale of the device lowers volume and area requirements for electrolytes and cell components, respectively, facilitating high-throughput, yet systematic studies of emerging chemistries and materials. As a representative use case, we characterize cell performance using two diagnostic configurations and a model redox electrolyte, common in flow battery literature. We also present a framework distinguishing marginal and total repeatability to quantify variability across independent cell builds and operators. Using cell polarization and galvanostatic cycling protocols, we demonstrate consistent performance across configurations and users. By coupling transparent design documentation with a quantitative repeatability framework, this work seeks to establish a reproducible foundation for bench-scale flow cell experimentation and to support cross-laboratory comparability in electrochemical research.

papers.title: NH3 Synthesis from 1.0 vol% Nitric Oxide Gas via Direct Electrocatalytic Reduction
papers.abstract: Ammonia is a promising zero-carbon energy carrier; however, its conventional production is energy-intensive and dependent on fossil fuels. The electrochemical reduction of nitric oxide offers a sustainable alternative for ammonia synthesis while simultaneously mitigating nitrogen oxide pollutants. In this study, a solid polymer electrolyte cell equipped with an anion-exchange membrane was employed to improve nitric oxide mass transport and suppress the competing hydrogen evolution reaction by establishing a localized alkaline environment. Using a copper catalyst supported on carbon, ammonia was successfully produced with a Faraday efficiency of 22%. The introduction of platinum as a secondary metal further enhanced the catalytic performance. Under continuous electrolysis at a current density of −50 mA cm −2 , the bimetallic copper–platinum catalyst achieved an ammonia formation rate of 2.2 mg h −1 cm −2 , a Faraday efficiency of 34%, and a nitric oxide-to-ammonia conversion of 23%. These results demonstrate an effective strategy for continuous ammonia electrosynthesis from dilute nitric oxide streams and suggest a promising approach for utilizing low-concentration nitrogen oxide sources.

papers.title: Efficient Photocatalytic Arene Hydrodehalogenation Using Hydrogen Terminated Nanodiamond and Visible Light
papers.abstract: The potential of diamond materials to act as a photocatalyst has been proposed in the past, based on the negative electron affinity of its surface, the position of the conduction band and the possibility to emit electrons from its surface also in liquid phase. However, actual experimental proof of this ability and studies of organic photocatalyis with diamond were lacking so far. Here, we report on the high photoredox activity of hydrogen-terminated detonation nanodiamond (DND-H) using visible light, giving access to redox potentials of about 3 V (vs SCE). Irradiation at 395 nm enables the dehalogenation of a broad range of aryl halides via a radical mechanism in good to excellent yields, making it suitable for the catalytic dehalogenation of halogenated environmental pollutants, e.g. persistent pesticides or chemical intermediates. The diamond catalyst is available on a kilogram scale and can be recycled, thus opening an opportunity for sustainable photoredox catalysis.

papers.title: Combinatorial synthesis of Ba-Zr-S-O thin films: cation ratio controls crystallization kinetics of BaZrS3
papers.abstract: BaZrS3 is a chalcogenide perovskite composed of earth-abundant elements that is of interest for photovoltaic (PV) applications. In the present work, BaZrS3 thin films were synthesized from oxide precursors with a spatially-varying cation ratio. The precursor thin films were deposited using combinatorial pulsed laser deposition and subsequently sulfurized in a tube furnace using different concentrations of H2S gas at temperatures from 800 °C to 1000 °C. Increasing the H2S partial pressure and/or the Ba concentration causes a transition from closed, dense nanocrystalline films to unconnected islands of large crystalline grains, indicative of enhanced mass transport kinetics, eventually leading to solid-state dewetting. These results suggest the presence of a Ba-S liquid phase that acts as a flux during BaZrS3 crystallization, for some processing conditions. Our results suggest that specific conditions are needed to stabilize this flux. The present work may help designing processes to fabricate BaZrS3 films at low temperatures, which remains an outstanding challenge.

papers.title: CONAN Build: Building functionalized or doped carbon nano-materials
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning the microscopic structure of nanoporous materials is essential for improving the performance of supercapacitors and other energy-storage devices. In this work, we present CONAN-build, an extension of our molecular dynamics analysis tool CONAN [J. Chem. Inf. Model. 2023, 63, 21, 6706–6716], which enables the interactive construction of complex nanostructures such as functionalized carbon nanotubes and nanoporous carbons. The tool provides a command-line interface and direct visual feedback via a graphical interface. This allows users to build pristine materials, add defects or functional groups, and dope materials for simulation studies. To demonstrate the program’s capabilities, we performed a case study on the ionic liquid 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate confined in carbon nanotubes. Negatively charged carboxylate groups functionalization significantly alters the ion count by making the pore entrance selective towards cations. This effect is diminished in larger pores. It suggests that surface functionalization near pore entrances may serve as an effective strategy to modify the electrochemical properties of nanoporous materials.

papers.title: Atomistic insight into the mechanism of substrate recognition and transport by the bile salt export pump (BSEP) using computational microscopy
papers.abstract: ABCB11, also known as the Bile Salt Export Pump (BSEP), is an essential member of the ABC transporter family that primarily exports bile salts across the bile canaliculi. ABCB11 undergoes extensive conformational transitions during its transport cycle. Although the recent cryo-EM structures provide a brief insight into the catalytic process, the detailed molecular mechanism of the substrate translocation and the role of cofactors in facilitating the transport cycle remain elusive. Given its structural homology with other ABC transporter proteins, ABCB11 is presumed to adopt an alternative access mechanism for its transport activity. However, the proposed mechanism is not characterized thoroughly. In this study, we have employed well-tempered metadynamics and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to decipher the overall transport mechanism of ABCB11 within a membrane environment. Our workflow incorporates enhanced sampling and systematic docking of substrates and cofactor molecules to map the full conformational landscape during the substrate transport of the protein. From the free energy surface of the Apo state, the ABCB11 structure in the minima has been identified, which subsequently served as a basis for analyzing substrate-bound, prehydrolysis, and post-hydrolysis states. Initially, the Apo form of ABCB11 adopts an “inwardfacing (IF)” conformation. Substrate binding induces conformational flexibility, allowing the protein to access occluded and distinct “IF” conformations with varying degrees of NBD separations. Furthermore, the nucleotide binding drives conformational transitions in the ABCB11. From the free energy surface, we have identified a catalytically potent, collapsed conformation primed for hydrolysis. Hydrolysis drives the receptor to adopt a more collapsed conformation, thereby facilitating the “inward-facing” to “outward-facing” conformational switch, which enables substrate release. Collectively, this work provides a comprehensive atomistic description of the entire transport cycle of ABCB11 and highlights the impact of substrate and cofactor binding on conformational transition that facilitates bile acid translocation.

papers.title: Electrooxidation of Chalcones to Vicinal Tricarbonyls (VTCs): A Gateway to Rapid Acquisition of Quinoxalines
papers.abstract: An environmentally benign, operationally simple transition-metal-free and external-oxidant-free electro-oxidative process has been established to synthesize a unique class of ketal-protected vicinal tricarbonyl derivatives starting from chalcones. The electrochemical oxidation of the electron-deficient chalcone double bond was achieved in an undivided cell using methanol as the solvent, with a graphite rod and a platinum foil as the anode and cathode, respectively, under air. The unprecedented ketal-protected vicinal tricarbonyl derivatives can readily be converted to respective quinoxaline derivatives in a one pot operation. A unique class of products, readily available starting material, inexpensive reaction setup, exclusive regioselectivity, high atom and pot economy are the synthetically attractive features of the newly discovered protocol.

papers.title: Stochastic Evaluation of Exciton–Exciton Annihilation Rate in 2D Molecular Aggregate
papers.abstract: Exciton-exciton annihilation (EEA) is a process by which two excitons combine to form a single high energy excitation. In molecular chromophore aggregates EEA is governed by microscopic two-exciton coherence that depends on long-range coupling and supramolecular geometry, motivating scalable quantum mechanical rate calculations beyond deterministic small-system diagonalization. Here, we develop a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)-accelerated stochastic method for computing finite temperature EEA rates in large 2D excitonic molecular aggregates. We demonstrated agreement with conventional deterministic matrix diagonalization for small and intermediate systems, while achieving an improved scaling of O(N 2 logN) from O(N 6 ) cost. This approach enables large-scale parameter sweeps and structure–function screening in realistic 2D morphologies. We close by exploring the role of uncorrelated and correlated disorder, temperature and inter-exciton coupling in EEA.

papers.title: moTSart: Accelerating Automated Transition State Search with Generative Models in a Low-Data Regime
papers.abstract: Transition states (TSs) are first-order saddle points on the potential energy surface, and thus the highestenergy structure on the (multi-step) minimum-energy reaction pathway that corresponds to a chemical reaction, determining the rate at which it proceeds. Locating TSs and thus elucidating reaction mechanisms is a computationally demanding and expertise-driven task. Recent automation strategies leverage heuristic rules or deep learning models to directly arrive at TS geometries from textual SMILES representations. However, standalone TS predictors lack robustness, whereas heuristic-based approaches lack scalability, limiting their applicability to reliable high-throughput reaction discovery under distribution shifts. Here, we present a generative machine learning framework embedded within a fully automated TS search pipeline and demonstrate accelerated high-throughput screening of bio-orthogonal click reactions as a representative case study. The automated framework enables scalable exploration of large reaction spaces and progressively learns, reducing the number of required quantum mechanical evaluations as additional reactions are processed. In our case study, continuous learning decreased the required TS optimization cycles by nearly 50% after processing only 540 reactions. By coupling generative modeling with physics-based validation in a scalable workflow, our work establishes a framework for data-driven reaction mechanism exploration and advances the development of autonomous computational discovery of chemical reactivity.

papers.title: Local operator–hydrodynamic closure of the molecular time-dependent Schrödinger equation via exact factorization
papers.abstract: For pure electron–nuclear states, the molecular time-dependent Schrödinger equation admits an exact factorization into a nuclear factor and a conditional electronic factor. On a star-shaped nodal patch of the nuclear marginal, a rank-one conditional electronic projector determines a canonical local electronic section by projector-defined parallel transport. In that canonical gauge, the exact dynamics are equivalent to an exact, canonically gauge-fixed evolution system with state variables given by the nuclear density n(R, t), a local nuclear phase S(R, t), and the conditional electronic projector P(R, t). The nuclear equations are the exact continuity and Hamilton–Jacobi equations of exact factorization. The electronic equation is an exact tangent-space projector evolution law that remains valid for the generally non-Hermitian exact-factorization electronic generator. The projector determines the quantum metric and Berry curvature pointwise, while the connection entering the closed equations is reconstructed from the projector by canonical transport. No adiabatic reduction, trajectory approximation, truncation, or compression is introduced.

papers.title: From Global Optimization to Transition State Search: An Automated Workflow for Surface Reaction Barriers
papers.abstract: Reaction barrier calculations present the major bottleneck in the systematic exploration of surface reaction networks in heterogeneous catalysis via atomistic simulations. Each transition-state search introduces a high-dimensional configuration space of initial and final-state combinations that must be explored to identify the minimum-energy pathway with the lowest activation barrier. Typically, this task is delegated to human chemical intuition as user input to, e.g. nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations, since its automation remains challenging. Here, we introduce a fully automated workflow for transition-state searches that requires no human intervention. Initial and final states are generated via global optimization and systematically combined through atom mapping, symmetry alignment, and heuristic selection to yield a tractable set of NEB calculations. We benchmark the workflow against diverse reactions and model surfaces from the OC20NEB database, where it identifies on average lower transition-state energies and produces minimum-energy pathways with high chemical fidelity to the target reactions.

papers.title: Dual Knotting Pathways in MJ0366: β-Sheet Strength Shape Folding Mechanisms
papers.abstract: Knotted proteins represent a rare class of biomolecules in which the polypeptide chain adopts a non-trivial topology. Such knots are often associated with enhanced thermal stability and structural robustness. The protein MJ0366 from Methanocaldococcus jannaschii, the smallest known trefoil-knotted protein, provides an ideal model system to investigate the mechanism of protein knot formation. In this study we have investigated how folding temperature and contact map definitions influence the dual knotting pathways of the trefoil-knotted protein MJ0366 using coarse-grained structure-based models. Our results show that folding and knotting are governed by the balance of stability among secondary structural interactions. At temperatures below the folding temperature (T<Tf), folding follows a multi-state pathway with non-identical intermediates that vary depending on the contact map. Additionally, we suggest that modulating β-sheet stability through mutations or environmental changes could tune the folding mechanism which in principle can be tested experimentally.

papers.title: WITHDRAWN
papers.abstract: Withdrawn at the author’s request due to presence of confidential research data.

papers.title: Scaling Carbon Removal to Gigaton Capacity using Pressurized Direct Air Capture
papers.abstract: Direct Air Capture (DAC) has the potential to roll back the effects of human-induced carbon emissions on our global climate. DAC technologies essentially extract carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to sequester it underground. The capturing process remains expensive due to the dilute concentration of CO 2 in the atmosphere. Current research primarily focuses on developing novel materials and solvents that can effectively reduce the energy requirements of the process. However, existing literature indicates that we have reached the minimum possible energy needed to capture CO 2 from the atmosphere. Instead, we present a new method that centers around maximizing the amount of air being treated. This process operates at high pressure to reduce contactor size by 70x, the main component of DAC facilities. It also delivers over 3100x better performance by increasing absorption capacity by ~7x and absorption rate by ~450x. The recommended solvent mixture is sourced from highly produced chemicals that are resistant to oxygen degradation. Our proposed solution leverages mature technologies that are highly integrated, so that it could be scaled to reach gigaton capacity. The next generation of DAC systems will need to focus on advancing turbomachinery and membrane technologies to achieve ultra-low CO 2 removal costs.

papers.title: A V4C3Tz//K0.04MnO2 supercapacitor cell in a 5 M LiNO3 electrolyte
papers.abstract: MXenes are excellent candidates for supercapacitor applications in aqueous electrolytes. Due to their two-dimensionality, which results in a high packing density, MXenes deliver a high energy per unit volume. However, as most MXenes perform in negative electrochemical windows, the challenge in building a full cell device lies on finding a suitable positive electrode that matches the high performance per unit volume of the MXene while being stable in the same electrolyte and enabling a suitable enhancement of the voltage range of the resulting cell. In the case of aqueous electrolytes, activated carbon electrodes have been traditionally used as the positive electrode counterpart of MXenes. However, its low density undermines the performance per unit volume. In this work we build a full cell using a V 4 C 3 T z MXene as negative electrode and cryptomelane-type K 0.04 MnO 2 as positive electrode and evaluate it in a 5 M LiNO 3 electrolyte. The full cell performed in a 1.8 V voltage range and showed a superior volumetric energy as compared to a V 4 C 3 T z //Activated carbon cell in a 3 M H 2 SO 4 electrolyte at low volumetric power (previously reported by us). The V 4 C 3 T z //K 0.04 MnO 2 cell also outperformed in volumetric energy other previously reported Ti 3 C 2 T z //MnO 2 and Ti 3 C 2 T z //Activated carbon cells evaluated in a water-in-salt electrolyte at a medium to high power per volume range. An aqueous and neutral electrolyte at standard concentration such as 5 M LiNO 3 brings environmental advantages versus acidic electrolytes and circumvents power performance problems brought in by highly concentrated electrolytes.

papers.title: The Hammerhead Fold – In-Solution Structure Validation of an Unusual Fold in a Major Streptococcal Virulence Factor, the M3 Protein
papers.abstract: M proteins are major virulence factors of Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS) and Streptococcus dysgalactiae subspecies equisimilis (SDSE), which have seen a recent surge in invasive infections on a global scale. Despite the importance of M proteins in the pathogenicity of bacteria, they have eluded high-resolution structure determination in their full-length physiologically relevant form, and little is known about their structure and functional dynamics. The publication of AlphaFold and particularly AlphaFold 3 has opened hitherto unknown possibilities for techniques complementing high-resolution structure determination. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy is well-suited for experimental protein structure validation. Here, we demonstrated this confirming a highly unusual N-terminal fold in the full-length M3 protein known to induce autoimmune rheumatic disease in humans.

papers.title: A Data-Efficient Machine-Learning Approach for Modeling the Photodynamics of All-trans Hexatriene based on Multireference Configuration Interaction Calculations
papers.abstract: Accurate simulations of excited-state photodynamics of polyenes remain challenging due to the high computational cost of multireference electronic-structure methods required to describe the coexistence of ionic and covalent states. In this work, active learning together with machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIP) trained on multireference configuration interaction with single and double excitations (MR-CISD) level energies and gradients is used to enable efficient and accurate nonadiabatic molecular dynamics for all-trans-hexatriene. A compact yet representative training set is constructed by reducing an initial pool of ~850k configurations to ~3k geometries while preserving the regions of configurational space relevant for the dynamics. The resulting model reproduces the topology of the excited-state potential energy surfaces and yields a physically consistent relaxation mechanism, characterized by a sequential S2 → S1 → S0 pathway and time constants in good agreement with experimental data. Analysis of representative trajectories provides mechanistic insight into the structural factors governing nonadiabatic transitions, including the key role of the terminal C=C bond elongation and identifies a notably broader and more diffuse structural distribution associated with the S1 → S0 transition in comparison to the more localized S2 → S1 decay pathway. Analysis of the torsional angles around the C=C double bonds reveals preferential isomerization at the central C3=C4 bond, providing semi-quantitative evidence for the initiation of cis-trans photoisomerization in the hot ground state. The MLIP simulations trained at high-level MR-CISD level are extremely efficient, enabling 200 trajectories running up to 800 fs in short time, whereas direct on-the-fly multireference dynamics simulations would be practically impossible at this MR level.

papers.title: Controlling Vertical and Lateral Growth of Copper and Ruthenium on Tungsten Dichalcogenide Monolayers for Interconnects and Metal Contacts
papers.abstract: The unique properties of tungsten based transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers (TMDs) drive significant interest for their use in a variety of applications, from heterogeneous catalysis, to future generation semiconductor device technologies. In these technologies the TMD monolayers are necessarily interfaced with a metal, such as a source and drain contact for use as a channel material in sub-nm transistors, an interconnect metal when used as a diffusion barrier, or as a support for a metal catalyst. The control of the morphology of the interfaced metal is critical to ensure optimal material performance for these target applications. Therefore, an atomic level description of how metals interact and grow on TMDs is needed. First principles studies of metal-TMD monolayer interactions have primarily focussed on the behaviour of single metal atom adsorption, substitutional metal doping, or pristine metal-monolayer interfaces. Consequently, there persists a clear gap in the understanding of metal growth on TMD monolayers and the drivers of vertical versus lateral growth. In this work, we present a density functional theory and ab initio molecular dynamics investigation of the adsorption, preferred morphology, and dynamics of Cu and Ru metal deposits on WS2 and WSe2 monolayers. Using metal cluster models of sufficient size to display a variety of potential morphologies, and by characterising the behaviour of the metal deposits with an ensemble of analytical shape descriptors derived from the gyration tensor, we develop a comprehensive and quantitative understanding of the structure, stability, dynamics, and morphology of deposited metals on tungsten TMD monolayers. We find that on both TMDs Cu prefers to form compact, vertically growing clusters, with molecular dynamics simulations showing a transition to a more compact metal shape and a further promotion of 3D growth over time. In contrast, Ru prefers to grow laterally on WS2. Ru present on WSe2 displays a preference for a lateral morphology as on WS2, but makes noticeably more compact deposits on WSe2 than on WS2. Dynamics simulations show that temperature further promotes growth in the preferred direction, thus driving both island growth and lateral deposition depending on the inherent preference for a growth mode. These results demonstrate clearly how the identity of the metal and the TMD layer contribute to the preferred growth mode and morphology. Additionally, we reveal the critical importance of dynamic cluster evolution over time in determining the final structure.

papers.title: Lessons Learned on Obtaining Reliable Conductivity Estimates from Molecular Dynamics Simulations
papers.abstract: The calculation of reliable ionic conductivities from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations is not a straightforward task, especially for strongly correlated systems, such as ionic liquids or highly concentrated electrolytes, where the Nernst–Einstein approach tends to fail. In this manuscript, we present the newly implemented conduct module for TRAVIS. It allows the calculation of the ionic conductivity using the Einstein–Helfand and Green–Kubo approaches, which explicitly include ionic correlations in their formalism. We provide a broad overview of accessible transport properties and compare methods and best practices for obtaining statistically reliable estimates of ionic conductivity and other physicochemical properties derived from electrolyte MD simulations, including transport numbers and the inverse Haven ratio. To validate our implementation and demonstrate the conduct module’s capabilities, we simulated the ionic liquid 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium dicyanamide ([EMIm][DCA]) as well as the ether-based electrolyte lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide in ethylene glycol dimethyl ether (LiFSI/DME).

papers.title: RAT-LAMP: Design and Characterisation of Conchimeric Primer Architectures Toward High-Density Solid-Phase Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification
papers.abstract: Solid-phase loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) offers a pathway toward low-cost, integrated molecular diagnostics, but practical implementation is limited by poor primer bioavailability and insufficient surface primer payload. RAT-LAMP ( R Nase- A ctivated T rigger for L oop-mediated isothermal AMP lification) and a conchimeric primer architecture are presented as a dual strategy to overcome these constraints. Conchimeras are concatenated multi-primer oligonucleotides composed of distinct LAMP primer species separated by RNA spacer residues, enabling on-demand primer release through RNase-mediated cleavage during amplification. The adoption of conchimeras reduces the number of distinct LAMP primer species competing for a fixed surface area from six to three. Chimeric and 81 to 84-base conchimeric primers were designed and evaluated targeting synthetic Dengue virus 1 DNA. The functionality of the designed primers was demonstrated for simultaneous RNase and polymerase activity under standard LAMP conditions. RAT-LAMP restored chimeric primer performance to near-unmodified levels (time-to-positive: 2.81 vs. 2.59 minutes for unmodified primers), confirming the feasibility of on-demand primer release. Conchimeric primer amplification was feasible following spacer optimisation (rCrG and rUrG designs), with RNase supplementation reducing batch-to-batch coefficient of variation by ∼ 4-fold (16.47% to 3.76%). Amplification using shorter conchimeras containing FIP and BIP confirmed that the rate-limiting primers (FIP and BIP) should not be concatenated with other primers. Notably, primers modified via 5′-phosphorylation for EDC surface immobilization produced a statistically significant improvement in amplification speed over unmodified primers (TTP: 2.36 minutes; p-value =0.0006). Together, RAT-LAMP and conchimeric primer architectures establish the component feasibility of high-density primer immobilization for solid-phase LAMP. They simultaneously address primer availability and surface loading constraints without increasing workflow complexity. Adoption of a three-species conchimeric system increases primer cost by only 1.4-fold over unmodified primers (£0.010/ test - conchimera vs £0.007/ test - unmodified). Regardless of the cost increase, at £0.010/ test, the adoption of conchimeras for solid-phase primer delivery would not significantly impact consumable cost.

papers.title: Hydration Free Energies of Alkali Metal and Halide Ions from Data-Driven Many-Body Potentials
How spin conductive are oligo(p-phenylenes) in trityl-based biradicals
papers.abstract: The relationship between structure and exchange coupling constant J is of interest for the rational design of molecular open-shell systems in the context of molecular magnetism, dynamic nuclear polarization, and quantum information science. However, even for the basic relationship between J and the distance r between two spin centers for the archetypal oligo( p -phenylene) bridge, there are only a few and contradicting experimental and theoretical data. We therefore synthesized a series of six trityl-[( p -phenylene) n=1-5 ]-trityl biradicals and used Electron Paramagnetic Resonance methods to extract J values in the range from 17.5 MHz to 235 GHz. We find a distance dependence parameter β of 0.11 Å -1 for unsubstituted and 0.67 Å -1 for substituted oligo( p -phenylene) bridges. This places unsubstituted oligo( p -phenylene)-bridges into the spin-conductor regime and highlights the tunability of conductance by substitution, i.e., increase of the dihedral angle between the phenylene units. DFT calculations employing low Fock-exchange fraction functionals exhibit some limitations in reproducing the experimental J value, particularly in the weak coupling regime. Furthermore, biradicals with n = 3-5 exhibit spin coherence of 1.2 µs at room temperature in the liquid state. These long coherence times, combined with the modular bridge design, position bistrityl systems as promising candidates for applications in quantum information technology.

papers.title: Design Rules for Selective N2 Reduction Through Electrolyte Chemical Potentials
papers.abstract: Metal-mediated nitrogen reduction offers a route to decentralised, low-carbon ammonia synthesis, but its selectivity is poorly understood and often attributed to the formation of a solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI). Here we show that ammonia selectivity in lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction is governed by the relative chemical potentials of lithium and proton carriers in the electrolyte, rather than by SEI composition. By independently tuning lithium-ion and proton-carrier chemical potentials across a range of salts, solvents and proton sources, we find that ammonia, hydrogen and unreacted lithium yields collapse onto a single descriptor defined by the difference between the Li + /Li and H + /H 2 potentials. Post-mortem analysis of electrode deposits shows that SEI formation correlates with lithium chemical potential but does not determine selectivity; instead, SEI growth primarily suppresses both N 2 reduction and H 2 evolution rates through passivation. These results explain previously observed bell-shaped selectivity trends and provide a thermodynamic framework for designing electrolytes and redox mediators for selective and energy-efficient ammonia synthesis.

papers.title: Synthesis and Comparison of Photophysical Properties of Anionic Diaryl [M(C^C)(CN)2] x-(M= Au III , Pt II ) Complexes
papers.abstract: The d 8 complexes A[Au(C^C)(CN)₂] and A₂[Pt(C^C)(CN)₂] (where C^C = 4,4′-bis(tert-butyl)-2,2′biphenyl-1,1′-diyl and A = NBu₄, K) were synthesized from [Au(C^C)Cl]₂ and [Pt(C^C)COD], which were themselves obtained from Sn(C^C) n Bu₂. These complexes are bright photoemitters but exhibit remarkable differences in the origin of their photoluminescence. The tin complex Sn(C^C) n Bu₂ displays blue/white photoluminescence originating from an admixture of ¹IL(C^C) and excimeric transitions. In contrast, the gold complexes exhibit green, long-lived phosphorescence (lifetimes up to 100 μs), which theoretical calculations attribute to ³IL(C^C) transitions. Although the platinum complexes show similar absorption and emission energies, theoretical calculations indicate an admixture with ³MLCT character in their emissive states. This is evidenced by: (i) luminescence lifetimes up to one order of magnitude shorter than those of the gold complexes under similar conditions; (ii) a greater contribution from ¹IL(C^C) fluorescence in solution, due to less efficient intersystem crossing (ISC); and (iii) reduced susceptibility to ³O₂ quenching, a consequence of the shorter triplet-state lifetime. The combination of water solubility, efficient ISC, and a long-lived triplet state with high sensitivity to dissolved O₂ endows K[Au(C^C)(CN)₂] with excellent catalytic activity in the photo-oxidation of p-bromothioanisole. This result underscores the potential of this class of Au(III) salts for photocatalysis in green solvents.

papers.title: CO-Degassing in a Segmented Slug Flow Reactor Enables Continuous Linear Alcohol Formation from Alkenes using a single, non-assisted Rh-catalyst by Switching Between Hydroformylation and Aldehyde Reduction
papers.abstract: We investigated the continuous, tandem catalytic reductive hydroformylation of 1-octene in a segmented slug flow reactor using a single catalyst enabled by CO degassing. Higher alcohols are of significant industrial importance and are traditionally produced through a two-step process. The use of rhodium-based catalysts offers advantages in terms of activity and selectivity towards linear alcohols; however, carbon monoxide (CO) inhibits catalytic activity in the subsequent reduction step. An innovative approach is presented here, where CO is selectively removed from the reaction mixture after hydroformylation utilizing a semi-permeable AF2400 membrane in a tube-in-tube setup to enhance reaction efficiency. The results demonstrated a notable improvement in yields, achieving 67.1% yield of l-nonanol with an impressive linear-to-branched (l/b) ratio of 10.6 after a residence time of only 27.6 minutes. This study highlights the significance of effective degassing and demonstrates the potential for sustainable optimization of reductive hydroformylation in continuous flow operations, showcasing that nearly full conversion can be achieved under optimized conditions with comparatively low catalyst loading of 0.5 mol.-%.

papers.title: Robust Delocalized Frenkel Excitons in Two-Dimensional Supramolecular Assemblies
papers.abstract: Efficient energy transport in nanoscale photonic and optoelectronic systems requires excitons to remain delocalized in the presence of structural and environmental disorder, a central challenge for real-world applications ranging from artificial light harvesting to quantum information processing. Here we show that Frenkel excitons in two-dimensional supramolecular nanomaterials preserve extensive delocalization even in the presence of intentionally embedded deep-energy traps. Using fluorescent trap molecules introduced during the self-assembly of double-walled molecular nanotubes, we created a model system in which traps are incorporated without compromising the host lattice’s structural integrity. Polarization-resolved microscopy of individual nanotubes reveals that exciton delocalization is remarkably robust against trap incorporation. Complementary theoretical simulations based on realistic molecular geometries reproduce the experimental behaviour and further demonstrate that excitons adaptively redistribute to avoid trap sites. These results establish that higher-dimensional supramolecular architectures can sustain efficient exciton transport under fabrication-relevant levels of disorder, highlighting a key advantage of multidimensional excitonic materials and pointing toward the similar behaviour expected in fully three-dimensional systems.

papers.title: An Experimental and Theoretical Investigation of the Electrochemical Reactivity and Electron Transfer Kinetics of Perindopril Erbumine
papers.abstract: This study explores the electrochemical properties of Perindopril Erbumine (PE) via cyclic voltammetry (CV) and correlates with density functional theory (DFT) calculations at the CAM-B3LYP level. CV experiments, conducted with a three-electrode system (glassy carbon working electrode, Ag/AgCl reference, Pt counter), revealed distinct oxidation and reduction peaks, indicating sequential oxidation processes, with scan rate studies (10–100 mV s⁻¹) confirming diffusion-controlled yet kinetically hindered electron transfer. DFT results show that PE exists as a neutral COOH···N hydrogen-bonded complex in the gas phase. Frontier molecular orbital analysis indicates a large HOMO–LUMO gap (7.78 eV), reflecting high kinetic stability, with the HOMO localized over amine and carbonyl groups, identifying preferred oxidation sites. The first adiabatic ionization potential (6.54 eV) correlates with the initial anodic peak, while the higher second ionization potential (18.44 eV) explains oxidation at elevated potential. Low electron affinity values account for the weak reduction response. These findings establish a diffusion-assisted, kinetically controlled sequential oxidation mechanism governed by intrinsic electronic structure.

papers.title: Spin Modulated Energetics in the Combustion of MnB2
papers.abstract: Manganese diboride (MnB2) possesses an unusually high enthalpy of combustion, especially compared to other transition metal diborides (TMB). Previous work attempted to shed light on the mechanism underlying the energetics of MnB2 through the lens of overcoordination. Deeper investigation of the electronic structure and properties of MnB2 revealed potential spin crossover (SCO) behavior. The dynamic coexistence of the stable high spin (HS) state and the unstable low spin (LS) state potentially explains the material’s previously observed metastability. Applying this theory, the energetic output was tempered through the combustion of MnB2 in the presence of a magnetic field to spin trap the electrons into the more stable HS state. This opens the door to modulation of energetic output and improved storage safety of solid state energetic materials.

papers.title: Scale-up of laminar co-flow method for selective precipitation from micro- to milli-fluidics
papers.abstract: The laminar co-flow method (LCM) is a promising separation approach that allows selective precipitation of minerals from complex feedstocks. LCM offers unique process control leading to high product purity and selectivity, but the method is in early stages of research with reported studies currently limited to experiments in microfluidic devices at low flowrates. Commercial implementation of LCM for critical mineral separation will require the scale-up of co-flow reactors through a combination of numbering- up and scaling-up to meet the flowrates required for industrial-scale processing. In this study, we experimentally evaluated LCM scale-up using selective precipitation of Mg(OH)2 from seawater as a representative chemistry. We successfully demonstrated the feasibility of scaling up LCM from microfluidic devices to the millifluidic-scale without performance loss and provide the first demonstration of continuous solids collection using LCM. We used computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling to identify critical scalability parameters. Our CFD model outputs showed alignment with experimental observations and that LCM will work in reactors up through 1 meter in diameter. The model also identified >1 Pa pressure drop across the reactor and <5% difference in fluid densities as design limits for maintaining a well-defined reactive interface for LCM. To be industrially relevant LCM will need further scale-up from millifluidics, and this is the first step toward designing larger LCM reactors.

papers.title: Chitosan-Gated Polycarbonate Nanochannels for Switchable Water and Cation Transport
papers.abstract: Biological membranes regulate transport by simultaneously responding to pH changes and ion binding. Emulating this logic, chitosan is introduced into the cylindrical nanochannels of multiporous polycarbonate ion-track-etched membranes via covalent immobilization or electrostatic adsorption. Chitosan is mainly deposited in the nanochannels, leaving outer-surface liquid–solid interactions unchanged. The channels remain open when dry, while upon hydration the polymer swells and modulates water and ion transport. Chitosan shifts the membrane from microfiltration to ultrafiltration via swelling-driven steric hindrance. Consistent with the reduced water flux, the flux of tris(2,2′-bipyridine)ruthenium(II) (Ru(bpy) 3 2+ ) decreases by ~75% and ~92% at pH 7.5 and pH 2.5, respectively, compared to pristine nanochannels at the same pH. The stronger limitation at pH 2.5 arises from combined steric hindrance and electrostatic exclusion by protonated chitosan. Salts provide an independent stimulus: at neutral pH, Ca 2+ chelation induces chitosan deswelling and increases water flux, whereas under acidic conditions, KCl mainly screens charges and eases cation passage. This simple biomimetic platform enables pH- and ion-triggered, bidirectional control, allowing limitation or acceleration of both water flux and cation transport on demand and advancing nanoporous materials for smart separations, selective ion handling, and adaptive flow regulation.

papers.title: Open Source Tools for Pressure Vessel Thermo-Mechanical Response and Safety Analysis—Applications for Depressurization, Overpressure Protection, Boil-off, and Fire Exposure
papers.abstract: This work presents an open-source Python-based framework for the dynamic simulation of pressure vessel thermo-mechanical response during blowdown, filling, fire exposure, and cryogenic boil-off. The framework solves coupled mass and energy balances integrated with detailed heat transfer correlations and mass flow models. A partial phase equilibrium approach is employed to capture the non-equilibrium thermal behavior between phases. The models are validated against five experimental datasets and commercial software, showing robust performance for both pure fluids and mixtures. Application case studies reveal that conventional steady-state sizing methods for pressure safety valves on gas-filled vessels can overestimate required capacities by up to a factor of six, as thermal degradation of vessel wall strength typically governs failure before overpressure. Analysis of composite hydrogen storage and LPG fire protection further demonstrates that transient thermal effects are often the limiting factor for safety. These results highlight the critical importance of dynamic simulation for risk-informed design, as simplified steady-state methods fail to capture the complex thermo-mechanical coupling essential for ensuring vessel integrity under emergency conditions.

papers.title: Quantitative Constraints on the Condensed-phase Reaction Rate Constants of Criegee Intermediates with H2O2 and H2O
papers.abstract: Although Criegee intermediates (CIs) govern important oxidation pathways and are key reactive species in environmental and atmospheric chemistry, the condensed-phase reaction rates of CIs with soluble trace gases, such as H2O2 and H2O, remain somewhat uncertain. Here, we use the well-characterized multiphase reaction of ozone with aerosolized squalene to examine the competitive reaction pathways of CIs with H2O2/H2O and aldehydes (forming secondary ozonides, SOZs). In the presence of gas-phase H2O/H2O2, synchrotron vacuum ultraviolet photoionization aerosol mass spectrometry shows elevated aldehyde concentrations accompanied by a marked decrease in SOZ formation, providing direct evidence for competing reactive sinks for CIs. Using the CI + aldehyde reference reaction in relative rate method, we quantify the condensed-phase bimolecular rate constants for CI + H2O and CI + H2O2 reactions. Using measured Henry’s law constants for H2O (Hcp = 0.12 M⋅atm-1) and H2O2 (Hcp = 0.51 M⋅atm-1) in a predictive kinetic model, the condensed-phase bimolecular rate constants for CI reactions with H2O2 (1.0 × 10-14 cm3⋅molecules-1⋅s-1) and H2O (9.0 × 10-17 cm3⋅molecules-1⋅s-1) are determined. These values are comparable in magnitude to analogous gas phase reactions, in contrast with other condensed-phase bimolecular reactions with CIs (e.g., with acids, alcohols and aldehydes), which are orders of magnitude smaller than gas-phase analogs. These results provide key insights into the elementary kinetic steps that determine the fate of CIs produced in environmental and organic aerosol oxidation reactions.

papers.title: Toward Selective Cleavage of Glucosepane Crosslinks: A Theoretical Framework for Lewis Acid-Catalyzed Nucleophilic Trapping and Photoredox Radical Cation β-Scission
papers.abstract: Glucosepane is the most abundant advanced glycation end-product (AGE) crosslink in aged human extracellular matrix, accumulating irreversibly due to the absence of any known endogenous cleavage mechanism. No validated method for cleaving glucosepane has been published. Here, we present a unified theoretical framework comprising two synergistic strategies for selective glucosepane cleavage. Strategy I exploits the thermodynamic ring-opening equilibrium of glucosepane’s bicyclic aminal core. Lewis acid (Zn2+) and mild acid catalysis enhance the equilibrium population of the ring-opened intermediate, which is irreversibly captured by α-effect nucleophilic scavengers. A central kinetic result—that the effective cleavage rate keff = ktrap × [scavenger] × Kopen is independent of the ring-closure rate kclose—renders the prediction robust against uncertain kinetic parameters. Conservative modeling predicts crosslink half-lives of 18 hours to 2.2 days under optimized conditions. Strategy II bypasses the thermal activation barrier entirely through visible-light photoredox catalysis. Single-electron oxidation of glucosepane's lysine-derived N1 nitrogen generates a radical cation that undergoes β-scission—irreversible ring-opening fragmentation. Selectivity arises kinetically rather than thermodynamically: only glucosepane's strained heterocyclic ring provides an irreversible fragmentation pathway for the radical cation, while off-target amine radical cations are harmlessly reversed by back electron transfer within nanoseconds. The two strategies are mechanistically synergistic: photoredox-generated ring-opened intermediates are the species that nucleophilic trapping captures irreversibly. Even partial radical cation damage ("photochemical priming") increases the ring-opening equilibrium constant by orders of magnitude, rendering thermal trapping viable for previously resistant molecules. We further introduce a threshold therapeutic model: partial crosslink removal (hypothesized at 10–30%) may suffice to restore matrix metalloproteinase access, re-enabling endogenous collagen remodeling and initiating a self-amplifying therapeutic cascade. Specific validation experiments are proposed that can test the framework using synthetic glucosepane and LC-MS analysis.

papers.title: Graph Symmetry and Kekulé Structure Localization Correlate with Carcinogenic Potency of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons
