papers.title: Direct Chromatography-Free Quantification of THC and CBD in Cannabis by CID and EI-Like Fragmentation Enabled by Dielectric Barrier Discharge Ionization
papers.abstract: A chromatography-free method was developed for the sequential quantification and differentiation of (±)-Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) using dielectric barrier discharge ionization (DBDI) coupled with high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry for identification of the target compounds and MS2 for elucidation. DBDI generated both even-electron ([M+H]+) and odd-electron (M+• ) precursor ions in a single ionization event, each subjected to collision-induced dissociation (CID). The resulting MS2 spectra matched both LC-MS/MS and EI-MS libraries, enabling compound matching without chromatographic separation. Optimal ionization conditions were determined to enhance both ion types, and multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) transitions were developed from the odd-electron species to enable sensitive and selective quantification in complex matrices. This approach achieved sub-ppm detection limits and accurate THC/CBD ratio measurements in cannabis extracts, using Standard Addition, demonstrating its applicability for rapid, high-throughput cannabinoid analysis.

papers.title: Light-triggered decoding of the hydrophobic effect in living systems
papers.abstract: The hydrophobic effect is central to biological organization, underlying membrane assembly, molecular recognition, and protein folding. Despite its importance, spatiotemporal control of hydrophobicity is challenging because it emerges from collective solvation free-energy effects around hydrocarbon frameworks whose C(sp3)–H bonds are chemically inert. Here we show that hydrophobic interactions can be encoded and decoded on demand under physiological conditions using water-soluble functional groups and visible light. Aliphatic carbon frameworks are encoded in charged radical precursors, significantly reducing the free-energy penalty of aqueous solvation. Light-triggered single-electron decarboxylation converts these precursors into nonpolar hydrocarbon products, restoring hydrophobic interactions. This transition drives emergent behaviors including membrane self-assembly, lipid-mediated signaling, and targeted protein degradation in living cells.

papers.title: Automated Workflow for Microkinetic and Reactor Mdeling for Dry Reforming of Methane
papers.abstract: Dry reforming of methane (DRM) is an industrially and environmentally important reaction that converts CH4 and CO2 into syngas and serves as a useful model reaction for studying complex catalytic behavior. We present an automated multiscale computational workflow that links molecular-level modeling, microkinetic analysis, and reactor design by leveraging established reaction mechanisms and rate laws from prior studies. The framework enables rapid construction of microkinetic models and direct coupling to plug-flow reactor simulations, allowing precitions of conversion, surface-species evolution, pressure drop, and reactor perfomance as functions of catalyst loading, reactor length, and time on stream. Applied to DRM, the workflow captures methane conversion trends, dominant surface intermediates, and axial temperature-and pressure-dependent behavior under experimentally relevant conditions. This study demonstrates that automated multiscale modeling provides a scalable route for connecting fundamental catalytic kinetics with reactor engineering and process optimization.

papers.title: Exploring the Role of Excitonic Coupling in Polariton Formation
papers.abstract: J-aggregates are supramolecular structures assembled from organic chromophores, where collective interactions among monomeric units yield novel photophysical properties such as ultranarrow linewidths, increased peak absorption coefficients, and superradiant emission. J-aggregates are often used as substrates to prepare exciton-polaritons, hybrid quasiparticles formed by strongly coupled light and material excitations. However, the role of aggregation in exciton-polariton formation is often overlooked. In this work, we fabricate planar, Fabry-Pérot cavities containing a monomeric and J-aggregated thiacarbocyanine dye and perform angle-resolved transmission spectroscopy to elucidate the role of intermolecular dipolar coupling on polariton formation. We find that the monomer and J-aggregate cavities display similar coupling strengths of ℏΩ R = 168 ± 4 meV and ℏΩ R = 203 ± 1 meV, respectively. Most coupling criteria suggest that both monomer and J-aggregate cavities display strongly coupling. However, the J-aggregate cavity displays narrowed transmission peaks with distinctive anticrossing in both the experimental transmission and simulated absorptance, while the monomer does not. We ultimately classify the monomer as intermediately coupled while the J-aggregate is clearly strongly coupled. Our results suggest that excitonic coupling among monomers in J-aggregates mitigates inhomogeneous disorder effects and facilitates polariton formation, ultimately reinforcing J-aggregates as optimal molecular substrates for strong coupling experiments, particularly those aimed at leveraging delocalization effects.

papers.title: Do Chemically Modified Oligonucleotide Therapeutics Require Environmental Risk Assessment?
Subcritical extraction optimizes the milk thistle value chain: Balancing disproportionate economic-health gains with marginal environmental trade-offs
papers.abstract: The industrial development of Silybum marianum has accelerated in recent years, yet its processing chain, characterized by the long-standing sequence of mechanical oil removal followed by solvent-based silymarin extraction, has remained unchanged for years and lacks a structurally integrated sustainability evaluation framework. In this study, three common oil extraction pathways-solvent extraction (SE), mechanical pressing (PE), and subcritical butane extraction (SBE)-were treated as a system-level decision variable. A unified multi-endpoint life-cycle framework integrating carbon footprint (CF), economic value (EV), and a benefit-risk-based health performance index (HPI) was established based on experimentally derived inventories. PE achieved the lowest carbon emission, whereas SBE delivered the highest economic value and superior health performance. Under an environmentally-priority structure, PE represents the preferred pathway. In contrast, when economic return is prioritized, SBE becomes optimal. Transitioning from PE to SBE led to a moderate increase in carbon emissions (2%), accompanied by a substantial rise in economic value (151%) and a slight improvement in health performance (4%). Under expanded oil commercialization scenarios, economic gains were further amplified (176%). These findings not only provide a new perspective on enhancing profitability within the milk thistle industry, but also provide decision support for balanced technology selection in multifunctional agro-food systems.

papers.title: Enhanced Abiotic RNA Homopolymer Formation in Recirculated Microdroplet Reactions
papers.abstract: The air-water boundary of Earth’s oceans is a global reservoir for organic-compound accumulation and surficial chemistry. Sea-spray aerosols offer largely unexplored kinetic and thermodynamic advantages for chemical reactions and provide a natural cycle that supports unique abiotic chemistry. Here, airborne microdroplets were used as reaction vessels to form short-chain RNA oligomers from pre-activated nucleotides of adenosine, cytidine, guanosine, and uridine. Microdroplets (3 to 5 µm) were produced from bulk solution, condensed, and recirculated to mimic the natural system. Reaction products were analyzed via matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-ToF MS). Homopolymer formation from adenosine and uridine was enhanced, whereas oligomer formation from cytidine and guanosine was no different between microdroplet and bulk synthesis, indicating a preferential selection for adenosine and uridine. Tandem MS experiments of nucleobase dimers revealed that homo-nucleobase interactions dictated oligomerization. Including oligonucleotide formation shown here, all four major classes of biomolecules, including lipids, peptides, and sugars, have now been synthesized abiotically in microdroplet reactors. The enhanced RNA oligomer formation shown here, without catalysts or additives, highlights the importance of droplets as complex environments with broad implications for prebiotic chemistry, including as a novel selection mechanism between nucleotides and a source of homopolymer tracts that are conserved in modern life, such as poly(A).

papers.title: Mechanistic Insights into Synergistic VFA and NH3 Recovery Using a Hybrid BPMED–HFMC System
One- and Two-Electron Coordinatively-Induced Reduction of N-Heterocycles by Divalent Rare Earth Terphenyl Anilide Complexes
papers.abstract: Molecular rare-earth (RE) complexes in the divalent oxidation state have been used as potent one-electron reductants, yielding bonding motifs not accessible elsewhere in the periodic table. A deeper understanding of the chemical properties which dictate their reducing power is required to tame their reduction potentials and unlock new controlled reactivity. Here, we report the electrochemical characterisation of a series of divalent bis -(tethered)arene complexes, [M II (NHAr i Pr6 ) 2 ] ( 1M , M = Y, La, Sm, Eu, Yb, Tm, Lu; NHAr i Pr6 = {N(H)C 6 H 3 -2,6-(C 6 H 2 -2,4,6- i Pr 3 ) 2 }), and their reactivity towards the nitrogen heterocycles pyridine and 4,4′-‍bipyridine. Complexes 1Y , 1La , 1Tm , and 1Lu reduce 4,4′-bipyridine and reductively couple pyridine to afford the dimeric [{M III (NHAr i Pr6 ) 2 } 2 (m-N 2 C 10 H 8 )] ( 2M , M = Y, La, Tm, Lu) and [{M III (NHAr i Pr6 ) 2 } 2 (m-N 2 C 10 H 10 )] ( 3M , M = Y, La, Tm, Lu) respectively. These results contrast with electrochemical measurements, which place the RE(III/II) reduction potentials for all 1M complexes as insufficiently reducing for either heterocycle. These results imply the reactions proceed through coordination-induced reduction. Synthesis of 2M complexes also results in the formation of 4,4′-bipyridine radical species, which are probed by NMR, EPR, and UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopies.

papers.title: Quantifying the Number of Dark, Gray, and Bright States as a Function of Spectral Overlap in Polaritonic Systems
papers.abstract: Strong exciton-photon coupling can steer photophysical processes. However, the picture where it leads to two polaritonic and a manifold of optically dark states is now questioned. Instead, a picture where inhomogeneous broadening results in a partial photonic contribution to the dark states has gained ground. To understand the consequence of these dark and so-called gray states, they first need to be experimentally quantified. Here we use angle-resolved emission, coupled to rate equation modelling to quantify the absolute number of states in optical cavities. In addition, we also estimate the fraction of states that are gray by means of computer simulations. We find that the number of gray states is proportional to the overlap between the energy of the dark-and polaritonic states. This knowledge can be applied to all previous and future studies to interpret how detuning affects the relative number of dark and gray states and, consequently, polaritonic dynamics.

papers.title: Vapor-Deposited, Enzyme-Functionalized Coatings Sustain Anti-Biofilm Activity against S. aureus and S. epidermidis via Foul-Release Mechanism
papers.abstract: Biofilms formed by Staphylococcus species pose persistent challenges in healthcare and food processing environments due to their resistance to conventional cleaning and antimicrobial strategies. Immobilized biofilm dispersal enzymes (BDEs) offer a non-bactericidal control approach by degrading the extracellular matrix to weaken biofilm adhesion and cohesion, but implementation is often constrained by substrate surface chemistry and solvent compatibility. Here, we report an all-dry, substrate-versatile initiated chemical vapor deposition (iCVD) approach that deposits poly(glycidyl methacrylate) (pGMA) thin films to enable covalent immobilization of representative BDEs, proteinase K (PK) and DNase I (DN). We show that immobilized PK and DN retained activity and exhibited species- and enzyme-specific antibiofilm effects without bactericidal activity, potentially reducing selection for resistance under repeated exposure. PK-functionalized surfaces (pGMA-PK) reduced Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus aureus biofilms by >99% and 94% compared to the pGMA control, whereas pGMA-DN showed modest activity against S. aureus only. Partitioning and quantification of planktonic, adherent, and sloughed fractions suggested species-dependent antibiofilm modes of action for pGMA-PK. For S. epidermidis , immobilized PK weakened biofilm adhesion, causing biofilm sloughing from pGMA-PK surfaces under gentle rinsing; active-site inhibition reduced sloughing, implicating PK-mediated proteolysis in S. epidermidis biofilm destabilization, an effect that notably persisted over three exposure-rinse cycles. In contrast, incubation with pGMA-PK doubled planktonic S. aureus , suggesting an inhibition of initial adhesion rather than removal of established biofilms. Together, these results demonstrate the efficiency of non-bactericidal, vapor-deposited BDE coatings and highlight species-dependent Staphylococcal responses that inform antibiofilm surface design for clinical and food-processing applications.

papers.title: Electrons Meet Confined Electrolytes: Redefining the Electrochemical Interface
papers.abstract: From the age of the mercury electrode to the era of sustainable development, the landscape of electrochemistry has transformed. Eighty years after David C. Grahame’s monumental review of the electrical double layer, electrochemical devices are no longer defined by simple planar interfaces, but by nanoporous electrodes and complex electrolytes. This feature article explores the frontier of this evolution, redefining our fundamental understanding of interfacial thermodynamics, reaction kinetics, and ion transport through experimental advances and multiscale modeling. As we look beyond Grahame’s idealized models, the synthesis of theory and experiment offers a new paradigm for engineering the next generation of electrochemical systems for energy storage and chemical transformation.

papers.title: RETRACTED: Qualitative Assessment of Natural Deep Eutectic Solvents for the Sustainable Recovery of Polyphenols from Citrus Peel Waste
papers.abstract: Retracted by the author for inaccuracies in the data.

papers.title: A Statistical Mechanics Perspective on Memory and Forgetting in Nonequilibrated Polymer Films
papers.abstract: Polymer systems prepared far from equilibrium often retain long-lived memory of their processing history, manifested experimentally as molecular recoiling stresses and their anomalous relaxation behavior. Relaxation may therefore be viewed as the gradual erasure of stored nonequilibrium memory (forgetting). Experiments on spin-coated polymer thin films reveal relaxation behavior that lies beyond the scope of conventional equilibrium polymer dynamics and continuum viscoelastic descriptions, which only partially explain it. Yet a unifying statistical-mechanical framework for these observations has remained elusive. In this Perspective, I argue that such phenomena can be understood as the non-Markovian regression of constrained conformational entropy. Pivoting from Onsager’s regression hypothesis, the theory of dynamics of nonequilibrium variables, and the Mori–Zwanzig projection-operator formalism, molecular recoiling stress is identified as a slow nonequilibrium variable governing relaxation in nonequilibrated polymer systems. Projecting the microscopic dynamics onto this variable leads naturally to a stress-projected generalized Langevin equation with a history-dependent memory kernel. This minimal coarse-grained description accounts for stretched-exponential stress relaxation, Arrhenius temperature dependence, and the experimentally observed scaling of relaxation times with polymer chain length. The aim is not to introduce new microscopic models, but to provide a simple and general statistical-mechanics framework that rationalizes history-dependent stress relaxation in polymers and clarifies how polymers gradually forget their preparation history far from equilibrium. More broadly, this framework suggests that polymer memory and slow relaxation arise from the regression of constrained conformational entropy stored during nonequilibrium preparation, with topological constraints acting on nonequilibrium polymer ensembles to generate persistent, history-dependent mechanical responses.

papers.title: Boc-Protected Covalent Organic Framework Exhibiting Self-Immolating Behaviour and Antiviral Activity
papers.abstract: Covalent organic frameworks are mostly static materials despite their construction via reversible covalent bonds. This can be beneficial for applications requiring highly stable materials, but detrimental where a controlled or triggered disassembly is required. We have realized a self-immolating material, that can also serve as an antiviral material. The self immolative property is incorporated into a COF via an Boc aminefunctionalized linker that can be cleaved by acid or heating. Upon Boc deprotection a free primary amine is formed, which can cleave the COF-linkages through intralayer backbiting and interlayer transimination resulting in complete loss of order. Comparable COF system without the self-immolating linker retain their crystallinity under identical deprotection conditions, confirming the role of the Boc protected amine groups. Furthermore, we evaluated the self-immolating COF BocTA-TAPT and two control systems, TA-TAPT COF and OMeTA-TAPT COF, for their in vitro antiviral activity against HCoV-229E. These three COFs show novel antiviral activities, and the best-performing material exhibited 89.92% of inactivation of the virus within 15 min. This system could lead to triggered self-immolating COF materials, which release cargo on demand in biological applications without resulting in bioaccumulation.

papers.title: How to Handle Hard-to-Purify Polymers: Ammonium Sulfate Precipitation of rPEG as a Prototype for Amorphous and Flexible Polymers
papers.abstract: This work introduces a simple and effective method for purifying both amorphous and semicrystalline, flexible hydrophilic polymers by using ammonium sulfate precipitation (ASP), a technique commonly used in protein purification. ASP exploits the salting-out effect at high ionic strength to precipitate water-soluble polymers, leaving other substances in solution. We successfully purified amorphous and semicrystalline copolymers of ethylene oxide (EO) and racemic glycidyl methyl ether (GME), known as randomized PEG (rPEG), using ASP. The workup was performed from organic reaction media, yielding isolation yields of up to 97% while efficiently removing the solvent, low-molar-mass impurities, and salts resulting from the synthesis. High purity of the isolated polymers was confirmed by NMR spectroscopy, size-exclusion chromatography, mass spectrometry, and atomic absorption spectrometry. Owing to its cost-effectiveness and rapid implementation, ASP represents a viable alternative to conventional purification methods such as dialysis and high-pressure liquid chromatography and has the potential to purify a wide range of hydrophilic polymers beyond rPEG, e.g. for biomedical application.

papers.title: Overcoming Cathode Coating Inhomogeneity: The Role of LiF Interlayer in Enabling Conformal LiNbO3 Protection on LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 for All Solid-State Batteries
papers.abstract: Ni-rich cathode active materials (CAMs) paired with argyrodite solid electrolytes (SEs) such as Li 6 PS 5 Cl (LPSCl) are promising for high-energy density and inherently safer all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs). However, severe (electro-)chemical incompatibilities at the CAM/SE interface lead to parasitic reactions and the formation of resistive interphases. These interfacial degradations impede lithium-ion transport, limit rate capability, and ultimately trigger capacity fading upon cycling. Therefore, developing a stable, ionically conductive, and chemically robust CAM/SE interface remains a critical challenge. In this work, we report an efficient dual-surface-coating strategy based on ultrathin LiF and LiNbO 3 layers applied to LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 (NCM811) cathode particles. Surface fluorination via a controlled CHF 3 gas-phase reaction converts adventitious Li 2 CO 3 into a conformal LiF inner layer, while simultaneously promoting the formation of a uniform LiNbO 3 outer coating. This synergistic LiF/LiNbO 3 architecture effectively protects the CAM surface while facilitating fast interfacial lithium-ion transport. As a result, the modified NCM811 cathode exhibits markedly reduced interfacial resistance and significantly improved specific capacity at high current densities when coupled with LPSCl. Comprehensive structural, chemical, and electrochemical characterization provided in this study elucidates the pivotal role of a homogenous coating in stabilizing the CAM/SE interface, offering a viable pathway toward durable, high-performance Nirich ASSBs.

papers.title: Data-driven design of chiral covalent fragments using high-throughput chemoproteomics and machine learning
papers.abstract: A significant barrier in translating biological insights into therapeutic targets is the limited availability of high-quality chemical probes for target validation. Chemoproteomic profiling of covalent small molecules has dramatically accelerated the discovery of ligandable binding sites across the human proteome. However, the limited specificity and selectivity of initial hits often hinders their effectiveness in evaluating the functional consequences of ligand binding. To address this challenge, we developed a data-driven strategy that integrates chemoproteomic profiling of enantiomerically pure pairs of cysteine-targeting electrophilic fragments (enantiopairs) with machine learning (ML) to design fragment libraries optimised for proteome-wide selectivity. ML-guided library evolution produced a second generation enantiopair library markedly enriched in selective and stereospecific interactions relative to the first generation library. This approach identified high-quality enantioselective binding events with 205 cysteines, the majority not previously liganded. These findings establish a general framework for designing covalent fragment libraries to deliver higher-quality initial hits.

papers.title: Ligand and Counteranion Effects in Cyclometalated Pt(II) Diphosphine Complexes: Photophysics, Singlet-Oxygen Generation and Photocatalysis
papers.abstract: Two families of cyclometalated [Pt(C^N)(P^P)]X [C^N = 2-phenylbenzothiazolate (pbt), 1-phenylisoquinolinate (piq)] complexes have been synthesised and characterised. This allows us to establish structure–property relationships across variations in the C^N ligand (pbt vs. piq), the diphosphine backbone [P^P = 1,2-bis(diphenylphosphino)benzene (dppbz), 2,3-bis(diphenylphosphino)pyrazine (dpppyz), 2,2’-bis(diphenylphosphino)-1,1’-binaphthalene (BINAP) and bis[2-(diphenylphosphino)phenyl]ether (DPEphos)], and the counteranion [X= PF6-, NO3-, [Al(ORF)4]-]. Single‑crystal X‑ray diffraction reveals well‑defined trends in coordination geometry, with wide‑bite‑angle diphosphines inducing pronounced distortions that correlate with weakened emissive behaviour. The photophysical study shows that the nature of the C^N ligand predominantly governs the excited‑state energy landscape: pbt complexes emit in the yellow region with high efficiencies, whereas the more conjugated piq derivatives display red‑shifted phosphorescence. In solution, several complexes exhibit dual fluorescence–phosphorescence emission. All complexes act as efficient triplet sensitizers, displaying high singlet‑oxygen quantum yields. Guided by their increased photophysical stability and higher solubility, two Krossing-type anion [Al(ORF)4]- based salts were selected as catalysts for the photo-oxidation of p-bromothioanisole under homogeneous conditions. While the pbt derivative shows limited activity, due to catalyst degradation under near‑UV irradiation, the piq analogue operates efficiently under mild blue‑light excitation (460 nm), achieving 100% conversion with only 1% catalyst loading in 9 hours.

papers.title: A modular approach to functionalized azetidines. Preparation of a bioactive Ciprofloxacine analogue.
papers.abstract: In 1924, Bruylants reported a reaction between aminonitriles (from ketones) and organomagnesium compounds. During the past 100 years, all possible ketones have been successfully used in this reaction except for one – N-Boc azetidinone. Here we report why that is and how to solve that problem.

papers.title: Ligand-Directed Lysine Labelling of CRBN Enables Chemical Interrogation of a Key E3 Ligase Without Genetic Modification
papers.abstract: Cereblon (CRBN) is the central substrate receptor of the CUL4 E3 ligase and a cornerstone of targeted protein degradation (TPD), yet no chemical tools exist to directly interrogate CRBN itself. We report ligand-directed, site-specific labelling probes for CRBN that install a bioorthogonal click handle directly onto the native protein surface. This chemical modification allows modular attachment of functional tags, enabling downstream functionalisation of CRBN for assay development in patient-derived samples and in cells that are difficult to genetically manipulate. Guided by computational reactivity predictions and structural distance mapping, we designed lysine-targeting probes based on thalidomide and phenyl-dihydrouracil scaffolds and validated their ability to covalently label CRBN in recombinant, lysate, and cellular contexts. Crystal structures of CRBN in complex with representative probes confirm a conserved binding mode anchored by the core scaffold, whilst conformational flexibility at the NASA linker corroborated by molecular docking, enables sampling of proximal lysine residues. Proteomic analysis revealed highly selective modification at Lys300 and Lys407, with no detectable off-target reactivity despite the presence of 50 putative nucleophilic residues. These probes provide the first non-genetic strategy to directly access and functionalise CRBN, expanding the TPD toolbox and enabling earlier evaluation of CRBN-targeting therapeutics in clinically relevant settings.

papers.title: Lessons learned on obtaining reliable conductivity estimates from molecular dynamics simulations
papers.abstract: The calculation of reliable ionic conductivities from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations is not a straightforward task, especially for strongly correlated systems, such as ionic liquids or highly concentrated electrolytes, where the Nernst–Einstein approach tends to fail. In this manuscript, we present the newly implemented conduct module for TRAVIS. It allows the calculation of the ionic conductivity using the Einstein–Helfand and Green–Kubo approaches, which explicitly include ionic correlations in their formalism. We provide a broad overview of accessible transport properties and compare methods and best practices for obtaining statistically reliable estimates of ionic conductivity and other physicochemical properties derived from electrolyte MD simulations, including transport numbers and the inverse Haven ratio. To validate our implementation and demonstrate the conduct module’s capabilities, we simulated the ionic liquid 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium dicyanamide ([EMIm][DCA]) as well as the ether-based electrolyte lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide in ethylene glycol dimethyl ether (LiFSI/DME).

papers.title: The Kinetics of Chymotrypsin by Non-Linear Analysis
papers.abstract: While the hydrolysis of the serine protease alpha-chymotrypsin is used throughout pedagogical texts during discussions of enzyme kinetics, the experiment is rarely included in the laboratory curricula. Reasons include the pre-steady-state "burst" phenomenon, and the fact that the steady state rate does not follow simple Michaelis-Menten kinetics. Herein we describe a non-linear kinetic analysis of the hydrolysis of alpha-chymotrypsin that is accessible to the undergraduate, and results in values comparable to those reported in the literature.

papers.title: Precursor design principles for area-selective atomic layer deposition of alumina: quantifying the role of Lewis acidity, steric repulsion and dimerization in surface adsorption
papers.abstract: In atomic layer deposition (ALD), precursor adsorption plays a critical role in determining growth characteristics. This is particularly important in area-selective ALD (AS-ALD), where adsorption on the non-growth surface (NGS) leads to selectivity loss. In this context, both the ability of a precursor to access reactive surface groups on the NGS and the strength of its binding are key parameters governing the selectivity in experiment. Adsorption on the NGS is strongly influenced by the precursor’s substituents, which control Lewis acidity, steric demand, and propensity for dimerization. We applied energy decomposition analysis for extended systems (pEDA) to a set of commonly used aluminum precursors to quantitatively assess how these factors affect adsorption energetics on SiO2 as the NGS, with trimethoxypropylsilane (TMPS) as small-molecule inhibitor (SMI). Using fluoride ion affinity (FIA) as a metric for Lewis acidity, we find that this largely governs the trends in precursor bonding to both the surface and the SMIs. Notable exceptions are precursors bearing branched alkyl substituents for which steric repulsion dominates over Lewis acidity. Lewis acidity furthermore determines whether adsorption between the SMI layer remains energetically favorable. In this regime, steric effects—Pauli repulsion and deformation of the SMI layer—substantially weaken the adsorption. Dimerization generally reduces adsorption energies. This weakening effect is less pronounced, however, when adsorption takes place within the inhibitor layer. Based on these insights on bonding energetics we recommend targeted modifications of existing aluminum precursors and propose systematic strategies for precursor design aimed at minimizing interactions with the NGS.

papers.title: Direct Access to Carbenoids from Alkyl and α-Acyloxy Halides for Boron Homologations
papers.abstract: Summary: Despite the widespread utility of carbenoids in boron homologations, practical challenges in accessing unstabilized gem-halometal carbenoids limit their broader synthetic application. A major bottleneck is the historical reliance on gem-dihalide precursors, which restricts the accessible substrate scope. Bypassing gem-dihalides via direct deprotonation of unactivated alkyl halides offers an ideal but historically elusive alternative due to competing base-mediated elimination and substitution reactions. Here we introduce a straightforward deprotonation/boron homologation protocol for both alkyl and α-acyloxy halides using hindered amide bases (over 50 examples). The method was effective for both primary and secondary alkyl halide substrates, tolerating a wide range of functional groups including base-sensitive moieties. The α-acyloxy boronic esters, generated via an efficient aldehyde addition and homologation sequence, readily undergo diverse downstream substitutions with Grignard and organolithium nucleophiles. Finally, 11B NMR studies reveal how the Lewis acidity of the alkyl boronic esters dictates the buffering of the lithium amide base, providing a mechanistic rationale for boronic ester ligand selection across different alkyl halide substrates.

papers.title: Deterministic Error Propagation in Kinetic Kd Determination: General Theory with Application to Surface-Based Assays
papers.abstract: 2 ABSTRACT: Accurate determination of equilibrium dissociation constants (Kd) from kinetic measurements requires understanding how systematic errors in concentration and signal propagate into errors in rate constants kon and koff and further in the resulting Kd computed as koff/kon. Here, we present a deterministic, platform-independent framework for error propagation that applies to any method in which reversible 1:1 binding between a ligand (L) and a target/analyte (T) is monitored through time-resolved association and dissociation traces under pseudo-first-order conditions, where the total concentration of T (T0) remains effectively constant during the association phase. The analysis yields closed-form expressions for the relative error in Kd and reveals a triphasic dependence of |ΔKd/Kd| on T0/Kd, including a low T0/Kd regime in which Kd is intrinsically robust to systematic error. Because these features arise from the structure of the kinetic equations, they are general to both solution-and surface-based assays, regardless of detection modality. In this framework, the measured signal is proportional to the amount of LT complex (C) formed, and the maximal proportional response Smax corresponds to the signal that would be observed if all binding sites of L were fully occupied by T. To illustrate how the general theory manifests in practice, we apply it to surface-based measurements in which Smax is established independently and show that accurate kon, koff, and Kd values can be obtained from time-resolved traces acquired at T0 values far below the true Kd. We also outline practical limitations, including the requirement that kon and koff be resolvable from the measured traces, and discuss how the theoretical conclusions relate to established experimental strategies such as reference binding partners, off-rate screening, and softwarebased correlation diagnostics. This work provides a general theoretical foundation for understanding accuracy constraints in kinetic Kd determination and clarifies how these principles apply when implemented in practical surface-based measurements widely used for molecular interaction analyses.

papers.title: Systematic Helical Complexity Imparted by Chalcogen Atoms in Gallium Chalco-Iodide Tetrahelices
papers.abstract: Low-dimensional materials with main group elements manifest unique bonding motifs and exhibit strong axis-dependent responses. In particular, extended lattices with 1D helical motifs have been sought for their ability to host such physical states, and further for their ability to host unique quantum states due to their spring-like and chiral ordering. However, owing to their rarity, the difficulty in experimentally realizing 20 modular classes of freestanding, all-inorganic helical materials with tunable structures has limited the physical understanding of their structure- and composition-dependent properties in experimentally realizable systems. Here, we present a new helical 1D van der Waals (vdW) crystal, GaTeI, to complete the 1D gallium chalco-iodide crystal series. Through the realization of GaTeI, we study the profound influence of the identity of the chalcogen site to the crystalline order and helical structure of the exfoliable 1D vdW 25 III-VI-VII class. By analyzing the local coordination environment and helical parameters of the Ga(S, Se, Te)I series, we establish the systematic stretching of the helical structure that is driven by the rigid interchain interactions and the distortion of the tetrahedral building units along the chain. Our results highlight how the identity of the chalcogen strongly dictates the projected geometric cross-section of the helical chains to form unusual helical motifs such as the Boerdijk-Coxeter tetrahelix in GaSeI, and the non-natural 30 helical cross-sections such as the “squircle” in GaSI and the corrugated motif in GaTeI. Given the range of accessible helical compositions, we also demonstrate the chalcogen dependence of the bandgaps that cover a broad spectral window spanning the visible to the UV regime. These findings present an experimentally accessible and modular group of helical structures that underscores how fine tuning of the constituent atoms

papers.title: A Multi-Functional and Secure Photoresponsive Proteasome Inhibitor
papers.abstract: Precise external control of biological processes represents a central interest in the life sciences. Specifically designed molecular tools are ideally suited for this purpose and consequentially have found widespread applications including fundamental studies in biology or pharmaceutical drug development. Introducing photoresponsiveness to modulate biological activity of a molecule offers heightened levels of control by adding adjustable spatial and temporal resolution. Here we present a next step of capabilities in which photoresponsiveness of a small molecule inhibitor is coupled with a customizable secondary function. This multi-functional biochemical tool is based on MG132 – a potent proteasome inhibitor – whose activity is securely photocaged and thus rendered lightresponsive. At the same time, an alkyne group is introduced into the structure allowing for facile late-stage attachment of a second functionality via simple click-chemistry. The heightened utility is showcased by stably linking a fluorophore, allowing to monitor the spatial distribution of the photoactivatable inhibitor within living cells. This multi-level photoresponsive molecular tool opens up a vast space of opportunities for programmable and customizable biological activity control.

papers.title: RAT-LAMP: Design and Characterisation of Conchimeric Primer Architectures Toward High-Density Solid-Phase Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification
papers.abstract: Solid-phase loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) offers a pathway toward low-cost, integrated molecular diagnostics, but practical implementation is limited by poor primer bioavailability and insufficient surface primer payload. We present RAT-LAMP (RNaseActivated Trigger for Loop-Mediated isothermal AMPlification) and a conchimeric primer architecture as a dual strategy to overcome these constraints. Conchimeras are concatenated multi-primer oligonucleotides composed of distinct LAMP primer species separated by RNA spacer residues, enabling on-demand primer release through RNase-mediated cleavage during amplification. The adoption of conchimeras reduces the number of distinct LAMP primer species competing for a fixed surface area from six to three. Chimeric and 81 to 84-base conchimeric primers were designed and evaluated targeting synthetic Dengue virus 1 DNA. The functionality of the designed primers was demonstrated for simultaneous RNase and polymerase activity under standard LAMP conditions. RAT-LAMP restored chimeric primer performance to near-unmodified levels (time-to-positive: 2.81 vs. 2.59 minutes for unmodified primers), confirming the feasibility of on-demand primer release. Conchimeric primer amplification was feasible following spacer optimisation (rCrG and rUrG designs), with RNase supplementation reducing batch-tobatch coefficient of variation by ∼ 4-fold (16.47% to 3.76%). Amplification using shorter conchimeras containing FIP and BIP confirmed that the rate-limiting primers (FIP and BIP) should not be concatenated with other primers. Notably, primers modified via 5′-phosphorylation for EDC surface immobilisation produced a statistically significant improvement in amplification speed over unmodified primers (TTP: 2.36 minutes; p-value =0.0006). Together, RAT-LAMP and conchimeric primer architectures establish the component feasibility of high-density primer immobilization for solid-phase LAMP. They simultaneously address primer availability and surface loading constraints without increasing workflow complexity. Adoption of a three-species conchimeric system increases primer cost by only 1.4-fold over unmodified primers (£0.010/ test-conchimera vs £0.007/ test-unmodified). Regardless of the cost increase, at £0.021/ test, the adoption of conchimeras for solid-phase primer delivery would not significantly impact consumable cost.

papers.title: MolSurf3D: Integrating Molecular Surface Geometry with 3D Structural Representations through Physics-Constrained Multimodal Alignment
papers.abstract: We present MolSurf3D, a unified multimodal learning framework that integrates molecular surface geometry with three-dimensional structural representations for enhanced molecular property prediction and generation. Despite recent advances in equivariant neural networks and multimodal molecular modeling, existing methods treat molecular geometry and surface properties in isolation, overlooking critical physicochemical information encoded in molecular surfaces such as electrostatic potential, hydrophobicity, and curvature. MolSurf3D addresses this gap through three key components: (1) a Surface-Geometry Dual Encoder (SGDE) that independently encodes molecular surface features via geodesic convolution and 3D geometric features via equivariant message passing, with bidirectional equivariant cross-attention for information exchange; (2) a Physics-Constrained Cross-Modal Alignment (PC2A) module that enforces quantum mechanical constraints including energy conservation and valence rules during contrastive learning; and (3) a Surface-Guided 3D Generation (SG3G) module based on an equivariant diffusion model conditioned on surface fingerprints. Experiments on QM9 and CrossDocked benchmarks demonstrate that MolSurf3D achieves state-of-the-art performance, with MAE of 2.1 meV for HOMO energy on QM9 and Vina Score of-7.28 on CrossDocked, outperforming existing methods including Chem3DLLM.

papers.title: pH-Inverted Histidine-Rich Nanochelant 5H-EAF for Electrostatic Dust Mitigation and Cation Detoxification in Lunar Regolith: Enabling Lightweight In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) for Artemis Missions
Alternative mechanisms for fullerene growth: the spiral of “stick”, “handle”, and “horn” intermediates
papers.abstract: Traditionally, fullerene growth is considered to proceed via C 2 insertion. Based on theoretical calculations, this study proposes a novel mechanism for fullerene growth that involves the classical “stick” and “handle” intermediates as well as the “horn” intermediate introduced herein. A comparison with the reaction energy barrier of the traditional C 2 direct insertion mechanism indicates that the growth mechanism proposed in this work is a competitive pathway to the traditional C 2 insertion mechanism, and this new mechanism is further extended to fullerene derivatization. Furthermore, this work also investigates the C 4 insertion mechanism and proposes a possible formation pathway for C 3v( 1911)-C 64 .

papers.title: Discovery and Investigation of Novel Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) Degrading Enzymes through Metagenomic Mining
papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are highly persistent fluorinated chemicals linked to widespread environmental contamination and elevated cancer risk. Its ongoing contamination of Indian water sources(such as the ganga river) raises a national issue. Their exceptional stability arises from strong C–F bonds, making biodegradation challenging. Fluoroacetate dehalogenases (FAcD) can cleave monofluorinated substrates through an SN2 mechanism, but steric and electronic barriers limit activity against larger PFAS, and the lack of known homologs constrains their potential. This study aimed to identify novel FAcD homologs with enhanced catalytic versatility by mining metagenomic datasets. Fifty-one environmental samples were assembled into MAGs (Metagenome Assembled Genomes) using standard protocols, annotated using Bakta, and converted into 1024-dimensional ProtTrans embeddings. An XGBoost classifier trained on known dehalogenases screened candidate proteins. Of 583 proteins scoring above 0.9, conserved-motif filtering via BlastP and catalytic site analysis using fPocket narrowed the set to 20 novel proteins, three annotated as Epoxide Hydrolases. Site-specific docking using AutoDock4 against 20 representative PFAS ligands showed that novel receptors exhibited a mean binding affinity of –7.23 kcal/mol versus –6.38 kcal/mol for reference proteins. About 25.5% of the novel proteins demonstrated strong binding (≤ –8 kcal/mol), nearly double the proportion in 249 reference sequences (13.8%). A correlation between pocket volume and binding affinity indicated increased binding strength for pockets between 400–800 Å3. This study identifies 20 novel proteins with catalytic potential toward PFAS degradation, with findings suggesting a previously unrecognized role of Epoxide Hydrolases in PFAS chemistry.

papers.title: When Do Models Win? A Learning Curve Benchmark for Molecular Property Prediction in Low-Data Regimes
papers.abstract: In many molecular property prediction tasks, such as drug discovery and OLED material design, labeled data are often limited to only tens to thousands of samples due to high experimental costs. Despite the rapid development of machine learning models, it remains unclear which model classes are most effective under such low-data regimes and how their performance evolves with increasing data. In this work, we present a comprehensive learning curve benchmark across traditional machine learning methods, graph neural networks (GNNs), transformer-based molecular language models, and hybrid architectures. We systematically vary the training data size from 50 to 3,000 samples and evaluate performance on QM9, ESOL, Lipophilicity, and BACE datasets using scaffold splits with repeated trials for statistical robustness. We further propose two hybrid models combining GCN and ChemBERTa with different fusion strategies—concatenation (GTCA-Cat) and cross-attention (GTCA-CA)—and analyze their data efficiency through ablation studies on both transformer layer depth (2/4/6) and fusion strategy. Our results reveal that (1) hybrid models substantially improve over single-modality GCN in low-data regimes for physicochemical property targets (e.g., 32.1% RMSE reduction on ESOL at N=50), (2) simple concatenation fusion generally outperforms or matches cross-attention due to reduced overfitting and improved stability, (3) deeper transformer layers (depth=6) consistently outperform shallower configurations across most targets and data regimes, (4) clear crossover points exist where traditional kernel-based methods outperform deep learning models depending on the task type, and (5) PaiNN, despite having access to DFT-optimized 3D coordinates on QM9, fails to outperform 2D-based models across all training sizes, suggesting fundamental limitations of equivariant 3D architectures in low-data regimes. Importantly, we identify regime-dependent model optimality: deep learning models dominate continuous physicochemical property prediction (e.g., ESOL, Lipophilicity), while kernel-based methods can be more effective for bioactivity prediction (e.g., BACE) across most data scales. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for model selection under data scarcity and highlight the importance of learning curve analysis as a principled tool for understanding model behavior.

papers.title: Quantum assembly theory defines molecular complexity from electron density topology
Can cavity prediction algorithms help in docking experiments?
papers.abstract: Blind docking is a method for predicting a binding mode of a ligand with a protein without any prior information about a binding site. Some tools allow this type of docking experiment directly, others, including some established tools, require binding site information being passed as an input. In this latter case, one can use cavity prediction tools and use the results of their prediction as an input in these docking calculations. However, it is still unclear if the results of these predictions can be reliably used in protein-ligand docking and what is the best technical way to pass this information to the docking algorithm. In this study we estimated the applicability of the binding pocket prediction tools in docking experiments to address this gap in knowledge. We use four different computational tools for cavity prediction and use the best predicted cavities represented in different ways to run GOLD docking calculations. Analysis of subsequent use in docking highlights that Fpocket and CAVIAR are the best performing cavity prediction tools in this context. Further analysis shows that accurate binding site input does not guarantee accurate binding pose predictions and, even with the predicted cavities, the more restrained the input is, the more reliable the docking results are.

papers.title: Silicon and Low Pt Loading Improves Redox Dynamics and Regenerability in PtGa Propane Dehydrogenation Catalysts
papers.abstract: The increasing propene demand has accelerated the development of on-purpose propane dehydrogenation (PDH) technologies. Because of rapid catalyst deactivation caused by the high operating temperature, frequent catalyst regeneration cycles are required in industrial processes. While efficient Pt-Ga based PDH catalysts have been developed, the origin of the promotional effect of Si and the need of only small amounts of Pt to improve catalyst regenerability are not fully understood. Herein, we find that incorporating Si and decreasing the Pt-loading in Si-containing PtGa-catalyst supported on alumina, that is prepared via a surface organometallic chemistry approach, improve both stability and regenerability of the catalysts. Detailed analyses of in-situ/operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy confirm that the increased PDH performances correlate with a regeneration of Pt-Ga interaction due to enhanced Pt-Ga redox dynamics.

papers.title: Non-natural amino acid nomenclature for HELM monomer registration
papers.abstract: The growing interest in studying modified and cyclic peptides is constrained by limitations in how their chemical information is encoded, represented, and analysed. Traditional sequence formats such as FASTA only allow working with linear and natural peptides. HELM and BILN formats provide more versatile and extendible notation systems for the representation of peptides with non-natural monomers or cyclic arrangements. HELM is a notation that uses a database as a source of monomers where these are defined on their structure, identifier, and attachment points. While structural representations are canonicalized using established methods, there is currently no widely accepted convention for naming peptide monomers. In this manuscript, we develop on top of the guidelines proposed by Pistoia Alliance for the naming of non-natural amino acids for their representation using HELM. Our nomenclature extends on modifications of side chains and backbone, naming of homo amino acids and peptoids, and resolves ambiguous cases using a combination of systematic and pragmatic rules.

papers.title: Influence of Ligand Charge and Pi-Expansion on DNA Binding Ability of Protic Ruthenium Complexes with Light-Activated Anticancer Activity
C6-ROMP Enabled by Structure-Guided Monomer Design for Chemically Recyclable Polymers
papers.abstract: Cyclohexene, a minimally strained cyclic olefin, presents a long-standing challenge for ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) due to its inherently low ring strain energy. In this study, we present a rational monomer design framework for cyclohexene-derived monomers that leverages adaptive ring strain modulation via fused five-membered heterocycles—including carbonate, carbamate, acetal, silyl ether, and boronic ester motifs—to enhance polymerizability while enabling closed-loop recycling. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and experimental thermodynamic analyses reveal how monomer conformation, ethenolysis ring strain energy (ERSE), and substituent effects govern ROMP thermodynamics and ring-closing metathesis depolymerization (RCMD) efficiency. An ERSE threshold of approximately 4.3 kcal/mol is identified as necessary for effective polymerization under mild conditions. Additionally, entropy differences driven by substituent flexibility significantly impact depolymerization temperature and efficiency. The resulting polymers exhibit tunable thermal properties, with glass transition temperatures ranging from −42 to 120 °C and efficient depolymerization performance. This study provides practical design principles for the development of sustainable functional polymers with predictable reactivity and recyclability.

papers.title: Molecular Mechanisms of KIT Receptor Dimerization and Oncogenic Activation Revealed by Multiscale Simulations
papers.abstract: The receptor tyrosine kinase KIT is essential for cell proliferation and differentiation, and its aberrant activation contributes to cancers such as acute myeloid leukemia and gastrointestinal stromal tumors. KIT activation normally requires stem cell factor (SCF)-induced dimerization, whereas oncogenic mutations can drive ligand-independent signalling. Here, we employ multiscale molecular dynamics simulations based on the Martini 3 coarse-grained (CG) force field to investigate the dimerization mechanisms of full-length KIT in both wild-type (WT) and oncogenic mutant forms within a realistic membrane environment. For the WT receptor, simulations capture SCF-driven dimerization through a cooperative “zipper-like” mechanism involving sequential domain-domain interactions. In contrast, the T417I, Δ418–419 mutant forms stable dimers spontaneously in the absence of SCF, stabilized by enhanced D5–D5 hydrophobic contacts. Back-mapping and atomistic refinement yielded the first all-atom (AA) structural model of the full-length KIT(T417I, Δ418–419) mutant, consistent with the V-shaped extracellular conformation observed experimentally. This study provides mechanistic insight into KIT activation and establishes a Martini 3 based framework for simulating receptor assembly and guiding the design of antibodies or small molecules that disrupt aberrant dimerization.

papers.title: Silanol Functionalization of Amorphous Silica Surface from Density Functional Theory Simulations
papers.abstract: Amorphous silicates are among the most widely used supports in heterogeneous catalysis, yet the development of accurate atomisticallydetailed models remains a major challenge. Their structure is composed of SiO4 tetrahedral units arranged into siloxane rings of varying sizes, which gives rise to substantial surface heterogeneity. Although this heterogeneity plays a central role in determining surface reactivity, it also makes the experimental characterization of amorphous silica particularly difficult. Density functional theory (DFT) simulations offer a route to probe the properties of individual sites within this disordered network and to establish structure–reactivity relationships. In this work, we use large cluster models of amorphous silica treated at DFT level to investigate the thermodynamics of the surface silanol functionalization reaction. We find a broad distribution of functionalization energies across clusters, with significant variation even among sites with the same ring size, showing that reactivity cannot be described by ring size alone. To rationalize this, we construct smaller models of silica sites and analyze the functionalization energy as a function of effective model volume. Our results show that large-scale reorganization accompanies surface functionalization, which needs to be properly accounted for to obtain converged reaction energies.

papers.title: Head-to-head comparison of nanoparticle analyzers used for characterizing nanomedicines
papers.abstract: The characterization of nanomedicines, often formulated as drug-loaded nanoparticles, is critical for understanding, optimizing, and ensuring their quality, safety, and therapeutic efficacy. The expansion of nanomedicine research and development, largely driven by the success of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) in enabling the vaccine and therapeutic potential of nucleic acid-based molecules, has sparked the development of new analytical technologies for nanoparticle characterization. Given the growing diversity of established and emerging methods, it can be challenging to comprehend their strengths, limitations, and appropriate use cases. This complexity complicates both tool selection and the interpretation of analytical data in research and development. To address these challenges, we provide a comprehensive overview of 14 nanoparticle characterization tools that are commercially available or accessible at core facilities and are geared toward, at a minimum, estimating the size of nanoparticles. This assessment includes distinguishing between single-particle and bulk (ensemble) characterization methods and evaluating about 20 nanomedicine and tool parameters, including particle size, size distribution, zeta potential, chemical composition, the ability to study nanomedicines in complex biological fluids, as well as sampling frequency and minimal sample volume required for highthroughput applications. While we focus on applications with LNPs, liposomes, and extracellular vesicles, the tool comparison presented here also supports decision-making when choosing a tool for analyzing other lipid, viral, polymeric, protein, metallic, and metal oxide nanoparticles. The tools discussed here can provide overlapping and complementary information; in light of this, we recommend integrating single-particle and bulk measurements to comprehensively assess the quantitative and qualitative properties of nanomedicines.

papers.title: Rational Design of Single-Phase High Entropy Oxides via Large Language Model Data Mining and Explainable Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The rational design of high-entropy oxides (HEOs) is currently hindered by the scarcity of structured property data in the scientific literature. In this work, we present an end-to-end materials informatics framework that couples Large Language Model (LLM) data mining with interpretable machine learning to predict single-phase stability in HEOs. We deployed agents based on gpt-oss-120b to extract compositions, phases, and synthesis methods from unstructured scientific abstracts. Combined with regularexpression routines, the LLM-based agent achieved an accuracy of 96% in database generation despite the complexity of the task, including on-the-fly inference of relative cation proportions. Subsequently, a range of machine-learning models was trained in an exploratory multi-class classification setting to distinguish canonical HEO crystal structures using several variants of the primary databases obtained by combining different feature subsets. For this task, an XGBoost classifier achieved an F1-score of 86% in a seven-class classification problem, and the best-performing database variant combined primary and statistical features. This optimal database representation was then used to train a neural-network binary classifier to distinguish perovskite from non-perovskite compositions, achieving 97.9% classification accuracy on the test set, whereas the Goldschmidt tolerance factor reached only 67.3% on the same data. These results indicate that the proposed methodology can support the design of HEO compositions with target properties and substantially outperforms traditional descriptor-based approaches. Furthermore, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis revealed that high-entropy perovskite phase stability is governed by a critical interplay between geometric factors, such as the sum of cation radii, and electronic descriptors, including Sanderson electronegativity and atomization enthalpy. Overall, these findings demonstrate that LLM-driven data mining can overcome data bottlenecks and enable the discovery of physical design rules for complex multicomponent ceramics.

papers.title: PET-Trackable Carborane-Conjugated Star-Shaped Poly(2-oxazoline) Scaffold with High Boron Payload and Improved Aqueous Solubility for Boron Neutron Capture Therapy
papers.abstract: Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) requires substantial tumor boron delivery, yet carboranes, boron-rich BNCT building blocks, suffer from poor aqueous solubility and suboptimal in vivo behavior despite exceptional boron density and stability. We report a modular star-shaped poly(2-oxazoline) (POx) scaffold that carries high carborane payload and can be followed by positron emission tomography (PET). An alkyne-bearing POx was conjugated with azidopropyl meta-carborane, yielding PBMM- m CB 20 -EIP that remained highly water-soluble (300 g/L, ~34 g/L of boron, 20 carboranes/star). PBMM- m CB 20 -EIP exhibited good cytocompatibility in CAL 27 and FaDu head-and-neck cancer cells and showed higher cell-associated boron concentration than the clinical agent sodium borocaptate. A DOTA-modified analogue was prepared and radiolabeled with gallium-68 for PET imaging. In healthy mice, [ 68 Ga]Ga-DOTA-PBMM- m CB 20 revealed extended blood circulation (17 %ID/g) at 90 min, predominant renal clearance, and low background uptake. These results provide a baseline for macromolecular engineering of this carrier and irradiation-timing optimization in future tumor models.

papers.title: Self-consistent biased fine-tuning for highly accurate reaction-specific machine-learning interatomic potentials
papers.abstract: An algorithm for the black-box generation of high-quality system-specific machinelearning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for gas phase reactions in the electronic ground state is presented. It relies on the self-consistent fine-tuning of a MLIP foundation model, where the message-passing atomic cluster expansion (MACE) is taken as an example, based on data collected from biased samplings along the reaction coordinate of interest with the Caracal program. The reaction is first sampled with the foundation model at different temperatures, and then the sampling is repeated with the fine-tuned model until the errors of selected energies and gradients with respect to the high-level reference method falls below a chosen threshold. In this paper, this method is benchmarked systematically by alternating the amount of collected training data and the MACE MLIP architecture, such that an optimal compromise between speed and accuracy can be obtained. To make a direct comparison of reaction rate constants between MLIP and the reference method possible, two gas phase reactions with analytical potential energy surfaces from the literature have been chosen: The internal proton transfer in malonaldehyde and the proton exchange between methane and an

papers.title: Interpretable Metal-Chemistry and Minimal-Context Descriptors for MOF Water and Activation Stability: A Reproducible Benchmark of Descriptor Sufficiency, Split Sensitivity, and Screening Utility
papers.abstract: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are widely studied for gas storage, separations, catalysis, sensing, and electrochemical conversion, but these functions matter only if the framework survives activation and remains stable in water or humid environments. Yet MOF stability prediction still sits awkwardly between empirical chemical intuition and machine-learning models built from descriptors that are often difficult to interpret or reproduce. Here, we present a chemistry-led benchmark that tests how far stability prediction can be advanced using transparent descriptors, including metal identity, mixed-metal character, open-metal-site information, coarse topology, porosity, and compact thermophysical terms. Using two cleaned CoRE MOF-derived benchmark tables, the activation-stability resource (ASR, 1372 entries) and the framework-survival resource (FSR, 1192 entries), we model continuous solvent and water stability, include thermal stability as a supplementary regression task, and assess threshold-based screening at 0.6, 0.7, and 0.8. Random Forest models with the most complete descriptor regime perform best overall, with water stability consistently more predictable than solvent-removal stability. However, random splits are markedly more optimistic than grouped splits by metal family and topology, exposing a substantial interpolation–extrapolation gap. Overall, the results show that simple, chemically interpretable descriptors contain meaningful stability signal, but credible extrapolative claims require chemically aware validation.

papers.title: Directional folding and kinetic partitioning govern structural plasticity in the HIV-1 frameshifting element
papers.abstract: Programmed −1 ribosomal frameshifting (−1PRF) at the gag-pol junction of HIV-1 is regulated by a slippery heptamer and a compact but conformationally heterogeneous downstream RNA element. Here we combine directional-landscape analysis, kinetic pathway partitioning, and atomistic dynamics to examine how motif-targeted mutations reorganize the accessible fold space of the HIV-1 frameshifting element. The directional landscapes indicate marked 5′/3′ asymmetry: when sequence length was extended downstream to mimic post-ribosomal refolding, the designed 2_3 and 2_1 topologies were sampled more broadly than during upstream growth. The integrated target-motif occupancy for 23MUT1 was 0.35 in downstream landscapes versus 0.22 upstream, whereas 21MUT1 showed corresponding values of 0.22 and 0.15. Trajectory-based kinetic analysis ranked 23MUT1 and 21MUT1 as the most selective mutants for the 2_3 and 2_1 targets, respectively. Their endpoint target yields reached 68% and 61%, compared with 8% 2_3 and 12% 2_1 occupancy in the wildtype ensemble, and their median first-passage times were 84 and 71 ms. The same two mutants also displayed the most favorable thermodynamic separation from competing folds, with ∆∆𝐺 values of 1.7 and 1.3 kcal mol−1. In the MD/PCA analysis, 23MUT1 and 21MUT1 retained their target topologies for 81% and 76% of sampled frames and exhibited smaller mean backbone RMSD values than wildtype (4.3 and 4.7 Å versus 5.8 Å). PCA further indicated that wildtype dynamics are dominated by global junction opening, whereas the mutants shift variance toward more localized hinging and loop-breathing modes. Taken together, the results support a mechanistic picture in which directional exposure, kinetic competition, and dynamic stabilization jointly determine which HIV-1 frameshifting architectures are accessible during translation and refolding.

papers.title: Probing the Quantum Nature of Intramolecular Vibrational Energy Redistribution in HCCH - H2CC Isomerization Using High-Resolution Photoelectron Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: High resolution photoelectron spectra of vinylidene anions (H 2 CC¯ and D 2 CC¯) are reported using variations on slow electron velocity-map imaging of cryogenically cooled anions (cryo-SEVI). This work builds on previous studies aimed at exploring the coupling between neutral H 2 CC and HCCH isomers. One-photon photodetachment (PD) spectra with improved cooling and signal levels probe very weak transitions to vibrational levels of H 2 CC in which the ν 6 rocking mode is excited; this is the vibrational mode most strongly coupled to isomerization. In addition, vibrationally resonant two-photon detachment (VR2PD) experiments are carried out that probe PD from vibrationally excited anion levels to the same neutral ν 6 states and other low-lying vibrational levels of neutral vinylidene. The experimental spectra show a clear boundary in spectral complexity near the predicted isomerization barrier height, indicating that vinylidene and acetylene states above the barrier are strongly mixed whereas states below the barrier are largely localized in their respective wells. This mixing is, however, largely absent in the cryo-SEVI spectra of D 2 CC¯. Comparison with quantum dynamics calculations based on an accurate full dimensional potential energy surface provide insight into the connection between the H 2 CC-HCCH isomerization reaction and the vibrational structure of vinylidene, revealing pathways of intramolecular vibrational energy flow in the quantum state space of this prototypical system.

papers.title: Layer-by-Layer Assembly of End-Functional Zirconium Phosphonate Multilayers for Multifunctional Pretreatments of Aluminum Surfaces
papers.abstract: Aluminum with its unique combination of strength, lightness, and recyclability is popular choice for a wide range of applications in the packaging, automotive and construction sector. Even though its corrosion properties are more favorable compared to other structural metals such as steel, the economic burden of corrosion-related damages remains significant. This study introduces an approach to corrosion protection of aluminum surfaces through the creation of ultra-thin yet highly protective zirconium phosphonate multilayer coatings. The process involves the formation of a α,ω-bisphosphonic acid self-assembled monolayer (SAM) directly on aluminum, followed by a layer-by-layer (LbL) deposition approach using simple alternating dip-coating into α,ω-bisphosphonic acid and Zr(IV) salt solutions. While the hydrophobic alkyl sublayers contributed to inhibiting water and ion penetration, a functionalization of the surface was achieved by using different end-functional phosphonic acids as the terminating layer, In this way, the resulting multilayer structures gave rise to simultaneously excellent corrosion performance, particularly also against pitting corrosion and in near-application settings, improved surface wetting as required for forming, as well as a remarkable bonding performance under corrosive conditions due to the synergistic interplay of covalent bond formation to the adhesive and corrosion protection due to the Zr(IV)-linked multilayer assembly.

papers.title: Solution-Borne Protective Carbon Monolayer Coatings
papers.abstract: Carbon nanocoatings have emerged as high-performance solutions for the surface protection of engineering materials, especially in systems containing small precision components. For these applications, it is crucial that the nanocoating be continuous and defect-free even at thicknesses on the order of a few nanometers. High-energy vacuum deposition techniques are well-suited for this purpose but expensive and difficult to scale up to large areas or high-volume production. Here, we report a unique solution-borne method for preparing ultrathin, functional carbon nanocoatings under ambient conditions. A phosphonic acid surfactant conatining a highly reactive all-carbon hexayne segment forms a self-assembled monolayer on aluminium oxide that can subsequently be converted into a continuous, surface-bound carbon monolayer. The obtained coatings significantly reduce corrosion and secondary electron generation on aluminium substrates, demonstrating their effectiveness for surface modification and protection.

papers.title: Single-Chain Folding of a Synthetic Macromolecule and Two Metal Atoms Provides a Precise Globular Tertiary Structure
papers.abstract: Macromolecular folding underlies function in biological systems, yet analogous compact, globular tertiary structures remain rare in synthetic chemistry. Although shape-persistent foldamers and metal-templated knots have been realized, crystallographically resolved globular architectures arising from intramolecular folding of single non-peptidic macromolecules are unknown. Here we introduce metal–organic knedels (MOKs): compact single-chain globules formed by intramolecular folding of single synthetic macromolecules around multiple metal centers. Specifically, a uniform 2.6 kDa oligomer bearing eight pyridyl donors and three naphthyl linkers undergoes diastereoselective assembly with two Pd(II) centers to afford a discrete complex, MOK-1, where covalent tethering enforces a unique low-symmetry fold and cavity shape not typically accessible in conventional high-symmetry assemblies, as confirmed by NMR spectroscopy, mass spectrometry and single-crystal X-ray diffraction. These findings define a new class of metal–organic architectures and establish intramolecular folding as a strategy for constructing globular synthetic systems.

papers.title: On the Consequences of Categorical Partitioning in Novel Peptide Discovery: Database-Free Peptide Identification via Hierarchical Fragmentation Constraints and Computer Vision
papers.abstract: Peptide identification in tandem mass spectrometry relies on spectral matching against sequence databases, limiting discovery of novel peptides and requiring platform-specific calibration. We present a dual-modality framework for database-free peptide sequence reconstruction combining thermodynamic droplet encoding with categorical fragmentation network analysis. The framework maps MS/MS spectra to three-dimensional S-entropy coordinates (Sk, St Se) derived from physicochemical properties (hydrophobicity, molecular volume, electrostatics), then converts ions to thermodynamic droplets generating characteristic wave patterns amenable to computer vision analysis. Hierarchical fragmentation constraints validate fragment-parent relationships through five physical principles: spatial containment (64% ś 4% overlap), wavelength hierarchy (fragments 22% parent size), energy conservation (80% retained), phase coherence (perfect lock, Cϕ = 1.0), and charge redistribution (correlation R = 0.52 with S-entropy). Validation on 1,000+ spectra achieves 91% ś 4% hierarchical consistency, with 100% bijectivity (reconstruction error = 0) confirming information preservation. Categorical fragmentation network analysis reveals peptide ladders as phase-locked oscillatory cascades with scale-free topology (P(k) ∼ κ−γ , γ = 2.3 ś 0.4), enabling PTM localization via phase discontinuity detection: 88.7% accuracy versus 61.3% for MaxQuant, with 23Ö computational speedup for tri-phosphorylated peptides. Platform independence is achieved through categorical invariance: ladder topology features (b/y series completeness, complementarity, regularity) exhibit coefficient of variation < 2.1% across four instrument platforms (Waters Synapt, Thermo Orbitrap, Sciex TripleTOF, Bruker timsTOF). Zeroshot model transfer (train on Orbitrap, test on Waters) maintains 89.3% sequence determination accuracy, versus 54.7% for intensity-based methods requiring per-platform calibration. Sequence reconstruction via minimum-entropy Hamiltonian path traversal through fragment graphs (mean 100 ś 50 nodes, 300 ś 350 edges) achieves 42% ś 18% partial match rate without database queries, with hierarchical constraints improving accuracy by +18 percentage points.

papers.title: From Kinetic Gateways to Thermodynamic Locking: Unveiling the Dynamic Adsorption Landscape of CO on Pt(111)
papers.abstract: The adsorption of CO on Pt(111) serves as a benchmark system in surface science, yet resolving the discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental observations regarding site preference and structural evolution remains a challenge. Here, we present a comprehensive coverage–temperature study that combines generalized simulated annealing on a high-precision potential energy surface (PES) with molecular dynamics-based free energy calculations. Our statistical analysis reveals that surface relaxation plays a decisive role. It enhances the stability of top sites at low coverage and accurately captures the adsorbate-induced surface distortion at saturation (0.750 ML), driving the densely packed adlayer into a symmetry-broken configuration proximal to the bridge sites. Crucially, free energy landscapes reveal a non-monotonic evolution of surface mobility. A critical “kinetic gateway” at ~0.611 ML was identified, where migration barriers between top, bridge, and hollow sites nearly vanish, creating a highly fluid phase that facilitates complex changes of adlayer structure. In contrast, at the saturation limit, the CO adlayer becomes thermodynamically locked into deep potential wells with high diffusion barriers, indicative of a rigid “catalyst poisoning” state. These findings bridge the gap between zero-temperature static models and finite-temperature experimental realities, offering a unified theoretical framework for understanding the dynamic interplay between thermodynamic site competition and kinetic accessibility.

papers.title: Tubocapsenolide A Overcomes Oxaliplatin Resistance in Colorectal Cancer by Targeting the PLK1-CEP55-ESCRT Axis to Suppress Nuclear Budding and Mitochondrial-derived Vesicles Extrusion
papers.abstract: Oxaliplatin (L-OHP) is a first-line chemotherapeutic agent for both advanced colorectal cancer (CRC) and postoperative adjuvant therapy. However, the development of acquired L-OHP resistance remains a major clinical obstacle. Here, we identify Tubocapsenolide A (TA), a natural withanolide isolated from Tubocapsicum anomalum , as a potent antitumor agent that not only suppresses CRC growth but also effectively reverses acquired L-OHP resistance. Using a PROTAC-based target deconvolution strategy combined with biophysical validation, we demonstrate that PLK1 is the direct functional target of TA. PLK1 is aberrantly overexpressed in L-OHP-resistant CRC and negatively correlates with patient sensitivity to L-OHP. Mechanistically, overexpressed PLK1 hyperphosphorylates the adaptor protein CEP55 to recruit the ESCRT machinery, driving a previously unappreciated PLK1-CEP55-ESCRT-dependent vesicular extrusion process. This enables resistant cells to rapidly clear L-OHP-induced damage through γ-H2A.X⁺ nuclear budding and TOM20⁻/PDH⁺ mitochondrial-derived vesicles, thereby preserving organelle integrity and promoting cell survival. By directly binding and inhibiting PLK1, TA disrupts the CEP55-ESCRT-dependent membrane scission machinery, leading to intracellular accumulation of damaged components. Consequently, it triggers severe nucleolar stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, ultimately inducing death in L‑OHP‑resistant cells. Collectively, our findings uncover a novel PLK1-CEP55-ESCRT-driven vesicular extrusion mechanism underlying L-OHP resistance and establish targeting this axis as a promising therapeutic strategy for chemorefractory CRC. TA represents a valuable lead compound for the development of new treatments against L-OHP-resistant CRC.

papers.title: Mass-Balance Separation-Limits Framework for Efficient PVSA Cycle Design
papers.abstract: Pressure vacuum swing adsorption (PVSA) is a key technology for gas separations, yet its cycle design and optimisation remain computationally demanding. This work introduces a mass-balance-informed workflow that significantly reduces the number of simulations required for PVSA cycle design. By applying separation-limit analysis and material balance constraints, we define theoretical bounds on product purity and recovery, thereby narrowing the parameter space requiring detailed evaluation. The heavy product-to-feed ratio (H/F) is identified as a critical design variable, and the optimisation problem is framed around achieving target separation performance at specific H/F values. The methodology is demonstrated through the design of a PVSA for nitrogen rejection, using ZSM-5 at a feed flow rate of 1000 Nm3/h. Two adsorption cycles are evaluated to illustrate the approach. Results show that this strategy enables rapid feasibility screening, guides cycle refinement, and accelerates process development without reliance on extensive simulations.

papers.title: Real-time imaging reveals and quantifies heterogeneous molecular damage in double network hydrogels
