Self-driving labs (SDLs) that combine automated electrodeposition with machine-learning-guided decision-making could accelerate discovery in these complex, high-dimensional parameter spaces, but they face practical challenges. Notably, automated electrodeposition platforms need a continuous supply of pristine electrode surfaces, preservation and logging of electrodeposited samples, and the ability to easily incorporate non-electrochemical, downstream characterization. To overcome these challenges, we developed a modular, affordable, and accessible automated electrochemistry platform that uses a roll-to-roll design to enable continuous electrodeposition experiments. The roll-to-roll architecture enables easy integration with downstream characterization techniques in a conveyor-belt fashion, and electrodeposited samples are stored by rolling up the spent electrode material. We performed 300 identical Cu electrodeposition experiments over 35 hours, demonstrating high repeatability and continuous 24/7 experimentation. We demonstrate the use of our platform for an autonomous campaign, employing a vision-guided Bayesian optimization (BO) workflow to tune electrodeposition parameters and additive concentrations to achieve a visible-light-absorbing Cu deposit. An interpretable machine-learning approach was used to identify benzotriazole as a key additive for controlling the brightness of deposited Cu films. The roll-to-roll design enabled preservation of samples and offline analysis with scanning electron microscopy, providing insight into the impact of benzotriazole on the morphology of the deposited films.

papers.title: Multiplexed SERS Profiling of Gout Biomarkers in Sweat via Polymer-Mediated Ag Nanoflakes
papers.abstract: Personalized management of gout requires profiling multiple metabolites over time. 3 Sweat offers a non-invasive matrix for such profiling. However, simultaneous detec-4 tion of trace metabolic precursors amidst a complex chemical background remains a 5 major analytical challenge. Here, we report a flexible, multiplexed surface-enhanced 6 Raman spectroscopy (SERS) platform engineered to monitor a gout biomarker panel: 7 uric acid (UA), xanthine, hypoxanthine, and creatinine. The sensor is fabricated via 8 in-situ droplet-grown Ag nanostructures on microwell-patterned polydimethylsiloxane 9 (PDMS), ensuring robust mechanical integration. We demonstrate that polyvinylpyrroli-10 done (PVP)-mediated synthesis is critical for optimizing performance. PVP drives a 11 morphological transition from spherical nanoparticles to sharp-edged Ag “nanoflakes,” 12 while reducing competitive adsorption from abundant sweat interferents. The opti-13 mized platform achieves an LOD of 5 µm for UA, a two-fold improvement over un-14 modified analogs, with a linear quantification range of 5–100 µm. Clinical potential 15 was validated by analyzing real human sweat, identifying UA in 16 of 20 samples and 16 capturing diet-induced metabolic fluctuations. Furthermore, the device exhibits exceptional mechanical resilience, retaining signal stability under 50% tensile strain and cyclic fatigue. This work advances a robust, high-sensitivity pathway toward wearable chemical sensing by bridging plasmonic nanofabrication with sweat-based multiplexed monitoring.

papers.title: Predominant proton insertion during electrochemical cycling of ε-VOPO4 in a non-aqueous Ca ion electrolyte
papers.abstract: Calcium-ion batteries (CIBs) have attracted much attention for next-generation energy storage due to the abundance of calcium source and the low reduction potential of Ca2+/Ca. Recent studies have reported promising electrochemical results for Ca-ion intercalation in several electrode materials, yet only few provided structural evidence for true Ca-ion intercalation. This raises the concern that the alleged Ca-ion electrochemistry is derived from proton insertion. Herein, we investigate the electrochemical cycling of a VOPO4 electrode in an aprotic Ca electrolyte with trace water to clarify the charge storage mechanism. While electrochemistry, elemental analysis, and X-ray absorption spectroscopy results seem to support Ca-ion intercalation in the VOPO4 electrode, X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy results unequivocally show proton insertion as the predominant charge storage mechanism. The apparent variation of Ca content in the electrode with the state of charge is attributed to the formation and dissolution of Ca-containing precipitates on the surface of VOPO4 particles. Our work demonstrates the high propensity of proton participation in the intercalation reaction in Ca-ion batteries and the necessity of structural evidence in understanding reactions in multivalent electrochemical systems.

papers.title: Single-Chain Folding of a Synthetic Macromolecule and Two Metal Atoms Provides a Precise Globular Tertiary Structure
papers.abstract: Macromolecular folding underlies function in biological systems, yet analogous compact, globular tertiary structures remain rare in synthetic chemistry. Although shapepersistent foldamers and metal-templated knots have been realized, crystallographically resolved globular architectures arising from intramolecular folding of single nonpeptidic macromolecules are unknown. Here we introduce metal–organic knedels (MOKs): compact single-chain globules formed by intramolecular folding of single synthetic macromolecules around multiple metal centers. Specifically, a uniform 2.6 kDa oligomer bearing eight pyridyl donors and three naphthyl linkers undergoes diastereoselective assembly with two Pd(II) centers to afford a discrete complex, MOK-1, where covalent tethering enforces a unique low-symmetry fold and cavity shape not typically accessible in conventional high-symmetry assemblies, as confirmed by NMR spectroscopy, mass spectrometry and single-crystal X-ray diffraction. These findings define a new class of metal–organic architectures and establish intramolecular folding as a strategy for constructing globular synthetic systems.

papers.title: Nuclear Quantum Effects at Metal-Water Interfaces
Why Seeding Works When Nucleation Barriers Vanish
papers.abstract: Crystallization is a process governed by the interplay between nucleation and growth. While crystalline seeds are known to reduce nucleation barriers and accelerate crystallization under nucleation-limited conditions, their influence when nucleation is not the limiting step remains poorly understood. This creates a mechanistic puzzle in systems where nucleation barriers are already negligible, yet seeding still accelerates crystallization. The synthesis of zeolites is a quintessential example of growth-limited crystallization in which seeds accelerate the process despite negligible homogeneous nucleation barriers. Using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations—validated across two zeolites and the unrelated case of ice crystallization—we establish that growth-limited crystallization produces many small, misoriented crystallites whose slow coarsening into larger domains controls the emergence of X-ray-detectable crystallinity. Local crystalline order, structural coherence, and X-ray detectability are therefore kinetically decoupled milestones: the first can be reached rapidly while the latter two lag significantly. Seeds resolve this lag by imposing a common orientational registry on nascent crystallites, enabling their coherent coalescence into large seed-bound domains. This early coherence-building step produces a crystallite-size asymmetry that accelerates subsequent coarsening, advancing the onset of X-ray-detectable crystallinity without necessarily increasing the nucleated fraction. We conclude that under growth-limited conditions, the apparent induction period observed in powder X-ray diffraction reflects the time required to build long-range coherence, not the time to form crystalline material. Accordingly, seeds function not primarily by reducing nucleation barriers but by enforcing spatial coherence, thereby shortening the time required to develop long-range order detectable by X-ray diffraction.

papers.title: Modeling the sensitivity of large-scale virtual screening to scoring function accuracy, artifacts, and library composition
papers.abstract: Large library docking has emerged as a productive approach for ligand discovery, yet a quantitative framework for understanding how docking performance responds to methodological improvements has been lacking. Here, we develop such a framework by modeling large-scale experiments for three docking campaigns, where 2,544 ligands were synthesized and tested across the scoring landscape (poor scores, mediocre scores, high scores). We find that the observed experimental hit-rate curves can be accurately reproduced by a simple bivariate normal distribution model, where dock score is interpreted as a noisy predictor of binding free energy. To account for the plateauing and subsequent drop in hit-rates often seen at highly favorable docking scores, we add a term for high-ranking docking artifacts, a well-documented phenomenon observed across targets. From this model, three predictions about the sensitivity of docking performance emerge. First , even slight improvements in scoring accuracy would substantially improve both hit-rates and hit affinities: quantitatively, a 0.1 increase in the correlation between docking score and binding affinity would justify accepting a ~10-fold increase in computational cost per molecule, arguing for reinvestment in scoring function accuracy over further library expansion alone. Second , docking artifacts, while hard to anticipate, can come to dominate top-scoring lists as libraries grow. Physically testing molecules across a range of log-normalized ranks (pProp) is therefore essential to identify the peak hit-rate for a given campaign. Third , pre-filtering a library to enrich for molecules with appropriate physicochemical features increases the intrinsic hit-rate and substantially boosts docking performance, particularly at tera-scale, with effects comparable to a meaningful improvement in scoring accuracy. Beyond docking , the model’s parameters (affinity distribution, score-affinity correlation, artifact frequency) can be fit to any screening method with sufficient experimental data, providing an objective basis for benchmarking and comparing virtual screening approaches. These findings offer a practical framework for optimizing large-scale virtual screening as chemical libraries continue to grow.

papers.title: Cost-Effective Solid-state NMR of Fungal Glucans: A case study on Schizosaccharomyces pombe
papers.abstract: Solid-state NMR provides molecular-level insights into fungal cell walls, but full 13 C-enrichment is costly and limits biological replication. Here, we show that 10% 13 C-glucose labelling in Schizosaccharomyces pombe is sufficient to resolve the major carbohydrate resonances and quantify glucan composition with high reproducibility. We then examined cell wall composition at two temperatures, both in whole cells and in extracted wall fractions. Interestingly, whole cell spectra indicated minor, non-significant changes with temperature, while extracted walls revealed differences between the rigid glucan matrices with β-1,3-glucan especially enriched at 36°C. Together, these results establish low-level 13 C labelling as a cost-effective strategy for fungal solid-state NMR and highlight the complementary strengths of whole cell and extracted wall-level analysis in uncovering how the effect of elevated temperature is encoded in cell wall architecture.

papers.title: MODEL OF THE HENRYS: FOUNDATIONS FOR PREDICTING TRANSPORT COEFFICIENTS
papers.abstract: Henry Eyring’s absolute rate theory provides a microscopic picture of liquid transport based on molecular jumps, while Henry Frank’s free volume theory relates entropy changes to an effective cage volume in condensed phases. In this work, we integrate these two frameworks to obtain the Model of the Henrys (MotH), a unified description of transport phenomena based on the (re)movement of molecules within a system. Starting from Eyring’s viscosity expression, we replace vaporization energies by residual energies, and express the free volume via Frank’s entropy–free-volume relation using residual entropy. The resulting model contains a small set of molecule-specific parameters. We demonstrate that viscosity, self-diffusion coefficient, and thermal conductivity of alkanes, alcohols, carbon dioxide, and water can be described in good agreement with experimental and molecular dynamics data over wide temperature and pressure ranges. Analysis of the fitted parameters confirms Frank’s original idea that free volume is primarily controlled by molecular size, whereas activation energies are strongly family-dependent, with associating fluids showing high activation energy. Furthermore, we show that MotH provides a theoretical foundation for empirical entropy scaling relations. Finally, we show that activation energy, free-volume, and entropy-scaling models are complementary rather than competing concepts.

papers.title: Lignin-stabilized polystyrene dispersions as nanoplastic reference materials
papers.abstract: In natural aquatic systems, nanoplastics rapidly acquire organic coatings or so-called eco-coronas that govern their environmental behavior. In contrast, laboratory-made reference nanoplastics rely on artificial surfactants, forming non-natural coatings that enable small size and colloidal stability while failing to replicate these environmentally relevant interfaces. To address this limitation, we developed environmentally relevant polystyrene (PS) nanoplastic models by incorporating three lignin biopolymers, including softwood kraft lignin (SKL), hardwood kraft lignin (HKL), and acetylated softwood kraft lignin (ACL), through anti-solvent precipitation. By combining gravimetric analysis, machine learning-assisted particle sizing, and high-resolution interfacial analysis, we propose mechanisms governing dispersion stability. Systems that formed thick or continuous layers around PS particles showed poor performance, as ACL induced bridging-driven aggregation (~42% recovery), while HKL promoted strong self-association (~22% recovery). In contrast, an optimal 2% SKL formulation achieved high mass recovery (~90%, compared to ~46% for the uncoated PS benchmark) and produced uniform, well-dispersed particles (median size ~110 nm). Notably, SKL formed a thin stabilizing layer together with a distinct formation of lignin nanoparticle surrounding the PS cores. This interfacial architecture enhanced electrosteric stabilization while maintaining colloidal stability. At higher SKL loadings, excess lignin disrupted this balance, leading to reduced stability likely due to depletion flocculation caused by enrichment of free lignin nanoparticles in the continuous phase. Overall, this work provides a mechanistic basis for designing environmentally relevant nanoplastics and highlights the potential of lignin as a sustainable material for stabilizing and studying such systems.

papers.title: Addressing Steric and Electronic Limitations in Nickel Photoredox C–N Cross-Coupling Reactions
papers.abstract: Nickel–photoredox catalysis provides a powerful platform for C–N cross-coupling; however, reaction conditions that accommodate both electron-rich and sterically hindered aryl halides remain elusive due to sluggish oxidative addition and pervasive off-cycle catalyst deactivation. Here, we report a general and robust nickel–photoredox dual catalytic system that overcomes these limitations through the synergistic combination of a simple bipyridine ligand and alkylamine additives. This strategy enables high-yielding C–N bond formation across a broad range of electronically and sterically demanding electrophilic substrates, while mitigating steric constraints at the nucleophilic nitrogen center and substantially accelerating reactions that were previously slow or inaccessible. Mechanistic studies, including competition experiments, ligand-variation profiling, and in situ coordination analyses, indicate that the enhanced performance arises from dynamic ligand interplay and efficient stabilization and reactivation of off-cycle nickel species. A multivariate linear regression (MLR) model demonstrates that electronic effects contribute roughly twice as much as steric effects to oxidative addition kinetics under these conditions.

papers.title: Stereodivergence in the Matteson Reaction
papers.abstract: The Matteson homologation is a highly versatile method for the stereoselective insertion of carbenoids into boronic esters. Through iterative application of the process, complex chiral molecules can be synthesized. The stereoselectivity of the reaction is determined by a chiral diol incorporated in the boronic ester. Upon iterative application, this results in an efficient use of chiral pool starting materials. With that, however, comes limited stereochemical variability. This review delves into boronate homologations that can address these particular limitations and highlights unsolved problems in the field.

papers.title: Scenario-Driven Multicriteria Evaluation of CCSIntegrated Waste-to-Energy Treatment Technologies: A Decision Support Framework for Sustainable Municipal Waste Management in the Nordic Region
papers.abstract: Norway’s long-term climate strategy emphasises reducing the environmental impact of waste management by mitigating fossil CO2 emissions, particularly through the integration of carbon capture and storage (CCS) in municipal Waste-to-Energy (WtE) systems. WtE facilities are important because they play a year-round role in district heating. This study applies an Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP)-based Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) framework to evaluate technologies treating Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) in Trondheim, incorporating CCS retrofits at 85% and 95% capture rates. The model comprises four main criteria, twelve sub-criteria, thirteen key indicators, and eight deciding factors, which are weighted based on local performance data. These weights were processed through a scenario modelling interface to evaluate different WtE system configurations reflecting Trondheim’s existing infrastructure and potential future upgrades. The results show that retrofitting the city’s incineration plant with a 95% capture unit yields the highest composite score, improving environmental performance over the current arrangements; however, the integrated assessment also quantifies the trade-off that higher capture increases auxiliary energy demand and annualised costs, implying diminishing marginal benefits when moving from moderate to very high capture rates. The presented approach provides a transferable, data-driven tool for municipal decision-makers not only in Trondheim but worldwide to evaluate CCS unit retrofits of WtE plants under changing waste streams. By adapting to regional waste composition and policy constraints, the framework can support strategic planning for low-carbon, integrated waste management systems globally.

papers.title: Crucial Impact of Dinuclearity and Linker Length on Electrochemical CO2 Reduction to Methanol
papers.abstract: Herein, we demonstrate the critical role of dinuclear active-site frameworks in enabling electrochemical CO 2 -to-methanol (e-MeOH) conversion. While a structurally analogous mononuclear Fe complex exhibits no MeOH formation under identical conditions, dinuclear Fe/Fe and Cu/Cu systems promote the multi-hydride transfer steps required for e-MeOH production. Under homogeneous conditions, controlled potential electrolysis (3 h, 1 mM catalyst) with Fe/Fe and Cu/Cu complexes affords global Faradaic efficiencies (GFEs) of 22% and 24%, respectively, with high product selectivity toward e-MeOH (~90% and ~85%). Changing the linker length has a pronounced impact on electrocatalytic MeOH production performance. Molecular electrodes featuring a –CH2–pyridine linker outperform their –CH 2 –CH 2 –pyridine analogues, leading to enhancements in MeOH selectivity of ~20% for Fe/Fe and ~17% for Cu/Cu systems. Notably, Cu/Cu catalysts containing electrode incorporating – CH 2 –pyridine linkers consistently surpass their Fe/Fe counterparts, delivering more than twofold higher FEs for e-MeOH production over the initial 3 h of electrolysis. Collectively, these findings identify dinuclearity, metal identity, and linker structure as key parameters governing multi-electron CO 2 reduction to MeOH, establishing design principles for efficient electrocatalyst and molecular electrode architectures for sustainable CO 2 valorization.

papers.title: Mass Production and Doping of Graphene Using Low-Temperature Rapid Joule Heating
papers.abstract: The mass production of high-quality graphene and its functionalized derivatives remains a critical bottleneck for widespread industrial application. This study presents a versatile and energy-efficient rapid Joule heating (RJH) platform that enables the 100 gram-scale synthesis of graphene at significantly reduced surface temperatures. By leveraging a unique temperature gradient within the reactor, we demonstrate the successful synthesis of turbostratic graphene at a surface temperature as low as 800 °C, with optimal structural quality achieved at 1000-1200 °C. This low-temperature process preserves the quartz reactor, drastically reducing operational costs and enabling a single-batch yield of nearly 500 g. Furthermore, we develop a one-step, low-temperature RJH strategy for the efficient doping of graphene with boron and nitrogen. Maximum doping levels of 2.58 at.% (B at 800 °C) and 3.56 at.% (N at 400 °C) are achieved, with the doping temperature dictating the chemical configuration and resulting properties. Boron doping promotes thicker platelets, while nitrogen doping facilitates the formation of few-layer graphene. The scalability and robustness of this approach are validated through 500-gram scale syntheses. This work establishes low-temperature RJH as a powerful, green, and scalable platform for

papers.title: Designing transferable transition state guided collective variable via
A Tetra-Propionate-Functionalized Phenazine as a Low-Potential and Stable Negolyte Species for Durable Aqueous Organic Redox Flow Batteries
papers.abstract: Low-cost, long-lifetime aqueous organic redox flow batteries can store massive electricity from intermittent renewables, thus holding great promise for long-duration, grid-scale energy storage applications. Here, we report five phenazine derivatives with varied substituents or with the same substituent introduced at different positions. Of the five molecules, 2,2',2'',2'''-(phenazine-2,3,7,8-tetrayltetrakis(oxy))tetrapropionic acid (T4PEPz) shows excellent thermal stability in both oxidized and reduced states, as evidenced by time-dependent proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, a low redox potential of –0.66 V vs. SHE, and high aqueous solubility of 1.17 M at pH 14. The Pourbaix diagram, combined with in situ infrared spectroscopy and pH monitoring, further confirms a reversible two-electron, two-proton transfer mechanism. When paired with ferro-/ferricyanide positive electrolyte, the battery exhibits a high open circuit voltage of 1.24 V at 50% state of charge, and the 0.6 M T4PEPz-based flow battery retains approximately 97.5% of its initial capacity after 560 cycles over 73 days, corresponding to fade rates of 0.0045%/cycle and 0.0342%/day. The molecules reported in this work both enrich the phenazine-based negative electrolyte library and advance low-cost, long-lifetime, and high-performance phenazine-based flow batteries.

papers.title: Fluorene-Containing Hydrogenated Polypentenamers
papers.abstract: Understanding structure–property relationships of new all-hydrocarbon polymers is particularly important for developing next-generation polyolefin materials with enhanced thermal, mechanical, and optical properties. Herein, cyclopentenes spiro-fused to fluorenes are reported as a new class of monomers for ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP). Equilibrium ROMP of 1 using Grubbs catalysts, conducted at low temperatures and high monomer concentrations, afforded high-molecular-weight polypentenamers, which were subsequently hydrogenated. Precise control over polymer molecular weights, successful chain extensions, evaluation of the polymerization enthalpy, and complete depolymerization back to monomer 1 were achieved. Hydrogenated copolymers of 1 with cyclopentene and substituted analogues of 1 were also synthesized with various incorporation ratios, exhibiting widely tunable thermal, mechanical, and optical properties. Incorporation of fluorene units led to higher glass transition temperatures, Young’s modulus, and refractive indices, while orientation birefringence became more negative. This work established spiro-fused cyclopentenes as unprecedented ROMP monomers, offering a new platform for polyolefin analogues.

papers.title: Enhancing Mass Spectrum Comparison for Volatile Compounds
papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry is an analytical technique widely used to identify compounds in a chemical matrix. However, spectral identification and similarity evaluation of mass spectra remain challenging. In this paper, we present the adaptation, retraining, and evaluation of deep-learning methods originally developed for liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) to gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) identification and structural-similarity assessment. We evaluated the performance of these methods on classification, ranking, and regression tasks. Our results show that Spec2Vec models adapted to GC-MS data perform well in identifying and measuring structural similarities between volatile compounds, extending the capability of this approach to non-tandem MS data.

papers.title: Cobalt-Catalyzed [2σ+2π] Cycloaddition via Site-Selective Capture of Bicyclobutane Diradical
papers.abstract: Strained bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs) have emerged as versatile precursors for accessing highly reactive intermediates, enabling unconventional bond constructions through strain-release pathways. Herein, we report a cobalt(II)-catalyzed strategy that combines thermal activation of BCBs with selective radical capture by Co(II) to afford head-to-head fused bicyclo[2.1.1]hexanes (BCHex). We propose that thermal activation of the BCB generates a reactive diradical intermediate, which is intercepted by a tailored bidentate phosphine Co(II) cationic complex via oxidative radical coupling, followed by a [2σ+2π] cycloaddition with indoles. Mechanistic investigations, including 31P NMR spectroscopy, cyclic voltammetry, and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) studies, provide insights into the plausible reaction pathway. The involvement of paramagnetic Co(II) species is consistent with the broad features observed in both EPR and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra of the catalyst. In addition, four structurally distinct Co(II) complexes were synthesized, fully characterized by UV-Vis and Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, and evaluated as catalysts for the transformation. The cationic nature of the Co(II) species was further confirmed by phosphine oxide trapping experiments and single-crystal X-ray crystallography.

papers.title: Long Fluorescence Lifetime Molecular Rotors Based on the 4,4′-dicyano-BODIPY core
papers.abstract: Environmentally sensitive fluorescent probes with extended emission lifetimes are valuable for studying live cells by fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM). Here we demonstrate that substituting the fluorine atoms in BODIPY-based fluorescent molecular rotors with cyano groups results in viscosity-sensitive probes with significantly longer emission lifetimes. The new probes were used to measure the viscosity of the plasma membrane in Gram-positive bacteria.

papers.title: Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase
papers.abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than through concerted global motions or equilibrium fluctuations. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.

papers.title: Scaffold-Based Evaluation Metrics for Fair Comparison of Molecular Generators
papers.abstract: Molecular generators enable the exploration of chemical space to identify novel compounds with desirable properties. However, assessing their performance remains challenging due to the structural diversity and volume of the generated molecules. Commonly used evaluation metrics, focusing on chemical validity and novelty, do not fully align with the primary goal of molecular generation: the discovery of new biologically active compounds. To address this limitation, we introduce scaffold-based metrics that enable a fair comparison by evaluating a generator’s ability to recover biologically relevant scaffolds absent from the input set. We applied the scaffold Recovery Score (RS), SEt scaffold Diversity (SED), and Absolute SEt scaffold Recall (ASER) metrics to compare several molecular generators, including Molpher, DrugEx, REINVENT, and Graph-based genetic algorithm. The proposed scaffold-based metrics provide a realistic framework for evaluating and optimizing molecular generators for their practical use in drug discovery scenarios, particularly in the design of focused virtual chemical libraries. The metrics are available as open-source in a GitHub repository at https://github.com/filvaleriia/scaffold-based-metrics.

papers.title: WITHDRAWN
papers.abstract: Withdrawn at the author’s request because it was posted without approval of all contributors.

papers.title: SrTiO3 Homogeneously Doped with Rh and La from a Metal-organic Framework Template
papers.abstract: Precise control over dopant content and dispersion remains a challenge in the synthesis of functional nanomaterials. Herein a heterobimetallic MOF, MUV-10(Sr), was used as a porous crystalline scaffold into which lanthanum and rhodium were introduced via incipient wetness impregnation for the synthesis of homogeneously doped SrTiO3:La/Rh nanoparticles. Conversion of MUV-10(Sr) to SrTiO3:La/Rh conserved the metal composition present in the precursor template. Doped MOF-derived materials demonstrated greater visible light absorbance than a conventionally doped counterpart. This is attributed to homogeneous dopant incorporation and greater selectivity for rhodium in the RhIII oxidation state. Ultraviolet-visible reflectance spectroscopy and structural refinement from powder diffraction data supports the claimed oxidation state selectivity. The product oxides were employed as photocatalysts for H2 production and demonstrated activity across their absorbance profile. Intercrystallinity and large particle size, however, are proposed to limit the efficiency of MOF-derived materials. The use of crystalline scaffolds as precursors for nanoparticle synthesis opens potential for greater control over material composition and morphology.

papers.title: CSP5: Large-scale Neural Chemical Shift Prediction from 2.5 Million Experimental NMR Spectra
papers.abstract: Accurate nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) chemical shift prediction remains limited by the small size and narrow chemical diversity of atom-assigned training datasets. Here, we address that bottleneck by leveraging the new NMRexp resource with weak supervision, training CASCADE-style graph neural networks with an optimal-assignment loss with datasets of approximately 1.2 million unassigned 13C spectra and 1.4 million unassigned 1H spectra alongside conventional assigned data. This joint training strategy substantially improves performance over assigned-only baselines: on held-out NMRexp data, 13C mean absolute error (MAE) falls from 1.46 to 1.05 ppm and 1H MAE from 0.316 to 0.134 ppm, while 13C performance on a test set from the assigned Exp22K dataset improves from 0.812 to 0.610 ppm. These gains also translate into better structure verification performance, with hard-decoy top-1 retrieval improving from 0.819 to 0.876 for 13C and from 0.589 to 0.801 for 1H. Taken together, these results show that large-scale unassigned literature spectra provide an effective training signal for more accurate and practically useful NMR prediction models.

papers.title: Solution-Processing of Metal-Organochalcogenides (MOCs) and Application in Thin-Film Transistors
papers.abstract: Metal-organochalcogenides (MOCs) have recently emerged as highly promising candidates for optoelectronic applications; however, their integration into devices has been severely limited by the lack of solution-processable routes, as most MOCs are insoluble in conventional solvents. Herein, we report a strategy that employs coordinating diamine solvents to solubilize and process four metal–thiophenolate complexes as a model group of MOCs, enabling the fabrication of high-quality thin films. A high solubility of 150-200 mg mL -1 (>600 mM) can be achieved with 1,3-diaminopropane (DAP). Using copper thiophenolate (CuSPh) as a model system, we elucidate the role of DAP acting as a liquid co-ligand for the dissolution and validate the restoration of the MOC structure upon solvent removal. DAP-based solutions allow for the fabrication of smooth, compact, and uniform films with thickness between 30-40 nm. Notably, solution-processed films of CuSPh with the underlying one-dimensional (1D) structure are demonstrated as a semiconducting p-channel in field-effect transistors, achieving a hole mobility of 5×10 -3 cm 2 V -1 s -1 which is comparable to single-crystalline nanorods of CuSPh. Our ‘ liquid ligand processing ’ concept provides a route for fabricating MOC films using standard solution-based methods and crucially unlocks the applications of MOCs in thin-film devices.

papers.title: Ultrafast dynamics of competing dimethyl disulfide photodissociation pathways
papers.abstract: The disulfide bond, in the form of cystine, plays a key role in protein structure and function. Dimethyl disulfide serves as a model system for understanding the fundamental properties of this unique chemical bond, including its response to UV photoexcitation. While photoexcitation at 267 nm is known to exclusively cleave the S–S bond on a sub-picosecond time scale, photoexcitation at 200 nm excites a mixture of electronic states of Rydberg and antibonding character along the C–S bond, resulting in competing dissociation pathways on an unknown timescale. Herein, we use mega-electron-Volt ultrafast electron diffraction and time-resolved velocity-mapped ion imaging to directly time the competing C–S and S–S bond dissociation pathways upon photoexcitation of dimethyl disulfide at 200 nm, finding sub-picosecond as well as unexpectedly long, picosecond lifetimes. Non-adiabatic mixed quantum-classical trajectories reveal pathways for each bond dissociation and help interpret experimental results through calculations of both experimental observables. We suggest that while the sub-picosecond dynamics arise from bond dissociation on the singlet manifold, picosecond dynamics arise from

papers.title: Local Chemistry-Guided Molecular Beam Epitaxy Growth of SnSe on MgO via Combined ReaxFF Modeling and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Subtle variations in local growth chemistry can fundamentally alter the morphology of layered chalcogenide thin films, yet the atomic-scale mechanisms underlying this sensitivity remain poorly understood. Here, we combine molecular beam epitaxy experiments, reactive molecular dynamics simulations, and machine learning analysis to establish a chemistry–structure relationship for SnSe thin film growth on MgO. Experimentally, we show that modifying the Sn:Se flux ratio and deposition sequence switches SnSe growth from three-dimensional island formation to laterally coalesced smooth films, accompanied by a pronounced reduction in surface roughness. Reactive molecular dynamics simulations reveal that this transition originates from an intrinsic chemical asymmetry between Sn and Se that alters adatom surface diffusion and aggregation behavior during growth. Se-rich environments stabilize surface passivation and promote lateral growth, whereas Sn-rich conditions favor vertical aggregation through rapid Sn clustering. To independently assess morphology trends without imposing physical assumptions, we apply an unsupervised machine learning framework to images rendered from the simulation snapshots. The resulting low-dimensional representation of surface morphologies recovers the same chemistry-dependent roughness trends observed experimentally and in simulations, providing data-driven validation of the underlying atomistic mechanisms. Because nanoscale roughness strongly influences carrier scattering, phonon transport, and domain stability in SnSe-based electronic and energy devices, these results provide a chemistry-guided framework for morphology control in layered chalcogenide thin films.

papers.title: β-Ketosulfones in Gewald and Friedlaender chemistry. Design, synthesis, structure and in silico ADMET assessment of products
papers.abstract: β-Ketosulfones represent highly reactive and underexplored scaffolds in heterocyclic chemistry. In this work, we investigated their utility in two classical transformations: the Gewald and Friedländer reactions. Using the cyclic β-ketosulfone dihydro-2H-thiopyran-3(4H)-one-1,1dioxide, we developed optimized conditions that enable regioselective access to 2aminothiophenes. The Et3N/DMF protocol at 60 °C provided the major isomer with excellent selectivity, while a complementary DABCO/EtOH system under microwave irradiation afforded the minor regioisomer. These findings highlight the crucial role of solvent, base, and activation method in steering regioselectivity. Extending the study to Friedländer chemistry, we achieved efficient one-pot syntheses of aminoquinolines from both six- and five-membered βketosulfones. Unlike in the Gewald reaction, these condensations proceeded regioselectively, affording the desired products exclusively. The structures of representative products were fully established by NMR and X-ray crystallography, supported by HMBC and NOE correlations. Overall, this study demonstrates the synthetic versatility of β-ketosulfones and introduces sulfone analogues of biologically relevant heterocycles, expanding the scope of SO2containing privileged structures in medicinal chemistry.

papers.title: Theoretical Insights into Designing β-M@Ni(OH)2 Electrocatalysts for Efficient Urea Oxidation
papers.abstract: Ni-based catalysts show great potential for the urea oxidation reaction (UOR) due to their high activity, low cost, and broad energy and environmental applications. Herein, we investigate two possible mechanisms for N2 formation on β-Ni(OH)2 using density functional theory (DFT) and further focus on the dehydrogenation steps of the intramolecular pathway over β-Ni(OH)2 and β-M@Ni(OH)2 catalysts (M = Cr, Fe, Co, Cu, Mo, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ir, Pt, and Au). The results show that the intramolecular pathway is energetically favorable on β-Ni(OH)2, and that the enhanced urea adsorption energy (Eads(urea)) over β-M@Ni(OH)2 originates from the upshift of the d-band center (εd) which is induced by M-doping. Gibbs free energy analyses identify β-Fe@Ni(OH)2, β-Co@Ni(OH)2, and β-Pd@Ni(OH)2 as promising catalysts with low limiting potentials. Furthermore, the urea adsorption strength shows a linear correlation with the calculated limiting potentials, suggesting that it can serve as an effective descriptor for urea oxidation toward N2 formation. This study provides theoretical guidance for the screening and design of highly active Ni-based UOR catalysts.

papers.title: A molecular ”thermometer” for measuring effective non-local exchange
papers.abstract: Non-local exchange (NLX) is a key ingredient for accurate density functional calculations, but its effective strength is often hard to quantify beyond simple global hybrids. To this end, we introduce a molecular probe based on the isomerization of hexaethynylbenzene to carbo-benzene, a reaction with exceptional sensitivity to exchange effects. Using the isomerization energy, we define a simple relative measure, 𝑡 X , that gauges the effective NLX of a method on a scale ranging from 0 for the local density approximation to 100 for Hartree-Fock. Across a broad set of density functional approximations, 𝑡 X closely tracks the formal Hartree-Fock exchange content of global hybrids, while revealing that most common GGAs, meta-GGAs, and global hybrids still provide too little effective exchange. Several range-separated hybrid, double hybrid, and some local hybrid functionals perform much better and closely approach the near-basis-set-limit coupled-cluster reference value of 𝑡 X = 60. The 𝑡 X values of various semiempirical quantum mechanical and machine-learned interatomic potential methods indicate that they empirically account for NLX effects to a varying degree. Thus, the proposed reaction serves as a compact thermochemical benchmark for assessing and developing methods that aim to reliably describe non-local exchange.

papers.title: Kinetic Landscape Framework for Persistent Luminescence: a disorder-based state space for decay kinetics and materials design
A Single Active-Site Water Molecule Encodes Two Distinct Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer Pathways in Fatty Acid Photodecarboxylase
papers.abstract: Active-site water molecules are increasingly recognized as functionally involved species in enzymatic proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET), yet whether a single water molecule can support distinct catalytic roles within the same active site remains poorly understood. Here, using a multiscale computational approach we show that a previously unidentified water molecule (denoted here Wat3) in fatty acid photodecarboxylase (FAP), a natural photenzyme that converts fatty acids into alkanes, mediates radical quenching via two mechanistically distinct PCET pathways. In the lower-barrier pathway (∆A ‡ ≈ 23 kJ·mol -1 ), Wat3 acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, stabilizing the transition state of a direct proton transfer from cysteine C432 to the alkyl radical (water-assisted PCET). In an alternative, higher-barrier pathway (∆A ‡ ≈ 42 kJ·mol -1 ), the same water molecule acts as a proton shuttle, relaying the proton from C432 to the radical in a quasi-concerted two-proton transfer (water-relay PCET). In both scenarios, the flavin semiquinone provides the electron. The water-assisted route dominates the kinetics under ambient conditions and is consistent with the experimentally measured ∼100 ns timescale. The water-relay pathway, though less accessible in FAP, represents a mechanistic alternative that may become operative in engineered variants or in other enzymes. Additionally, we characterize the fate of the CO 2 coproduct, showing that it reacts with the nascent cysteine thiolate to form a transient thiocarbonate adduct, providing a structural interpretation of previously unassigned electron density in crystallographic data. These findings highlight the ability of a single active-site water molecule to modulate radical PCET through distinct functional roles, with implications for understanding and engineering light-driven biocatalysts.

papers.title: Synergistic Magnetic, Piezoelectric, and Chiral Optical Effects in Fe-and Mn-Hybrid Metal Halides
Defect-Driven Local Structures in 3D Hollow Hybrid Perovskites Resolved by Solid-State NMR Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Metal halide perovskites (MHPs) are versatile semiconductors with high defect tolerance. Among emerging MHP architectures, the 3D "hollow" perovskites incorporating ethylenediammonium (en) dications represent a unique defect-stabilization paradigm by retaining structural order, stability, and performance. But the local chemical environments of defects that underpin bulk properties have remained unresolved, due to the inherently averaging nature of diffraction techniques. Here, we address this information gap by probing both crystallinity and defect-specific local structures in three representative hollow systems: enMAPbI 3 , enFAPbI 3 , and enFAPbBr 3 (MA: methylammonium; FA: formamidinium) using powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD), periodic density-functional theory (DFT), and solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (ssNMR) spectroscopy. Specifically, ssNMR allows to identify and quantify two distinct vacancy regimes: a low-en (below 30%) regime with predominantly trans en conformers that stabilize the framework by simultaneously generating Pb vacancies; and a new high-en (above 30%) regime where conformationally tilted en dications lead to distortions in PbX6 octahedra and crystallinity features. Modulated by the non-covalent interactions, insights into defect sites can be obtained by analyzing 1D 1 H, 207 Pb, and 2D 1 H- 1 H and 1 H- 14 N correlation NMR spectra acquired at a high magnetic field (21 T) with fast magic-angle spinning (MAS). These findings help explain defect compensation mechanisms, reconciling correlated trends between bandgap evolution and stability across iodine-and bromine-based hollow perovskites. In addition, they provide a framework for rationalizing defectengineering strategies in hybrid perovskites and related metal halides.

papers.title: Characterizing Post-Fire Fine and Ultrafine Particles in the 2025 Eaton Fire Burn Zone and Nearby Areas
papers.abstract: Particle emissions may persist in wildland-urban interface (WUI) fire burn zones during the post-fire period, yet their characteristics remain poorly understood. Following full containment of the 2025 Eaton Fire, we conducted mobile and stationary aerosol measurements to characterize the spatial variability and temporal dynamics of fine and ultrafine particles within and around the burn zone. Our results show that the median PM 2.5 concentrations were slightly lower within the burn zone (inside the fire perimeter) than at locations >1000 m outside the perimeter (11.1 vs 12.0 μg/m 3 ), but the burn zone exhibited a higher frequency of PM2.5 spikes (2.8 vs 2.2 peaks/km) with greater peak prominence (9.0 vs 6.0 μg/m 3 ) and shorter durations (2.9 vs 7.5 s). These results indicate transient and intense PM2.5 emissions within the burn zone, which may not be captured by time-integrated measurements. In addition, particle number concentrations within the burn zone were higher than the urban background measured ~23 km downwind (1.2×10 4 vs 9.5×10 3 particles/cm 3 ). Distinct aerosol dynamics were observed within the burn zone that may contribute to elevated particle number concentrations, including (1) formation and growth of ultrafine particles and (2) shrinkage and disintegration of submicron particles. Together, these observations demonstrate that post-fire period represents an active and evolving phase of WUI particle emissions with important implications for human exposure and health.

papers.title: NextTopDocker: the largest-to-date docking power benchmark reveals that deep learning performs generally much worse than logistic regression models
papers.abstract: Predicting three-dimensional binding orientations of drug-like molecules remains challenging in structure-based drug design. Following AlphaFold’s success, end-to-end machine-learning (ML) docking frameworks have emerged, leveraging deep learning for pose generation. Yet, their performance is often assessed on small, outdated benchmarks containing only a few hundred protein-ligand complexes. We present “NextTopDocker,” a large, up-to-date, open-access data set for docking power assessment comprising 14,038 training and 5,201 test entries across 3,173 unique protein targets, constructed from the Protein Data Bank using a cold-ligand split. Developed entirely with open-source tools, it includes crystallographic structures, Smina-generated docking poses, and ligand-similarity-aware training subsets. With “NextTopDocker,” we benchmarked four state-of-the-art end-to-end ML docking frameworks, DeepDock, Interformer, SurfDock, and Uni-Mol Docking v.2, against classical (Smina) and hybrid (GNINA 1.3 and logistic regression using Smina and GNINA 1.3 scores) baselines. Despite sophisticated architectures, only Interformer matched the docking power of logistic regression on Smina poses, while others failed without post-docking physics-based refinement. Most raw ML-generated poses exhibited steric clashes and/or implausible geometries, underscoring the lack of intrinsic physical realism in current ML-based docking. Embedding physics-informed constraints directly into pose generation, rather than relying on downstream optimization, is essential for achieving valid, autonomous molecular docking. “NextTopDocker” is available at https://github.com/caominhtr/NextTopDocker and https://zenodo.org/records/17492994 .

papers.title: Digital Catalysis Platform (DigCat): A Gateway to Big Data and AI-Powered Innovations in Catalysis
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping catalysis research, yet its impact remains constrained by fragmented, heterogeneous, and non-standardized data. In this Commentary, we argue that the future of AI-driven catalysis depends critically on the development of data-centric infrastructures that integrate experimental results, theoretical insights, and literature knowledge. We highlight the Digital Catalysis Platform (DigCat 4.0) as an example of such an approach, combining large-scale curated datasets with tools for visualization, modeling, and machine learning. Building on this foundation, domain-specific AI agents enable automated data analysis, knowledge extraction, and catalyst design, transforming how researchers interact with catalytic data. We discuss how the convergence of big data, AI models, and automation may lead to closed-loop, autonomous discovery systems. Finally, we outline the current field-wide challenges and future opportunities in establishing reliable, interpretable, and scalable AI-driven workflows for catalysis in the data-rich era, while highlighting DigCat 4.0 as a foundation for subsequent platform evolution toward future releases (DigCat 5.0). Access DigCat 4.0 at https://www.digcat.org.

papers.title: Aerobactin mediates bacterial proliferation relevant to squid-Vibrio symbiosis
papers.abstract: Iron acquisition is a central determinant of microbial survival and symbiotic fitness in marine environments where the solubility of Fe(III) is extremely low. In the symbiosis between Vibrio fischeri and the Hawaiian bobtail squid (Euprymna scolopes), siderophore-mediated iron uptake is thought to play an important role during early colonization, yet the contribution of individual siderophores remains incompletely characterized. In this study, we report the total synthesis of the hydroxamate siderophore aerobactin and evaluate its chemical stability, iron-binding properties, and biological function in V. fischeri. Aerobactin was characterized by NMR and HRMS and shown to bind Fe(III). Stability experiments in artificial seawater showed that aerobactin degrades slowly, following first-order kinetics with a half-life of 564 hours. Quantification of iron in relevant growth media revealed concentrations of 11.7 µM in seawater tryptone (SWT) media and 1.26 µM in autoinducer bioassay (AB) media, requiring the design of iron-limited conditions using iron chelators. The biological activity of aerobactin was evaluated using growth recovery experiments with wild-type V. fischeri ES114 and mutants strains deficient in siderophore biosynthesis and transport (ΔiucABCD, ΔiutA, and ΔfhuCDB). Exogenous aerobactin restored growth in iron-limited environments in a concentration-dependent manner, particularly in the biosynthesis-deficient mutant, showing its functional role in iron uptake. Our findings support the use of AB-FeCit as the optimal media system. Collectively, the results link aerobactin and iron availability to bacterial growth dynamics, supplying quantitative insight into siderophore-mediated iron acquisition in a model marine symbiosis.

papers.title: Estimating the make-up of a blend in terms of its parent mixtures (e.g., reverse-engineering a wine blend) based on chemical fingerprints
papers.abstract: In the chemical, food & beverage, agricultural, and pharmaceutical industries, non-reacting complex mixtures are often blended to tune the properties of a finished product. Herein, we tackle the inverse problem of reconstructing the unknown make-up of a blend in terms of its parent mixtures based on chemical fingerprints. As an experimental case study, we estimate the volume percentages of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, and Cabernet Franc composing a Bordeaux red wine blend. For chemical fingerprinting, we measure the ethanol, sugar, and acid concentrations in the blend and each pure-varietal wine. A mass balance on each constituent over mixing (neglecting chemical reactions, evaporation, and excess volume) gives a system of linear equations, subject to a sum-to-one constraint, governing the make-up of the blend. To find the best approximate solution to this overdetermined system, we solve a constrained, scaled total least squares optimization problem—explicitly accounting for measurement errors in the chemical fingerprints. We predicted the Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, and Cabernet Franc content in each blend with an average error of <5 vol. %. Monte Carlo sampling and propagation of measurement errors provided uncertainty quantification. Such “computational unmixing” is useful for reverse-engineering blends across industries for authenticity verification, fraud detection, forensics, and quality control.

papers.title: Studying Formation of Single-Phase Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni Spinel High-Entropy Oxide with Simultaneous in situ X-ray Scattering and Absorption
papers.abstract: High-entropy oxides have emerged as a promising class of functional materials due to their tuneable compositions and resulting structural and electronic diversity. However, the synthesis of singlephase high-entropy oxides remains challenging, as the presence of multiple metals often leads to secondary phase formation. Understanding how composition and redox chemistry govern phase formation is therefore crucial for the rational design of these materials. Here, we apply rational design principles in a sol-gel synthesis to obtain a single-phase (Co0.5Ni0.5)(Cr0.33Mn0.33Fe0.33)2O4 spinel high-entropy oxide. Using quasi-simultaneous in situ X-ray scattering and X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we identify the formation of a nanostructured intermediate during synthesis. This intermediate reduces at higher temperatures to form the final high-entropy spinel phase, with Cr and Mn identified as the key redoxactive species during this transition. Modelling the extended X-ray absorption fine structure reveals the cation distribution of the final material, including the presence of Cr4+ and Mn2+ species in the tetrahedral site, which deviate from their expected oxidation states. We further show that the rare Cr4+ – typically inaccessible through commonly employed solid-state syntheses – forms in the intermediate and persists during product formation. These findings provide new insight into the redox requirements necessary for the formation of single-phase high-entropy oxides. Furthermore, we demonstrate that quasi-simultaneous in situ X-ray scattering and absorption is well-suited to probe the formation of complex materials such as HEOs, and we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first in situ structural characterization of HEO formation using this approach.

papers.title: Diagnosing Quantum Tunneling at Ambient Temperature through Rate–Driving Force Responsiveness
papers.abstract: Quantum mechanical tunneling can strongly influence chemical reactivity, yet experimental diagnostics for tunneling contributions remain limited. Here we derive a new diagnostic principle, identifying ratedriving force relationship as a general experimental observable of tunneling. We show that tunneling fundamentally reshapes the scaling relationship between reaction rate and thermodynamic driving force. Whereas classical transition state theory links this responsiveness solely to barrier height, tunneling depends on both barrier height and barrier width, producing responsiveness that exceeds classical predictions. This principle provides a simple experimental diagnostic for tunneling based on responsiveness analysis within a reaction family, complementing existing diagnostics that often rely on cryogenic temperatures or isotopic substitution. We demonstrate this derived principle using the syn elimination of selenoxides as a model system at room temperature. Because the diagnostic framework relies only on standard kinetic measurements, it is expected to be broadly applicable to reactions with measurable elementary kinetics.

papers.title: From C─H Feedstocks to Unnatural Amino Acids: Light Twist on the Classic Amidomalonate Synthesis
papers.abstract: Both linear and cyclic unnatural amino acids (UAAs) play a central role in drug discovery but remain challenging to access from feedstocks. Inspired by terpene biosynthesis, we designed a simple and unified olefin precursor that can be diverged into constrained cyclic motifs, including prolines, azepanes, carbamates, ethers, and lactones. To access this olefin precursor, we exploit the emerging Pd(I/II) cycle and demonstrate a three-component coupling. This visible light-promoted transformation converts readily available C–H donors, 1,3-butadiene, and amidomalonate esters into functionally rich α-tertiary amino acid precursors. We further show how this achiral motif can furnish enantioenriched UAAs through Liu’s dynamic kinetic resolution. In addition, we build a pyrrolizidine core found in various natural products from simple building blocks, including dichloroethane. Our approach represents a modern twist on the classic amidomalonate synthesis.

papers.title: Influence of Identity and Position of Ligand Substituents on Tris(amido) Yttrium Complexes
papers.abstract: Early transition metals have been reported to be effective C(sp3)-C(sp3) crosscoupling catalysts when paired with tris(amido) redox-active ligands. We developed a series of ligands to probe the effects of radical stabilizing groups and substituent position on yttrium tris(amido) complexes. We synthesized neutral yttrium complexes 1-Y – 3-Y which were characterized via NMR spectroscopy, single crystal X-ray crystallography, cyclic voltammetry, and UV-vis spectroscopy. Then, the single electron oxidized complexes 1-Yox – 3-Yox were synthesized as they are relevant intermediates in catalysis. These complexes were characterized via NMR, EPR, and UV-vis/NIR spectroscopy. DFT calculations were used to further elucidate the electronic structures of 1-Y – 3-Y and 1-Yox – 3-Yox. Complexes 1-Y – 3-Y were used as catalysts in a C(sp3)-C(sp3) cross-coupling reaction and initial rates were used to determine the influence of the substituents on catalysis. The results indicate that the identity and placement of the substituent impact the electronic structure of the complexes but have minor effects on catalysis.

papers.title: Biochar in Porous Protein-Based Materials for Fully Circular Single-Use Absorbents
papers.abstract: The pervasiveness of fossil plastics in the modern world is having numerous negative environmental and societal effects. While effective alternatives to fossil plastics have been developed to fit many use cases, no comparable alternatives to absorbent polymers yet exist. This study evaluated the effects that the inclusion of drupe-pit biochar powder in zein-gluten protein bioplastics had on the absorptive properties of the material. Four bioplastic formulations were produced and tested, one with no additives, one with sodium bicarbonate foaming agent, one with biochar, and one with both biochar and bicarbonate. These bioplastics were extruded and hot-pressed into sheets. The absorptive capabilities of each of these materials was evaluated. Their ability to absorb saline solution and limonene, a nonpolar liquid with low surface tension, was tested, and the size of pores was measured using a scanning electron microscope. Results showed that the inclusion of biochar reduced the efficiency of CO 2 -production in the sodium bicarbonate blowing agent, meaning biochar generally had a net-negative effect on absorptive capability. Despite this, samples containing biochar performed better on the limonene tests than those without, suggesting that the inclusion of biochar may be beneficial in select situations.

papers.title: The Heisenberg Fingerprint: Physics-Informed Molecular Similarity from Neural Network Potential Hidden States
papers.abstract: Scaffold hopping, the identification of functionally equivalent molecules with different chemical scaffolds, is among the most valuable and difficult operations in medicinal chemistry. Topological fingerprints are blind to it: Morgan fingerprints assign near-random similarity (mean Tanimoto 0.20) to confirmed scaffold-hopping pairs. Here we introduce the Heisenberg fingerprint (HFP), a 256dimensional molecular embedding derived from the hidden representations of pre-trained neural network potentials (NNPs) that reliably identifies scaffold hops. Per-atom features from a DFTtrained NNP backbone are pooled via multi-head attention and trained to correlate with 3D shape overlap, electrostatic potential similarity, and pharmacophore feature matching simultaneously, using 2 million molecular pairs with computed overlap targets. On 147 known scaffold-hopping cases, HFP assigns mean cosine similarity of 0.83 to pairs that Morgan fingerprints rate at 0.20. On 24 approved drugs spanning 12 therapeutic targets, including clinically validated scaffold hops such as Imatinib/Dasatinib and Sertraline/Escitalopram, same-target pairs are separated from cross-target pairs with Cohen’s 𝑑 = 1.83 (Mann-Whitney 𝑝 < 10−6), with 100% of scaffold-hop pairs scoring above the cross-target median. HFP improves virtual screening AUROC over Morgan fingerprints on LIT-PCBA (0.524 vs 0.481, winning 10 of 15 targets) and MUV (0.596 vs 0.534, winning 14 of 17 targets, non-overlapping 95% CIs). The approach is backbone-agnostic: we validate two NNP backbones (Egret-1 and MACE-OFF23) and show both produce effective embeddings with complementary strengths. The entire pipeline was completed for under $400 on cloud infrastructure. These results establish NNP hidden states as a practical source of physics-informed molecular descriptors, with particular utility for scaffold-hopping campaigns where topological methods fail.

papers.title: Investigating the Effects of Surface Chemistry and Pore Structure in Grafted PEM Fuel Cell Catalyst Layers
papers.abstract: The carbon support surface chemistry strongly influences ionomer interactions, water management, and electrochemical performance in polymer electrolyte fuel cell catalyst layers; however, studies that decouple these effects from Pt particle size remain limited. Here, diazonium grafting is applied to commercial 40 wt% Pt/Vulcan and Pt/Ketjenblack catalysts to introduce five aryl functionalities (–NO2,–NH2,–CF3,–COOH,–SO3H) spanning a wide range of polarities and wettabilities without altering Pt dispersion. Ex situ characterization (x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, thermogravimetric analysis, N2 physisorption, contact angle, and dynamic vapor sorption) confirms successful functionalization and shows that grafting on Ketjenblack occurs preferentially at external surfaces, reducing pore accessibility. In 5 cm2 single-cell tests, nitrogen-containing functionalities reduce cathode proton transport resistance, increasing current density at 0.7 V (1.20 vs 1.01 A cm-2, I/C=0.6). For hydrophilic and hydrophobic groups, optimal performance depends strongly on the ionomer-to-carbon ratio: hydrophilic functionalities enhance performance at low I/C (0.1) but become detrimental at higher I/C (0.6) due to increased water retention and unfavorable ionomer interactions. These effects are amplified for porous Ketjenblack, where pore blockage offsets gains from surface modification. These findings establish that surface functionalization and support porosity cannot be optimized independently, and suggest that next-generation mesoporous carbon supports could incorporate pore architectures compatible with surface modification.

papers.title: Chemoenzymatic Enantioselective Kinetic Resolution of γ-Nitro Chiral Alcohols: Efficient Access to Enantioenriched Cyclopropanes
papers.abstract: Lipase-catalyzed kinetic resolution offers an environmentally benign approach for the synthesis of enantioenriched chiral building blocks. Herein, we report an efficient kinetic resolution of racemic 3-nitro-1-aryl propanols using commercially available lipases at notably low catalyst loading, achieving excellent enantioselectivities (upto 97% ee). The synthetic utility of the enantioenriched products has been demonstrated through their transformation into enantiomeric pure 2-nitrocyclo propyl benzene derivatives.

papers.title: Shape-anisotropic artificial cells to uncover the impact of membrane curvature on protein aggregation
papers.abstract: Artificial cells are increasingly used to mimic and study cellular functions from a bottom-up perspective. However, their typically spherical geometry lacks the shape diversity of living cells. Cellular membranes adopt diverse shapes and morphologies to form membrane-bound organelles and carry out essential cellular processes such as movement, growth, and signaling. Therefore, we fabricate here shape-anisotropic artificial cells with both positive and negative membrane curvatures, and we demonstrate their potential by investigating the behavior of aggregating huntingtin protein at curved lipid membranes. The artificial cells consist of a shape-anisotropic microgel scaffold covered with a lipid bilayer. Encapsulating mutant huntingtin exon 1 protein in our anisotropic artificial cells led to its aggregation at the lipid membrane interface. We used fluorescent proteins as Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) probes to follow protein assembly and found that stronger negative curvatures enhanced protein aggregation the most and provided aggregates with a higher structural order. Moreover, protein aggregation at membranes reduces membrane fluidity. Hence, our shape-anisotropic artificial cells indicate that the sign and strength of curvature direct protein assembly, highlighting the importance of microscopic membrane curvatures in modulating membrane-mediated protein aggregation.

papers.title: Highly Amplified Enantioselective Recognition using Diastereomeric Fluorophore-Nanocellulose Adsorption Complexes
papers.abstract: Diaminodicyanoquinodimethanes is a family of molecules that exhibit enhanced fluorescence in the aggregate and solid states. Enantiomers of a novel chiral derivative, 7,7- bis (2hydroxyphenyl)ethylenediamino-8,8-dicyanoquinodimethane (( RR )BHPEDQ, ( SS )BHPEDQ) are shown to manifest fluorescence based enantioselective recognition of mandelic acid (MA); enantioselectivity factor ( ef ) of ~ 3 is obtained with nmols of the analyte. Relative stability of the complexes with ( D )MA and ( L )MA determined by fluorescence studies, is supported by CD and NMR experiments, and ab initio computations are used to model the intermolecular interactions. A prominent amplification of the ef is realized using the diastereomeric adsorption complexes of ( RR )BHPEDQ and ( SS )BHPEDQ with nanocellulose (NC), exploiting concomitantly, the enhanced fluorescence of the immobilized fluorophore and the chirality of cellulose. The high ef of 15 – 47 achieved at μM concentrations of the analyte and the sensor (~ 2 – 10 nmols of each), are unprecedented. A critical observation is that the weaker of the diastereomeric complexes elicits the higher ef values, amplified by more than an order of magnitude. Generality of the new paradigm for ef amplification is illustrated using several analyte enantiomers. Utility of the approach in the sensitive estimation of enantiomeric excess ( ee ) in mixtures is also demonstrated.

papers.title: Electronic Structure and Chiroptical Signatures of a Singlet Biradicaloid Beryllium Dimer
papers.abstract: We report the computational characterization of a novel symmetric binuclear beryllium complex supported by the ortho-hydroxy-benzothio-morpholide (oH-btm) ligand . Density functional theory (DFT) calculations at the TPSS/def2-TZVP level reveal a unique dimer featuring a direct, non-bridged Be–Be bond with a distance of 2.138 Å . Energy Decomposition Analysis (EDA) quantifies the interaction energy at -53.68 kcal/mol, stabilized by a significant orbital contribution of -38.51 kcal/mol and electrostatic attraction of -60.39 kcal/mol. Topological analysis of the electron density (QTAIM) confirms a (3,-1) bond critical point between the metal centres, while Electron Localization Function (ELF) analysis identifies a disynaptic V(Be, Be) basin with a population of 1.834 e, definitively characterizing the interaction as a formal covalent single bond. Furthermore, a high Fractional Orbital Density (FOD) of 2.0 localized on the beryllium core indicates significant multi-reference character, describing the complex as a stable singlet biradicaloid. Simulated absorption (TD-DFT) and Electronic Circular Dichroism (ECD) spectra reveal a prominent metal-cantered HOMO → LUMO transition in the visible region at 685.4 nm (f = 0.454), providing a distinctive optical signature for the direct Be–Be bond. These findings suggest that the oH-btm scaffold effectively isolates and stabilizes low-valent Be(I) centres through robust O, S-chelation, expanding the fundamental understanding of group 2 metal-metal bonding.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Inevitability of Biological Complexity: Resolution of Orgel’s Paradox through Partition Dynamics
papers.abstract: We prove that biological complexity emerges as thermodynamic inevitability from partition operations in bounded phase space. Orgel’s paradox—the circular dependency between information, catalysis, and metabolism—is resolved by identifying partitioning as more fundamental than any biochemical component. We establish the Charge Emergence Theorem: electric charge does not exist as intrinsic property but emerges from partitioning; unpartitioned matter has no charge. Electron transport partitioning generates charge as consequence, not precondition. Probability analysis establishes partition-first scenarios (P ∼ 10−6) exceed information-first scenarios (P ∼ 10−150) by factor 10144—not a quantitative but categorical difference. Membranes evolved as partition scaffolding, not compartmentalization structures; their measured potential (∼ −70 mV) emerges from partitioning. Nucleic acids evolved as partition structures generating charge (validated by C ∼ 300 pF capacitance), with information storage as evolutionary secondary function. Universal homochirality (L-amino acids, D-sugars, righthanded DNA) follows from electron spin coupling to

papers.title: Directing Assembly of Mesoscale Multi-Shell Morphologies of DNA Origami Crystals
papers.abstract: Nature builds hierarchically ordered materials, such as seashells, wood, and bones, through spatially and temporally regulated growth. Mimicking such capabilities in creating synthetic systems remains challenging, particularly in achieving multiscale organizations with the desired nanoscale arrangements and material morphology. Here, we introduce a DNA-based self-assembly strategy for constructing diverse multi-shell mesoscale morphologies from nanoscale lattices, enabling prescribed structural and compositional three-dimensional (3D) material mesoscale patterns. Using DNA origami frames as modular monomers, we direct anisotropic epitaxial growth through addressable DNA frame binding motifs and encapsulate nanoparticles (NPs) in desired 3D patterns. Sequential monomer addition under thermodynamically favorable conditions enables shell growth through heterogeneous nucleation while minimizing unwanted homogeneous nucleation. We demonstrate that DNA-encoded addressability enables epitaxial shell growth along specific lattice directions, yielding crystals with multilayered mesoscale organization, including tube-like (sushi roll) and plate-like (macaron) morphologies. Shell-specific NP lattice configurations and compositions are achieved through addressable and differentiated placement of NPs within each shell, as validated by small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) and cross-sectional scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). We further demonstrate an addressable release of NPs and reveal that shell modulates NP release kinetics. Together, these findings establish a modular platform for bottom-up fabrication of DNA origami crystals with programmable mesoscale morphologies, nanoscale structure, composition, and transport properties.

papers.title: Machine Learning-assisted Discovery of Unconventional Molybdenum Nitride Nano-facets as Hydrogen Evolution Electrocatalysts
papers.abstract: Transition-metal nitrides (TMNs) are promising electrocatalysts owing to their unique electronic structures and surface properties. Yet, the formation of metastable phases during particle growth is unavoidable in the traditional synthesis of TMNs. These metastable phases cannot be holistically depicted by conventional phase diagrams. Here, we use density functional theory (DFT) calculations in conjunction with thermodynamic analysis to establish particle-size-dependent phase diagrams for Mo nitrides (MoxNy), including both metastable and thermodynamically stable phases. To accelerate the identification of energetically favourable high-Miller-index facets of Mo nitrides, we complement our DFT approach with a machine learning (ML) model trained on computed results for low-Miller-index facets. Furthermore, we compute hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) free energy diagrams using DFT for both low- and high-Miller-index facets, uncovering that several previously underexplored high-Miller-index facets of Mo nitrides are not only stable but also catalytically active for HER. Our study elucidates the correlation between nanoparticle dimension and phase stability, predicts unconventional facets of Mo nitrides that serve as good catalysts in HER, and ultimately presents a computationally guided strategy to efficiently navigate the material discovery landscape and further discover robust and efficient catalysts for green energy conversion schemes.

papers.title: Quantum chemical energy-based cation-π interaction recovers protein-ligand docking poses in cationic pocket
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of ligand binding poses on protein is crucial for drug discovery. Current state-of-the-art methods recover fewer than 60% poses of crystallographic cation-π interactions in cationic binding pockets and yield many false-positive interactions. Common empirical scoring functions, which often target the minimization of geometric deviations (e.g., RMSD), can produce nonphysical poses or overlook key interactions critical for binding, such as cation-π interactions. We introduce QNCIdock, which captures important cation-π interaction within the cationic binding pocket at the high quantum chemical level. QNCIdock employs machine learning models to efficiently learn explicit quantum chemical cation–π interactions and thereby predict docking pose probabilities as functions of geometric descriptors, learned cation–π interaction energies and additional classical force-field contributions. QNCIdock successfully recovers 86% of ligand poses characterized by pronounced cation–π interactions within the top eight ranked configurations, representing nearly a twofold improvement over current deep learning-based methods. Moreover, its computational overhead is negligible relative to that of conventional docking methods, allowing an integration into high-throughput virtual screening workflows.

papers.title: Lipid Membranes from First Principles: Partition Geometry, Phase Space Boundaries, and the Emergence of Biological Computation
papers.abstract: We derive lipid membranes from first principles without invoking empirical biochemistry, beginning from a single geometric axiom: all physical systems occupy bounded regions of phase space admitting partition and nesting. From this axiom we prove that any bounded aqueous system at finite temperature necessarily generates amphiphilic boundary structures—lipid membranes—as the minimum-cost partition boundaries separating interior from exterior phase space. The derivation proceeds in four stages. First, we establish that bounded phase space requires partition boundaries with finite depth M, and prove that the minimum-energy boundary in a polar solvent is a bilayer of molecules with dual partition affinity (amphiphiles). Second, we derive the geometry of the lipid bilayer—thickness, area per lipid, bending modulus, and spontaneous curvature—from the compression cost of maintaining distinguishable leaflets. Third, we prove that membranes are not passive barriers but active computational surfaces: each lipid executes partition operations through conformational oscillations, and the collective membrane dynamics implements a categorical processor with temperature-dependent resolution. Fourth, we establish that membrane phase behaviour—gel, liquidordered, liquid-disordered—corresponds to distinct partition regimes, with lipid rafts emerging as regions of local partition extinction analogous to superconducting domains. The framework yields quantitative predictions matching experimental measurements: bilayer thickness d = 4.0 ± 0.2 nm, area per lipid AL = 0.64 ± 0.04 nm2, bending modulus κ = 20 ± 2 kBT , lateral diffusion coefficient D = 1–10 µm2/s, and gel-to-fluid transition temperature Tm = 314 ± 2 K for DPPC. All results follow from partition geometry with zero free parameters fitted to membrane data. The membrane emerges not as a contingent product of chemical evolution but as a geometric necessity of bounded phase space in polar solvent.

papers.title: Derivation of Nucleic Acid Structure from Partition Operations on Bounded Phase Space
papers.abstract: We derive nucleic acid structure from partition operations on bounded dynamical systems without invoking quantum mechanics or molecular biology.
