Beginning from the Bounded Phase Space Law—that all physical systems occupy finite phase space volumes admitting partition and nesting—we prove that electron transport in bounded systems necessarily generates four distinguishable partition states. These states correspond exactly to the four nucleotide bases A, T, G, C. We establish the Charge Emergence Theorem: elec-tric charge is not an intrinsic property of matter but emerges from partitioning; unpartitioned matter has no charge. The Composition Theorem proves that binding reduces partition depth, with the deficit released as binding energy—explaining base pairing as partition completion rather than electrostatic attraction. The double-helix architecture emerges as the minimal structure providing dual-partition stabilization. Experimental validation includes: (i) measured DNA capacitance C ∼ 300 pF derives from partition-generated charge; (ii) base pairing energies ∆G ∼ 2–3 kcal/mol equal partition depth deficits; (iii) helix geom-etry satisfies partition stability constraints. Cardinal coordinate transformation ϕ : {A, T, G, C} → R2 maps partition operators to geometric space, enabling information density Igeometric/Ilinear = Θ(log n). All results follow from two axioms with zero free parameters.

papers.title: On the Consequences of Categorical Partitioning in
papers.abstract: Peptide identification in tandem mass spectrometry relies on spectral matching against sequence databases, limiting discovery of novel peptides and requiring platform-specific calibration. We present a dual-modality framework for database-free peptide sequence reconstruction combining thermodynamic droplet encoding with categorical fragmentation network analysis. The framework maps MS/MS spectra to three-dimensional S-entropy coordinates (Sk, St Se) derived from physicochemical properties (hydrophobicity, molecular volume, electrostatics), then converts ions to thermodynamic droplets generating characteristic wave patterns amenable to computer vision analysis. Hierarchical fragmentation constraints validate fragment-parent relationships through five physical principles: spatial containment (64% ś 4% overlap), wavelength hierarchy (fragments 22% parent size), energy conservation (80% retained), phase coherence (perfect lock, Cϕ = 1.0), and charge redistribution (correlation R = 0.52 with S-entropy). Validation on 1,000+ spectra achieves 91% ś 4% hierarchical consistency, with 100% bijectivity (reconstruction error = 0) confirming information preservation. Categorical fragmentation network analysis reveals peptide ladders as phase-locked oscillatory cascades with scale-free topology (P(k) ∼ κ−γ , γ = 2.3 ś 0.4), enabling PTM localization via phase discontinuity detection: 88.7% accuracy versus 61.3% for MaxQuant, with 23Ö computational speedup for tri-phosphorylated peptides. Platform independence is achieved through categorical invariance: ladder topology features (b/y series completeness, complementarity, regularity) exhibit coefficient of variation < 2.1% across four instrument platforms (Waters Synapt, Thermo Orbitrap, Sciex TripleTOF, Bruker timsTOF). Zeroshot model transfer (train on Orbitrap, test on Waters) maintains 89.3% sequence determination accuracy, versus 54.7% for intensity-based methods requiring per-platform calibration. Sequence reconstruction via minimum-entropy Hamiltonian path traversal through fragment graphs (mean 100 ś 50 nodes, 300 ś 350 edges) achieves 42% ś 18% partial match rate without database queries, with hierarchical constraints improving accuracy by +18 percentage points.

papers.title: Reductive Deoxygenation of Aromatic Aldehydes and Ketones with Boron Triiodide
papers.abstract: Deoxygenation of carbonyls is an area of value in synthetic transformations because it allows for traceless utilization of carbonyl chemistry, a mainstay in synthetic manipulations. Since oxygenation patterns are common in biological settings, deoxygenation can also be used to valorize biologically-derived feedstocks such as lignin. Herein, we describe the use of potassium borohydride and iodine, two common and benchtop stable reagents, to generate boron triiodide in situ, which performs full deoxygenation of aryl aldehydes and ketones. For aldehydes, benzyl iodide products are formed, whereas for ketones the methine is produced. Byproducts upon workup are low toxicity boric acid and iodide salts, making the process practical and appealing for a wide range of applications.

papers.title: Evaluation of net reaction heat in photochemical processes excluding heat input from irradiation
papers.abstract: We have established a procedure for evaluating net reaction heat generated by photochemical processes. As a representative example, photochemical Wohl-Ziegler bromination was selected. Its reaction heat was measured independently of heat input from irradiation using an EasyMax system. Such precise evaluation can facilitate safe and efficient scale-up of photochemical reactions.

papers.title: Bench-Stable Iron Bipyridine Complexes as Long-Lived Catalysts for the Hydrodefluorination of Arenes at Room Temperature
papers.abstract: The iron(II) complex [Fe( tBu bipy)OTf 2 ] ( tBu bipy = 4,4’-ditertbutyl-2,2’-bipyridine, OTf = CF 3 SO 3 - ) was found an efficient and bench-stable precatalyst for the hydrodefluorination (HDF) of arenes upon in situ activation with NaHBEt 3 employing H 2 SiPh 2 as H source at room temperature. The identity of the bipy ligand as well as of the X type ligands in the precatalyst were key to enable high efficiency for the process. Polyfluorinated arenes containing a different number of fluorine atoms in different positions were hydrodefluorinated to afford exclusive products from single HDF or mixtures of arenes from single and sequential HDF. The system showed a remarkable efficiency for 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoroanisole, for which a TON of 31.6 was obtained at room temperature. The efficiency of the system increased at high temperature, catalyzing up to 5 HDF cycles for hexafluorobenzene at 100 °C. The highest catalytic efficiency was found for tetrafluoroarenes, followed by tri- and perfluorinated arenes. A marked preference for fluorine atoms located between C–F and C–H bonds was observed in tetra- and trifluoroarenes, the efficiency of the system being primarily governed by the number of fluorine atoms in this environment, while their relative positions determined the efficiency when the number was identical. Mechanistic experiments for the hydrodefluorination of 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoroanisole suggested that paramagnetic Fe(II) are responsible for catalysis. The high catalytic efficiency of the system was attributed to the extended lifetime of the catalyst resting states, arising from the robust five-membered chelate formed by the tBu bipy ligand, which prevented catalyst deactivation by ligand decoordination.

papers.title: A molecular ”thermometer” for measuring effective non-local exchange
papers.abstract: Non-local exchange (NLX) is a key ingredient for accurate density functional calculations, but its effective strength is often hard to quantify beyond simple global hybrids. To this end, we introduce a molecular probe based on the isomerization of hexaethynylbenzene to carbo-benzene, a reaction with exceptional sensitivity to exchange effects. Using the isomerization energy, we define a simple relative measure, 𝑡 X , that gauges the effective NLX of a method on a scale ranging from 0 for the local density approximation to 100 for Hartree-Fock. Across a broad set of density functional approximations, 𝑡 X closely tracks the formal Hartree-Fock exchange content of global hybrids, while revealing that most common GGAs, meta-GGAs, and global hybrids still provide too little effective exchange. Several range-separated hybrid, double hybrid, and some local hybrid functionals perform much better and closely approach the near-basis-set-limit coupled-cluster reference value of 𝑡 X = 60. The 𝑡 X values of various semiempirical quantum mechanical and machine-learned interatomic potential methods indicate that they empirically account for NLX effects to a varying degree. Thus, the proposed reaction serves as a compact thermochemical benchmark for assessing and developing methods that aim to reliably describe non-local exchange.

papers.title: Direct Observation of a Cross-Coupling Catalyst Intermediate via Single-Molecule Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Single-molecule measurements on molecular catalysts are uniquely poised to allow observation of unsynchronized chemical dynamics and transient intermediates that are not observable using traditional bulk techniques. However, single-molecule fluorescence spectroscopy is typically performed at nanomolar concentrations, far lower than typical synthetic conditions. Here, we use nanophotonic zero mode waveguides (ZMWs) to enable observation of the dynamics of a single operational catalyst under synthetically relevant reaction conditions. We deploy ZMWs to perform the direct observation of a previously hypothesized intermediate of Pd-PEPPSI (Pyridine-Enhanced Precatalyst Preparation, Stabilization, and Initiation), a well-known molecular C–C cross-coupling catalyst, by using a fluorescently labeled ligand to report on ligand binding and dissociation. Kinetic analysis of single-catalyst ligand dynamics reveals how the presence of cross-coupling reactants alters the underlying mechanism. This paradigm for single-molecule investigation of molecular catalysts at synthetically relevant concentrations is general for investigation of a wide variety of ligand and reactant dynamics.

papers.title: Trace-metal-assisted flash synthesis for fast-charging graphite anodes
papers.abstract: Graphite has remained the dominant anode material in lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), powering portable electronics and electric vehicles (EVs). However, sluggish Li+ diffusion kinetics in natural and synthetic graphite can severely limit charging rates. Overcoming this bottleneck requires the rational design of graphite architectures that enable rapid Li+ transport in LIBs. Here, we disclose a trace-metal-assisted flash (TMF) process for the millisecond synthesis of catalytic flashed graphite (CFGr) with exceptionally fast-charging capabilities. The TMF process induces in situ formation of trace nickel nanoclusters that catalyze ultrafast graphitization of amorphous carbon into highly ordered graphite within <1 s. Raman spectroscopy shows an exceedingly clean graphite material with ID/IG of 0.09, with calculations yielding a binding energy (Eb) of −2.297 eV, while diffraction reveals a sub-angstrom-level interlayer expansion (d002) of 3.4 Å. These afford an enhanced structural stability and Li+ accessibility. Consequently, optimized CFGr achieves a high reversible capacity of 347.4 mAh g−1 at 0.25 C and retains 158.8 mAh g−1 at 15 C with 80% capacity retention after 1000 cycles, outperforming the rate and cyclability of both commercial graphite and graphite prepared by flash Joule heating. The TMF route can replace conventional energy-intensive calcination, reducing energy use and emissions by over 80% and lowering the production cost of premium fast-charging synthetic graphite by ~80% to only US$0.84 kg−1. These findings establish a sustainable, scalable pathway to advance fast-charging graphite anodes into next-generation LIBs.

papers.title: Rapid extraction of acid-labile compounds into an aqueous phase using a mixer-settler under continuous flow conditions
papers.abstract: We have developed a methodology of rapid extraction under continuous flow conditions. Basic compounds with a tert-butoxycarbonyl protecting group, which are labile under acidic conditions, were extracted into an acidic aqueous phase by a mixer-settler under continuous flow conditions and immediately neutralized prior to their decomposition. This methodology could serve as a promising option for purifying drug substances during pharmaceutical production.

papers.title: Quantifying the Coherence Wall: FeMoCo Quantum Chemistry from 48 to 108 Qubits on IBM Heron r2
papers.abstract: We present a specialized noise-compensated computational pipeline for quantum chemistry on current NISQ hardware, comprising a multi-qubit extension of Aurora-DD, samplebased quantum diagonalization (SQD) with physical-symmetry post-selection, a classical DMRG multi-determinant ph-AFQMC route, and a Bayesian framework integrating DMRG priors with device-derived likelihoods. The distinguishing feature of the Aurora-DD component is a proxy observation paradigm, in which per-qubit phase corrections are inferred from bitstring quality indicators rather than from direct coherence measurements. Under the present Heron r2 conditions, this capability is required to recover the four-point spatial correlation scaling reported here at LUCJ depth ∼2,900. Using this pipeline, we obtain four results on the iron-molybdenum cofactor (FeMoCo). First, we report the first 108-qubit FeMoCo execution with a ph-AFQMC statistical standard error of ±0.67 mHa; this is not a chemical-accuracy claim, because the systematic phaseless bias remains approximately 1,103 mHa for single-determinant trials, but statistical precision is no longer the bottleneck at this scale. Second, the classical DMRG-MSD ph-AFQMC route achieves chemical accuracy (+1.07 mHa phaseless bias) at the 48-qubit scale. Third, four-point spatial correlation measurement shows monotonic amplitude decay with circuit depth (scale: 0.226 → 0.045). Fourth, an exhaustive Bayesian methodology search yields an out-of-fold ceiling of r ≈ 0.03 at 108 qubits, which we term a coherence wall—a conditional empirical observation under the specific Heron r2, shot-count, circuit-depth, and DMRG M = 800 reference conditions of this study, not a universal physical constant. Implementation details, IBM Quantum job IDs, and reference data are released publicly with this manuscript to enable independent verification.

papers.title: Quantifying the Coherence Wall: FeMoCo Quantum Chemistry from 48 to 108 Qubits on IBM Heron r2
papers.abstract: We present a specialized noise-compensated computational pipeline for quantum chemistry on current NISQ hardware, comprising a multi-qubit extension of Aurora-DD, samplebased quantum diagonalization (SQD) with physical-symmetry post-selection, a classical DMRG multi-determinant ph-AFQMC route, and a Bayesian framework integrating DMRG priors with device-derived likelihoods. papers.title: Passive Anti-Icing Strategies on Metallic Surfaces: A Review of Superhydrophobic and Slippery Liquid-Infused Coatings
papers.abstract: Ice accumulation on metallic surfaces presents persistent challenges across aerospace, energy, transportation, and infrastructure systems due to its impact on safety, efficiency, and structural integrity. In recent years, passive anti-icing strategies have gained significant attention as energyefficient alternatives to conventional deicing methods. This review examines the current state of passive icephobic surface engineering for metallic substrates, with a focus on superhydrophobic surfaces (SHS) and slippery liquid-infused porous surfaces (SLIPS). The fundamental mechanisms governing ice formation, including heterogeneous nucleation, wetting behavior, heat transfer, and ice adhesion, are first discussed to establish the key parameters influencing icing performance. SHS rely on micro/nanostructured roughness and low-surface-energy chemistry to reduce liquidsolid contact and promote droplet mobility, offering effective ice mitigation under dynamic droplet-impact conditions. However, their performance is limited by environmental instability, particularly under condensation and frosting, where wetting transitions lead to increased ice adhesion. In contrast, SLIPS employ a lubricated liquid interface that minimizes pinning and maintains low adhesion even in high-humidity environments, demonstrating superior performance under frosting conditions. Nevertheless, challenges related to lubricant depletion, durability, and long-term stability remain critical barriers to practical deployment. A comparative analysis highlights that SHS and SLIPS are optimized for different icing regimes rather than being directly interchangeable. Finally, future directions are outlined, emphasizing hybrid surface designs, improved durability, and scalable fabrication strategies for real-world applications on metallic systems.

papers.title: The Role of Electrochemically Reduced Tungsten in Deoxygenative Reactions
papers.abstract: Direct functionalization of carbonyl moieties in a deoxygenative fashion is emerging as a valuable synthetic tool in the preparation of organic compounds. Among the possible strategies, the use of transition metals provides access to formal carbonyl metathesis in a selective and efficient way. In particular, the use of tungsten has been underdeveloped despite its peculiar reactivity with oxygenated compounds. Hereby, the systematic investigation of cathodically reduced tungsten in deoxygenation reactions is presented. The reaction was performed in a continuous flow recirculation setup to circumvent technical limitations, streamlining the preparation protocol. The transformation was explored on different activated aldehydes, ketones, and diols (27 examples). Mechanistic investigation demonstrated the necessity of a thermal step to perform the C–O cleavage, as well as unprecedented evidence of an electron shuttling effect of W(IV) for the formation of ketyl radicals. Furthermore, Giese-like reactivity was accomplished when cinnamaldehydes were employed as substrates, revealing a convenient formation of p -terphenyl scaffolds (14 examples).

papers.title: CFD Analysis of CH4/CO2 Separation in a Zeolite Membrane Module
papers.abstract: The separation of CO2 from CH4 is important for natural gas purification and biogas upgrading. In this work, three-dimensional CFD simulations are performed to investigate the influence of inlet flow rate and internal hydrodynamics on CH4/CO2 separation in a tubular zeolite membrane module under experimentally relevant operating conditions. The complete shell-and-tube geometry is explicitly resolved, and the governing equations for mass, momentum, energy and species transport are solved in OpenFOAM using experimentally derived permeance values to represent membrane transport. The predicted CH4 molar fraction at the retentate outlet and CO2 molar flow rate at the permeate outlet reproduce the experimental trends over the investigated inlet flow rate range. The results show that increasing inlet flow rate reduces CH4 enrichment because of shorter residence times, while concentration polarization develops along the membrane and reaches up to about 12% at high flow rate and about 8% at low flow rate. Membrane use is also not axially uniform. At low flow rate, the first tenth of the membrane is used about five times more intensely than the last tenth, whereas at high flow rate the permeation remains nearly uniform along the active length. Streamline analysis further indicates that fluid originating from the high velocity core of the inlet has a greater tendency to permeate through the membrane. These results help clarify how inlet flow rate and internal hydrodynamics influence transport and separation performance in tubular zeolite membrane modules.

papers.title: Regime-Aware Model Selection for Reactive Transport with Asymptotic Completion
papers.abstract: Selecting an inappropriate transport model can introduce large errors in reactive flow prediction. We propose a regime-aware model selection framework for convection–diffusion–reaction (CDR) systems governed by the Péclet (Pe) and Damköhler (Da) numbers. The framework automatically identifies which combination of advection, diffusion, and reaction operators is physically valid for a given regime, and constructs stable reference trajectories using classical perturbation theory when standard numerical integration fails. At small Pe, a matrix-exponential solver provides an unconditionally stable reference via regular perturbation. At large Pe, a Van Dyke matched asymptotic expansion yields a composite solution with a boundary layer of thickness O(1/Pe). A stiff Radau solver handles high-Da nonlinearity where the asymptotic approximation breaks down. Model selection is performed by minimizing a joint residual-plus-rollout score against the regimeappropriate reference trajectory. Experiments on a 4 × 4 Pe-Da parameter grid and a cylindrical reactive-wall benchmark produce clean, physically interpretable regime maps with finite confidence margins across all conditions. A chemical source detection scenario shows that selecting the wrong model introduces source estimation errors exceeding four orders of magnitude, while the proposed framework stays below 0.25% error across all tested regimes, compared to a naive diffusion-only baseline that reaches 16,532%.

papers.title: The Mott-Jones Electron Crystal: Patterning Atomic Positions for Pseudogap Formation in Hume-Rothery Phases
papers.abstract: The valence electrons of Hume-Rothery intermetallics are envisioned to be so delocalized that together they approximate a freeelectron gas. And yet, electron count plays a key role in their structural preferences, with different structures exhibiting electronic pseudogaps at different numbers of electrons per atom. These features are generally attributed to the Mott-Jones (MJ) effect, in which the mixing of otherwise free electron states is induced by the presence of a periodic array of ions. This picture forges a connection between a structure’s unit cell dimensions and its preferred electron counts. Less clear, however, is how this relationship translates into the often complex local atomic configurations encountered in these materials. In this Article, we investigate this connection through the visualization of the partial electron densities associated with MJ planewave interactions. Over a series of structures with varying complexity (CuZn, AlCu3, AuAl2, Cu5Zn8, and Al4Ni3), a simple mechanism emerges. In each case, essentially the same partial electron density distribution is obtained, which we refer to as the BCC-derived Mott-Jones electron crystal. The atomic centers are placed within the channels in this density, corresponding to nodal surfaces in the underlying standing waves, with the different structures representing distinct ways of spreading atoms over these channels. These positions reinforce the splitting of s- and p- orbital character across the pseudogaps, while the contributions of additional reciprocal lattice vectors fine-tune this effect. We comment on the potential existence of other Mott-Jones electron crystal topologies, each with their own potential series of crystal structures.

papers.title: Overcoming the Energy Gap Law in Red Carbene-Metal-Amide Materials through Steric Carbene Engineering for Stable Exciplex OLEDs
papers.abstract: A carbene substituent engineering strategy has been introduced for quinoxaline-fused N-heterocyclic carbene (QuinNHC) metal-amide (CMA) emitters, enabling highly efficient and operationally stable red OLEDs. Systematic modification of the QuinNHC aryl arms at the meta- and para-positions with aryl and alkyl substituents reveals that 3,5-di-tert-butyl substitution delivers near-unity photoluminescence quantum yields and markedly suppressed non-radiative decay, effectively circumventing energy gap law limitations. Theoretical calculation and Huang-Rhys factor analysis reveal that the enhanced performance originates from suppression of key vibrational modes coupled to the bright singlet charge-transfer exciton, explaining the superior performance of the para-tert-butyl- and 3,5-di-tert-butyl substituted QuinNHC CMA materials. OLEDs based on the 3,5-di-tert-butyl CMA emitters exhibit bright orange-red to red emission at 596 and 620 nm. Maximum OLED external quantum efficiencies (EQE) reach 20% with minimal roll-off, retaining 11% EQE at luminance as high as 170,000 cd m-2, and achieving one of the longest reported CMA OLED operational lifetimes with LT97 = 140 h at 1000 cd m-2. This work establishes a CMA molecular design platform for deep-red to near-infrared organometallic TADF luminophores that overcomes intrinsic energy gap law constraints, advancing the development of stable, high-efficiency red OLEDs.

papers.title: Continuous Feedback at Scale: Closing the Instruction–Response–Feedback Loop in a Large Physical Chemistry Laboratory Course
papers.abstract: The classical structure of physical chemistry laboratory courses often relies on delayed, report- based assessment, which can hinder conceptual understanding and student engagement, particularly in large classes. In this study, we report the redesign of an undergraduate physical chemistry laboratory course aimed at closing the Instruction–Response–Feedback (I–R–F) loop through a scalable systematic implementation of continuous and structured feedback mechanisms. The course was offered to two cohorts of approximately 50 students each, one during the daytime and one during the evening, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Key elements included short post-laboratory assessments, weekly collective discussion sessions, and a final project in which students designed their own experimental scripts. Student self-assessment surveys and qualitative feedback collected at the beginning and end of the course indicate improvements in engagement, conceptual understanding, and perceived learning. The results show that effective closure of the feedback loop is feasible even in large laboratory classes and can significantly enhance the educational value of experimental physical chemistry courses.

papers.title: Sodium expulsion from sodium closo-hydroborates under electron beam induced bias
papers.abstract: Electron microscopy (EM) invites the opportunity to locally characterize the properties of solid-state electrolytes important for choreographing ion motion within next-generation solid-state batteries. Through the combination of inert gas transfer, cryogenic, time-resolved low-dose analytical electron microscopy, we observe that mixed-anion sodium closo -hydroborate, Na 2 (B 10 H 10 ) 0.5 (B­­­ 12 H 12 ) 0.5 (NBH), solid electrolyte suffers from electrostatic charging damage under bias of both transmission electron microscopes (TEM) and scanning electron microscopes (SEM). During the process of beam damage, crystalline ordering of NBH is lost, while particle morphology remains unchanged. In regions exposed to electron beams at a dose rate of 1-8 e - Å -2 s -1 , spectroscopy confirms vastly reduced sodium signal or even absent from irradiated NBH at total doses less than 80 e - Å -2 . Simultaneously, we detect the growth of sodium metal crystals on the unirradiated faces of NBH particles. An SEM experimental study revealed the maximum damage rate occurs at 2 keV with increasing energy prolonging the time before sodium extrudes. This work also highlights that cryogenic conditions, while highly effective in mitigating certain types of inelastic beam damage, are not the panacea for eluding beam sensitivity. Rather, comprehensive awareness of the underlying physics in competing damage mechanisms is paramount in condition selection for battery interface characterization.

papers.title: MULTI-LAYER SELF-LIMITING ELECTROSPRAY DEPOSITION USING VOLTAGE BIAS
papers.abstract: The self-limiting regime of electrospray deposition (SLED) is a highly adaptable means to coat complex 3D architectures and 2D templated surfaces. There are, however, drawbacks to this approach, including that (1) SLED coatings cannot be applied in multiple layers and (2) the generally-micron-scale thickness of SLED coatings is determined by the material and spray parameters, preventing nanoscale coatings such as those possible by atomic layer deposition or spin coating. This latter limitation can be circumvented by applying a secondary bias to the spray target, which reduces the SLED thickness and increases uniformity. Here, we demonstrate that the stepwise removal of bias can in turn result in the stepwise increase of the SLED thickness. We thereby demonstrate (i) trilayer polystyrene stacks with bias-controlled thickness, (ii) uniform trilayer coatings on a complex geometry, and (iii) mechanically robust nanocomposite using thermal capillary rise infiltration (CaRI) of electrosprayed bilayer films.

papers.title: Robust (n,m) Assignment of Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes from Electron Diffraction Patterns via Near-Neighbor Search and Cross-Check Correction
papers.abstract: The chirality (n,m) of single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) strongly influences their properties and growth behavior, creating a need for accurate and reproducible evaluation methods. Nanobeam electron diffraction (NBED) is a powerful approach for (n,m) assignment, but practical analysis is often affected by analyst-dependent steps, manual measurement errors, and sample tilt. Here, based on a previously reported calibration-free diffraction analysis framework, we developed a practical SWCNT chirality-assignment protocol that combines near-neighbor (n,m) search with cross-check correction under assumed manual measurement errors and tilt. Feature extraction and candidate screening were semi-automated using an ImageJ script and an Excel VBA macro, thereby reducing analysis time, improving reproducibility, and minimizing operator dependence. Using 2394 simulated NBED images covering CNT diameters of 0.4–2.3 nm, chiral angles of 0–30°, and tilt angles of 0.5–16.5°, with added noise, direct electron beam intensity, and beam-stop effects, the assignment accuracy improved from 71.6% for conventional TRUNC-based analysis to 97.7% with the proposed protocol. Errors in mean CNT diameter, mean chiral angle, and metallic CNT fraction were also nearly eliminated. The substantial improvement in assignment accuracy was primarily attributable to the newly introduced overlap ratio, which effectively reduced the ambiguity and instability present in the initial candidate discrimination.

papers.title: Dimensional crossover in ternary chalcohalide van der Waals crystals driven by the interplay of ionicity and topology
papers.abstract: Dimensionality is a concept tied to crystalline order, electronic states, and physical properties. While the chemical basis of dimensionality in inorganic 3D and 2D solids is known, the evolution of the 25 structure and physical states of 2D layers into 1D chains remains poorly understood. Here, we leverage solid solutions in the InTeI—InSeI series representing the emergent III–VI–VII van der Waals class to demonstrate the seamless chalcogen-driven dimensional crossover of the 2D layered phase (InTeI) to the sought-after 1D chain analogue (InSeI) that manifests helicity. Computational and experimental structures, bond valencies, binding energies, and Bader charges establish that bond ionicity scale with Se content which 30 define the electronic states and drive the stabilization of 1D helical chains from the more Te-rich 2D phase. This interplay between ionicity and dimensionality reconciles the structural evolution in III–VI–VII crystals and can be invoked to rationally design new low-dimensional materials.

papers.title: Functional-group-convergent synthesis of amides
papers.abstract: Amide bonds are ubiquitous in biology and synthetic chemistry, forming the backbone of peptides, proteins, pharmaceuticals, polymers, and natural products. Traditional amidation strategies typically rely on the inherent reactivity of carboxylic acids and amines, often requiring activating agents or pre-functionalized derivatives. Here, we report a functional-group-convergent (FGC) strategy for modular amide assembly from readily available starting materials. The method employs visible-light-mediated manganese-catalysed carbonylative amidation, proceeding via a synergistic radical–polar crossover cycle that merges radical and organometallic reactivity. Unactivated alkyl iodides, boronic acids, low-pressure carbon monoxide, and nitrogen-transfer reagents are converted directly into amides under mild conditions, with selective activation of C(sp3)–I bonds while preserving C(sp2)–I bonds. The approach tolerates diverse functional groups and enables 15N-labeled amide synthesis using isotopically enriched reagents. Its broad scope and chemoselectivity facilitate late-stage functionalization of complex drugs and natural products, exemplified by the efficient synthesis of Vorinostat and 15N-labeled (±)-Acoitremon.

papers.title: Stepwise Ring Expansion as a Biosynthetic Strategy for Macrocycle Construction
papers.abstract: Macrocyclic formation in natural products is typically understood to proceed through direct macrocyclization reactions. Here we demonstrate that complex macrocycles can instead be constructed through stepwise ring expansion of a pre-formed smaller scaffold. Genetic and biochemical analyses of luminamicin (1) biosynthesis revealed that a 10-membered ring is progressively transformed into a 14-membered macrocycle through two mechanistically distinct ring expansion steps. This process involves a cofactor-independent intramolecular acyl transfer and a radical-mediated oxidative rearrangement, which together reorganize a pre-assembled intermediate into the final macrocyclic framework. This stepwise remodeling strategy contrasts with canonical macrocyclization logic and provides a solution to the entropic and conformational constraints associated with the formation of large rings. More broadly, these findings establish stepwise ring expansion as a previously unrecognized biosynthetic strategy for constructing complex macrocycles and suggest new strategies for their chemical synthesis.

papers.title: Triethoxysilane-Catalyzed Hydroboration of Alkenes, Nitriles, Ketones and Esters: From Non-Covalent Interactions to a Hydrosilylation/Si-B Exchange Pathway
papers.abstract: Triethoxysilane was found an efficient precatalyst for the hydroboration of alkenes, nitriles, ketones and esters with pinacolborane (HBPin). The catalyst showed an excellent substrate scope including aromatic and aliphatic substrates affording the products in good to excellent yields. The system was found less efficient for the hydroboration of alkenes and Ealkenylboronate esters than that of alkynes, which could be traced back to the strength of the interactions between the multiple CC bonds of the substrates with HSi(OEt)3. The nature of the multiple CC bond (C=C vs C≡C) played the largest role in catalyst efficiency, the presence of a BPin substituent in the E-alkenylboronate esters not impacting the substrate conversion compared to that of terminal alkenes. The nature of aryl substituents in aromatic substrates exerted distinct effects on catalytic efficiency depending on the substrate class. Whereas the catalyst was sensitive to both the electronic and steric properties of terminal alkynes, catalytic efficiency in the hydroboration of aromatic nitriles was governed primarily by steric effects, with minimal sensitivity to electronic variation. Competition experiments allowed to unravel the catalyst preferences for the hydroboration of different types of functional groups, HSi(OEt)3 showing a significant preference for alkynes and alkenes over nitriles and ketones. Unlike in the HSi(OEt)3-catalyzed sequential hydroboration of alkynes, the fluorinated analog HSi(OCH2CF3)3 showed a comparable efficiency to HSi(OEt)3 for the hydroboration of nitriles, suggesting that the Lewis acidity at Si did not play a role in catalyst efficiency. The significant differences between alkynes and heteroatom-containing substrates could be traced back to the presence of a catalytically active species different from HSi(OEt)3 in the hydroboration of nitriles, ketones and esters. Additionally, intermediates from hydrosilylation of the multiple bond of nitriles were identified during catalytic turnover, supporting a mechanism involving H-Si bond addition across the multiple bond followed by Si-B exchange steps.

papers.title: Assessing Order in Liquid, Supercooled, and Crystalline Water
papers.abstract: Water has strong directional interactions and forms a network of hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) in aqueous solutions. In order to assess the nature of this network as a function of thermodynamic state, a generalized approach is introduced for enumerating the extended connectivity of H-bonding paths. By identifying and classifying rings formed from H-bonds where the donor-to-acceptor directionality can be considered, a ring summation factor metric can be constructed in a form comparable to the commonly used tetrahedral order parameter. This factor ranges between 0, where there is no closed path ring connectivity, and 1, where all potential H-bonds participate in unique closed paths. This new metric is used to explore the relative limits of water ordering in liquid, supercooled, and crystalline condensed phase systems. In liquid systems, network ordering is shown to depend on the specific state parameters and how different models for water perform at and outside of their commonly used conditions. As they are supercooled, water models that converge on a similar preferred crystalline form show a common ring distribution signature, indicating a universal characteristic ordering in the liquid environment preceding nucleation and crystal growth processes. The various crystalline ice polymorphs are observed to have unique degrees of order and distributions of ring sizes, and even different degrees of proton ordering can be identified using this approach. The detail of these findings allows for identification of and subsequent remedy of potential deficiencies in tetrahedrality for characterization of the structure of crystalline water.

papers.title: Digital Catalysis Platform (DigCat): A Gateway to Big Data and AI-Powered Innovations in Catalysis
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping catalysis research, yet its impact remains constrained by fragmented, heterogeneous, and non-standardized data. In this Commentary, we argue that the future of AI-driven catalysis depends critically on the development of data-centric infrastructures that integrate experimental results, theoretical insights, and literature knowledge. We highlight the Digital Catalysis Platform (DigCat) as an example of such an approach, combining large-scale curated datasets with tools for visualization, modeling, and machine learning. Building on this foundation, domain-specific AI agents enable automated data analysis, knowledge extraction, and catalyst design, transforming how researchers interact with catalytic data. We discuss how the convergence of big data, AI models, and automation may lead to closed-loop, autonomous discovery systems. Finally, we outline key challenges and opportunities in establishing reliable, interpretable, and scalable AI-driven workflows for catalysis in the data-rich era. Access DigCat at https://www.digcat.org.

papers.title: Model-informed strategies for mitigating platinum loss in polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cells
papers.abstract: Mitigating platinum loss in the cathode catalyst layer (CCL) of polymer electrolyte membrane (PEM) fuel cells remains a critical challenge for improving long-term durability. Computational modeling provides a powerful tool for evaluating mitigation strategies prior to experimental testing. Building upon our previously developed transient pore network model for platinum degradation, we systematically investigated microstructural and spatial design strategies enabled by the model’s pore-scale resolution. Microstructural modifications including variations in porosity and agglomerate size as well as spatial platinum distribution strategies were evaluated. Increasing porosity uniformly or near the membrane reduces total platinum loss but is detrimental to the performance, though introducing mid-CCL constrictions minimizes the performance sensitivity. Reducing agglomerate size enhances performance with negligible impact on degradation. Increasing platinum loading near the membrane by increasing particle sizes promotes more uniform degradation. A combined case study integrating the most favorable strategies demonstrates simultaneous improvements in the fuel cell performance, overall degradation, and degradation homogeneity relative to a base case. Overall, the results indicate that spatial and microstructural modifications can indeed provide effective ways to design more durable catalyst layers. Although individual strategies have distinct benefits and drawbacks, combining complementary approaches retains the advantages of each while minimizing their trade-offs. The limitations of the current study are discussed, along with directions for future experimental and modeling efforts aimed at translating these findings into the development of more durable catalyst layers for PEM fuel cells.

papers.title: The analysis of post-mortem fluorescent signatures in discarded cell lysate from DNA extractions: a comparative study between pig and human remains
papers.abstract: Post-mortem interval (PMI) estimation remains a complex yet crucial task in medico-legal death investigations, as accurate and reliable estimates could establish timelines and contextualize physical evidence. Taphonomic studies often use pig carcasses as human analogues, and while they perform well in some entomology experiments, recent comparative studies have shown interspecies differences in biomolecular degradation during decomposition. Further, few studies use fluorimetry, leaving the degradation of biological fluorophores understudied in both species. Herein, we integrated PMI analysis into DNA extraction protocols by probing typically discarded cell lysates, enabling multiple analyses from a single sample. Our dataset included human and pig remains: 50 biopsy punches collected from 14 human donors at the Research in Experimental and Social Thanatology (REST) facility in Québec, Canada and 21 biopsy punches from two pigs placed in Oshawa, Canada, with PMIs ranging from 0-1185 days (9.9-11281.7 accumulated degree days; ADD). An excitation-emission matrix was acquired for each lysate and deconvoluted using parallel factor analysis (PARAFAC) to identify individual fluorophores. PARAFAC models revealed similar fluorophores and time-dependent trends in both species. Tryptophan fluorescence decreased over time, while fluorescence between 400-500 nm increased as PMI progressed, attributed to an accumulation of fluorescent oxidation products and advanced glycation end-products. Although partial least squares discriminant analysis demonstrated fluorescence differences between species, principal component analysis did not yield species-specific groupings and displayed common PMI/ADD-related trends for both species. Our findings suggest that interspecies differences are not primarily driven by PMI/ADD, and that pig carcasses are a useful human analogue in taphonomic studies using fluorimetry.

papers.title: Giant barocaloric effect from spin crossover in a green nitroprusside framework†
papers.abstract: The interest in spin crossover for solid-state cooling is growing. We investigate the spin crossover transitions of [Fe(pyridine)2Fe(CN)5NO] and [Fe(pyrazine)Fe(CN)5NO] by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, high-pressure X-ray diffraction, magnetometry, and high-pressure calorimetry. The dehydrated form of the latter compound shows a reversible cooling effect (∆Tad,rev) of ∼15K at 1.2 kbar. This is high in the context of other reported spin-crossover barocalorics, and competitive within the field at large. The excellent performance results from a large barocaloric coefficient (dT1/2/dp = 35K kbar−1). In addition, the one-pot synthesis is simple and free from toxic solvents.

papers.title: Reconsidering molecular docking practices in aptamer research
papers.abstract: Molecular docking is increasingly used to study aptamer–target interactions, yet most studies rely on computationally generated aptamer structures rather than experimentally determined ones. This approach presents fundamental limitations, including structure prediction without the target molecule and the common conversion of RNA models into DNA by deleting the 2′-hydroxyl group, while neglecting the intrinsic differences between A-form RNA and B-form DNA. Using the theophylline aptamer, for which crystal structures are available for both RNA and DNA forms, we systematically examine these issues through a step-by-step analysis of the standard docking workflow. Docking-based selectivity predictions against caffeine, together with molecular dynamics simulations, further demonstrate the inconsistency and limited reliability of this strategy. Overall, current docking practices, when applied without experimental structures, can produce unreliable and potentially misleading interpretations of aptamer binding mechanisms.

papers.title: Improving Activity and Stability of Candida boidinii Formate Dehydrogenase Through Rational Active Site Engineering
papers.abstract: Formate dehydrogenases represent a highly attractive tool for nicotinamide cofactor regeneration to drive biocatalytic reductions and oxygenations by NADH-dependent oxidoreductases with formate as cheap, atom-economic, terminal reductant. However, despite the clear benefits over other recycling systems, native FDHs remain rather unpopular, mainly due to their intrinsic, low specific activity. While the active site architecture is generally highly conserved across many FDHs from very diverse origins, smaller patterns of dissonance in the active site's vicinity can serve as hotspots for the rational design of more effective variants. In this study, we have created a series of Candida boidinii FDH variants incorporating non-consensus amino acids found in Saccharomyces cerevisiae FDH. A double mutant (C23S/F285D) was identified that exhibits a significantly higher specific activity, an overall more desirable pH and temperature profile, and an improved stability profile.

papers.title: Hierarchical Quantum Mechanical Validation of a Novel Allosteric USP7 Inhibitor via DLPNO-CCSD(T) and Local Energy Decomposition Analysis
papers.abstract: Ubiquitin-specific protease 7 (USP7/HAUSP) is a validated oncology target whose inhibition reactivates p53-mediated apoptosis by destabilising its negative regulator MDM2. We report a tiered computational framework to identify and rigorously validate a novel allosteric USP7 inhibitor.. A focused library of 30 pyrimidine–sulfonamide derivatives was rationally designed using a combinatorial substitution strategy and screened against the allosteric sub-pocket of USP7 (PDB: 5N9R) using AutoDock Vina 1.2.3. Ligand L14 (C29H42FN7O3S; MW 587.75g/mol) emerged as the lead candidate with a binding affinity of −9.78 kcal/mol. Geometry optimisation at the ωB97X-D3/def2-SVP level (ORCA 5.0) yielded a binding energy of −71.70 kcal/mol. This was benchmarked by RI-MP2/def2-SVP (−40.78 kcal/mol) and confirmed by gold-standard DLPNO-CCSD(T)/def2-SVP (−71.38 kcal/mol; deviation = 0.32 kcal/mol), within the commonly accepted chemical accuracy threshold of 1.0 kcal/mol. Local Energy Decomposition (LED) analysis at the coupledcluster level established that the interaction is predominantly electrostatic in character (72.9%), supplemented by exchange (22.3%) and London dispersion (2.7%). Coordinate-level structural analysis confirmed that L14 engages the allosteric sub-pocket defined by ASP295 and PHE409, rather than the canonical catalytic triad. ADMET profiling demonstrated acceptable drug-likeness (one Lipinski violation), a predicted LD50 of 645 mg/kg (GHS Class 4), consistent with low acute toxicity, and an overall ProTox-3.0 safety score of 85.4%. To our knowledge, This is the first application of gold-standard DLPNO-CCSD(T) LED analysis to a USP7 allosteric inhibitor..

papers.title: PDB Manipulation Suite (PDBMS): A browser-based toolkit for PDB file manipulation, molecule building and biophysical analysis, easily extendable via reasoning models
papers.abstract: We present here the PDB Manipulation Suite (PDBMS), a modular hub of web apps and platforms designed for the seamless creation, edition, and analysis of biomolecular coordinate files. The PDBMS is written entirely for client-side execution in web browsers, providing a "zero-footprint" environment available out of the box at https://pdbms.altervista.org/ with zero installs, no downloads, and no registration. This architecture ensures that all calculations occur locally, meaning that sensitive data never leaves the user’s machine—critical for proprietary structural data—while maintaining the responsiveness of a local application. The suite is organized into specialized sub-platforms: PDBMS-tools for rapid structure editing, renumbering, format conversion and data mapping; Web-PackMol for the assembly of complex molecular systems; Web-MDA and the Conformational Ensemble Inspector for the deep analysis and inspection of molecular dynamics trajectories, BioEmu predictions, docking poses, and other kinds of ensembles. Example functionalities include a variety of analyses to infer structural details, dynamics and interactions across molecules and time or ensemble indexes, to aid in the visualization of various kinds of data including AlphaFold 3 confidence scores and outputs from modern NMR spectroscopy pipelines. Since the source code is inherently open and was developed largely with AI reasoning models at Google’s AI Studio, it is extremely easy to modify or add new functionalities at will. We demonstrate this by providing tools to assist the editing and visualization of outputs from modern software like NMRtist and Sparky; and also demonstrate how an AI agent built into the Web-MDA app can provide new functionalities on request. We hope PDBMS will provide an environment for structural bioinformaticians and molecular modelers to perform complex tasks while maintaining absolute data confidentiality, extreme portability across devices and operating systems, and maximal flexibility.

papers.title: A Modular, Versatile Rapid-Injection NMR System for Kinetic Analyses and Structure Elucidations
papers.abstract: Rapid-Injection NMR spectroscopy (RI-NMR) is a powerful technique which enables the accurate collection of kinetic data by initiating fast reactions within the spectrometer itself. Despite the promise of this technique as a tool for mechanistic analysis, the broad adoption of RI-NMR is hindered by the lack of cost- and space-efficient instrument designs which can be operated with negligible interference to the NMR facility. Herein, we introduce a streamlined RI apparatus which is compatible with most NMR spectrometers, requires no modification of the NMR instrument or probe, and may be easily transported to and from the laboratory. The injection volume is easily adjusted, and multiple injections of a single reagent or multiple reagents is trivial to perform. To highlight the advantages of our RI-NMR design, we apply RI-NMR to the investigation of reactions at non-ambient temperature, systems requiring sequential injections of reagents, and for the analysis of a multi-step reaction sequence in a single experiment.

papers.title: TWCS++: Uncertainty-Aware Consensus Scoring for Data-Scarce Virtual Screening
papers.abstract: Virtual screening for targets with fewer than 50 known actives remains an unsolved problem: individual classifiers memorize dominant chemotypes, docking scoring functions lack predictive power, and no method provides calibrated confidence estimates. We present TWCS-+-, a consensus scoring framework that addresses all three failure modes through (i) pretrained molecular representations (Uni-Mol, MolICLR) as frozen feature extractors alongside classical fingerprints, (ii) precision-weighted aggregation where each model’s contribution scales inversely with its predictive uncertainty, and (iii) conformal prediction intervals providing distribution-free coverage guarantees. Validated on NUDT5 (20 actives, ER-+- breast cancer target) and four additional targets spanning NUDIX enzymes and unrelated protein families, TWCS+-+- achieves scaffold-split AUC = 0.938 on NUDT5 with the smallest degradation from random-split metrics (A = 0.062) of any method tested. Retrospective recovery experiments show TWCS-+-+- identifies 3.8/5 held-out actives in the top 3% of ranked libraries, versus 2.6/5 for the best individual classifier. Scaling analysis reveals TWCS++ advantage grows as training data shrinks: at n = 5, TWCS-++ outperforms the best individual model by 5.4%. Applied to NUDT5, the pipeline identifies 10 candidates (80% novel scaffolds, zero Lipinski violations) with integrated ADMET profiling across 41 endpoints. All code and data are publicly available.

papers.title: MalarIA, A Machine Learning Pipeline for De Novo Identification of Oral, G6PD-Safe and Pediatric-Compatible Anti-Malarial Candidates via Latent Diffusion, Contrastive Learning and Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification
papers.abstract: Malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum kills approximately 600,000 people annually, predominantly children under 5 in sub-Saharan Africa. Emerging resistance to artemisinin-based combination therapies urgently requires novel anti-malarial compounds. We present MalarIA, an open-source computational pipeline combining: (1) a Random Forest model achieving rho=0.845 [95%CI: 0.840-0.849] in 5-fold cross-validation (N=23,202 ChEMBL P. falciparum IC50 measurements); (2) a Fourier Transformer VAE with Latent Diffusion (Classifier-Free Guidance) for de novo molecular generation with malaria-specific constraints enforced at generation time (oral bioavailability TPSA<90, G6PD safety, pediatric compatibility MW<450 Da); (3) molecular docking on PfCRT (PDB: 6UKJ) and PfDHFR (PDB: 1J3I) via AutoDock Vina v1.2.5; and (4) a V2.2 framework adding contrastive learning (triplet loss), Bayesian uncertainty quantification (500-tree RF), and topological latent space exploration (DBSCAN clustering). External validation using MAIP (consensus model from multiple pharmaceutical partners, EMBL-EBI, trained on 6.5 million bioactivity values) identified two priority candidates: MalarIA-009 (MAIP=82.33, at the top 1% threshold) and V22-008 (MAIP=85.47, within the top 1%), reproduced across three independent MAIP submissions. V2.2 Bayesian high-confidence candidates (uncertainty<0.3) achieve superior docking: PfCRT best=-9.47 kcal/mol vs -8.63 in V1. All results are purely computational predictions. No experimental validation has been performed. Structures available upon request.

papers.title: Structure-activity relationship study of antimicrobial peptide with cross-kingdom activity
papers.abstract: The widespread emergence of antibiotic-resistant pathogens poses a significant global health challenge and underscores the need for novel approaches to accelerate antimicrobial discovery. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have gained attention as promising candidates due to their broad-spectrum activity, including efficacy against multidrug-resistant bacterial strains. SAJO-2, an antimicrobial peptide developed by Sarojini and colleagues, features a tryptophan zipper-like motif incorporating a central DPhe-2-Abz unit, where 2-Abz functions as a conformationally constrained β-turn-inducing peptidomimetic scaffold. Modification of SAJO-2 in prior joint work from our groups through differential fluorination enhanced its antimicrobial potency; however, it also increased susceptibility to enzymatic digestion by βtrypsin. To address this limitation, the current research focuses on improving the overall efficacy of SAJO-2 through the incorporation of D-amino acids, beta backbone modifications, and a bulky pentafluorinated amino acid residue. All modified peptides exhibit resistance to enzymatic degradation, while antimicrobial activity was retained to differing degrees across organisms.

papers.title: Generalizing the Geometry–Property Noncorrelation: ADescriptor Informativeness Index for Organic Molecules
papers.abstract: The recent study by Joy, Kraus, Ricks, and Ess ( Organometallics 2025, 44, 1566–1575) revealed a striking finding for transition metal chemistry: across 686 experimentally char acterized Pd-Me complexes, the Pd-C bond length shows no correlation whatsoever with bond dissociation energy ( R2 = 0.00), despite perfectly predicting the intact bond’s force constant ( R 2 = 0.92) and electron density ( R 2 = 0.99). This observation, which challenges a cornerstone of chemical intuition, raises a compelling question about its generality beyond transition metal systems. In the present work, we introduce the Descriptor Informativeness Index (DII), a quantitative metric that measures the fraction of achievable predictive accuracy retained by a given descriptor subset relative to a full-feature machine learning model. We apply this metric to 11,736 organic molecules from the QM9 dataset across six quantum chemical properties and two structurally distinct molecule classes. Our analysis reveals that organic molecules retain substantial geometric informativeness (DII geo = 0.33–0.80), in clear contrast to the Pd-Me system (DII geo ≈ 0.00). However, geometric informativeness is not uniform: it is systematically lower in aromatic molecules (mean DII geo = 0.465) than in aliphatic molecules (mean DII geo = 0.637), with the largest suppression observed for electronic properties. These results contextualize the elegant findings of Joy et al. within a broader spectrum of geometry–property relationships, suggesting that the degree to which geometric descriptors inform molecular properties is governed by the interplay between delocalization and the nature of the target property

papers.title: What Can Atomic Force Microscopy and Quartz Crystal Microbalance Tell Us About Membrane Disruption?
papers.abstract: We investigated the effects of methyl-β-cyclodextrin (MβCD) on supported lipid bilayers (SLBs) using a combined approach of Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) imaging, force–distance (F–D) measurements, and Quartz Crystal Microbalance with Dissipation (QCM-D). This multimodal strategy enabled simultaneous assessment of mechanical and mass-related changes, revealing disruption pathways that depend on membrane composition. AFM imaging showed time‑dependent defect nucleation, with cholesterol-containing bilayers exhibiting the most extensive structural damage. Force–distance analysis across POPC, POPC/POPE (1:1), POPC/DPPC (1:1), and POPC/Chol (7:3) bilayers demonstrated that shifts in median rupture force and changes in mechanical heterogeneity can be decoupled. Pure POPC bilayers exhibited mild softening, POPC/DPPC (1:1) bilayers maintained mechanical resilience, and POPC/POPE (1:1) bilayers underwent pronounced destabilization characterized by increased heterogeneity. Cholesterol-containing bilayers retained resistance to penetration despite selective removal of mechanically weak regions. Statistical evaluation confirmed these trends and highlighted distinct mechanical transitions. Overall, our results show that MβCD-induced disruption is governed by lipid composition, phase behavior, and intrinsic membrane stress.

papers.title: Elucidating Sodium-Ion Storage Mechanisms in Bowl-Shaped Hierarchical Porous Carbon Anodes: A Combined Solid-State NMR and EPR Approach
papers.abstract: Understanding sodium-ion storage in carbon anodes is essential for producing efficient batteries via the design of carbon architectures with optimized pores, defects, and surface area. Previous mechanistic studies have mainly focused on hard carbon anodes with poorly defined structures, leaving the structural correlation with sodium storage unexplored. This work investigates sodium-ion storage in bowl-shaped hierarchical porous carbon anodes using a combined magnetic resonance spectroscopy approach. The material exhibits hierarchical porosity, 917.5 m 2 /g surface area and delivers a reversible capacity of 250 mAh/g at 0.1 A/g in aqueous sodium-ion batteries (ASIBs). Solid state magic-angle spinning nuclear magnetic resonance probes the local chemical environments of Na + ions confined within the carbon pore network, revealing distinct interactions between Na + ions different carbon domains and pore environments. Complementary variable temperature continuous-wave electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy enables differentiation between weakly adsorbed Na + ions and strongly interacting sodium species through voltage-dependent line shape and linewidth analysis. These studies reveal the potential-dependent evolution of sodium storage processes: adsorption, insertion, and intercalation, with direct correlation to their electrochemical signatures. This work establishes structure-mechanism relationship between hierarchical carbon architecture and Na+ storage pathways, providing mechanistic insight beyond conventional hard carbon and guiding design of advanced anodes for ASIBs.

papers.title: Distribution of Relaxation Times as a Generalized Function: Atomic Spectra and Power-law Tails in Blocking-Electrode Impedances
papers.abstract: The distribution of relaxation times (DRT) model is widely used to deconvolve electrochemical impedance spectra into timescale distributions. However, standard DRT formulations assume integrable impedance. This condition is violated by electrochemical systems with blocking boundaries where diffusion or charge accumulation causes the low-frequency response to diverge. We formulate DRT inversion in the space of tempered distributions and derive a distributional Fuoss–Kirkwood boundary-value relation in S ′(R), under explicit analyticity, growth, and boundary-value assumptions on the strip continuation of the impedance. In this setting, the DRT is determined by the strip boundary values of the impedance, with Dirac atoms from simple poles, derivatives of Dirac masses from higher-order poles, and power-law tails from non-integrable low-frequency behavior. This formulation clarifies reported discrepancies for capacitive and diffusive systems by making the boundary-value convention explicit and separating distributional identities from pointwise evaluations. We derive closed-form distributional DRTs for generalized resistor-capacitor (RC) circuits, constant-phase elements, and finite-length diffusion transmission-line models in multiple geometries, and establish relationships between the DRT and the distributions of diffusion and capacitive times.

papers.title: Tunable Dearomative Intermolecular Hydrofunctionalization of Heteroarenes via Acridine/Acridinium Photoredox Catalysis
papers.abstract: Development of mechanistically divergent steps in photocatalytic manifolds by distinct modes remains understudied, impeding their implementation in synthetic methodology. In this study, we present a tunable dearomative hydroetherification, hydroesterification, and hydroamination of heteroarenes via two distinct mechanistic pathways for the synthesis of C-2 regioselective C(sp3) enriched 3D complex dihydrobenzofurans and indolines under photoredox conditions from readily available feedstock. The reaction operates via two independent two mechanistically distinct pathways: the conventional HAT pathway and less explored radical-polar crossover pathway. This modular approach enables tuning of the reactivity by varying both acridine/LA and HAT reagent. This design strategy exhibits broad substrate scope, most importantly, exclusive C-2 selectivity of hydroetherification, hydroesterification, and hydroamination. The scope of this synthetic method was further demonstrated through late-stage modification of drug molecules, natural products, and bioactive candidates. Notably, the synthetic potential was revealed when primary alcohol reacted chemoselectively over tertiary alcohol. Furthermore, the reaction was extended to dearomative difunctionalization with excellent trans diastereoselectivity.

papers.title: Functional-group-convergent synthesis of amides
papers.abstract: ：Amide bonds are ubiquitous in biology and synthetic chemistry, forming the backbone of peptides, proteins, pharmaceuticals, polymers, and natural products. Traditional amidation strategies typically rely on the inherent reactivity of carboxylic acids and amines, often requiring activating agents or pre-functionalized derivatives. Here, we report a functional-group-convergent (FGC) strategy for modular amide assembly from readily available starting materials. The method employs visible-light-mediated manganese-catalysed carbonylative amidation, proceeding via a synergistic radical–polar crossover cycle that merges radical and organometallic reactivity. Unactivated alkyl iodides, boronic acids, low-pressure carbon monoxide, and nitrogen-transfer reagents are converted directly into amides under mild conditions, with selective activation of C(sp3)–I bonds while preserving C(sp2)–I bonds. The approach tolerates diverse functional groups and enables 15N-labeled amide synthesis using isotopically enriched reagents. Its broad scope and chemoselectivity facilitate late-stage functionalization of complex drugs and natural products, exemplified by the efficient synthesis of Vorinostat and 15N-labeled (±)-Acoitremon.

papers.title: Probing the Aqueous Electrochemical Degradation in NASICONstructured Na2.5V1.5Ti0.5(PO4)3 by Multinuclear NMR through the Interplay Between Paramagnetic and Diamagnetic Vanadium Ions
papers.abstract: Although Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a very powerful method for investigating battery materials, its application is often complicated by the inherent presence of paramagnetic transition-metal ions (e.g., V+3/+4, Mn+2/+3, Fe+2/+3, etc). These ions induce extremely large chemical shift ranges, severe line broadening, and rapid spin relaxation, which often prevents NMR signal detection. In this work, we demonstrate that the interplay between the oxidation states and magnetic properties of vanadium, such as the transition from paramagnetic V+3/+4 to diamagnetic V+5, provides a unique direct probe into the structure and degradation of vanadium-based electrode materials. By systematically analyzing the results of Na2.5V1.5Ti0.5(PO4)3 samples, ranging from pristine NVTP powder and as-prepared electrodes to electrodes subjected to electrochemical cycling, we have developed a comprehensive mechanistic model of NVTP electrochemical degradation in aqueous media. Our findings reveal that surface vanadium oxidation to V+5 and its subsequent dissolution, together with phosphate, are among the primary drivers of charge capacity loss. The formation of residual Ti-rich phases, which also become NMR-visible due to the absence of paramagnetic V+3/+4, results in insulating layer growth and additional capacity loss. These NMR observations establish a definitive framework for probing the structure and stability of vanadium-based electrodes, offering critical insights for advancing high-performance aqueous electrochemical devices.

papers.title: POMs-GibbsNet: A Deep Neural Network for the Prediction of Thermodynamic Parameters of Polyoxometalates
papers.abstract: Polyoxometalates (POMs) are versatile metal–oxo clusters with remarkable structural diversity and applications spanning catalysis, energy storage, and materials science. However, accurately predicting their thermodynamic properties remains computationally demanding due to the large system sizes and the cost of density functional theory (DFT) frequency calculations required to obtain Gibbs free energies. In this work, we present POMs-GibbsNet, a deep neural network designed to predict the thermal free energy correction (G−E) of polyoxometalates by combining graph-based molecular representations with DFT-derived descriptors. Molecular structures were encoded using variants of the AABBA autocorrelation graph kernel, which captures atom–atom, bond–bond, and atom–bond correlations together with quantum-derived features including QTAIM descriptors. POMs-GibbsNet was trained on a dataset of 1625 POM structures spanning 19 chemical systems. A multilinear regression model based on global molecular descriptors was first evaluated as a baseline, achieving R2 values of 0.84–0.92 but with relatively large prediction errors (RMSE 9 kcal mol−1). In contrast, POMs-GibbsNet captures nonlinear structure–property relationships and significantly improves predictive accuracy. External validation using POMSimulator reaction networks comprising over 9×104 reactions shows excellent agreement between predicted and DFT reaction energies (R2 > 0.99), with errors typically within a few kcal mol−1. Notably, simplified atom–atom autocorrelation descriptors already provide robust performance while reducing model complexity. These results demonstrate that POMs-GibbsNet enables efficient estimation of thermodynamic corrections in POM systems, providing a powerful framework for accelerating the computational exploration of polyoxometalate speciation and self-assembly across large chemical spaces.

papers.title: CO2 transfer radical addition and polymerization mediated by organic photoredox catalysts
papers.abstract: Decarboxylation and carboxylation are among the most essential reactions for generating active species and producing useful compounds. If both reactions are sequentially built in organic or polymer synthesis, atom-economical and environmentally friendly processes can be achieved. Here, we report CO2 transfer radical addition (CTRA) and CO2 transfer radical polymerization (CTRP) catalyzed by organic photoredox catalysts at ambient temperatures under visible light irradiation. CTRA enables the 1:1 radical addition of potassium carboxylates and methacrylates, resulting quantitatively in half malonate ester derivatives. The CTRP of methacrylates proceeds via reversible decarboxylation of dormant carboxylate species, resulting in polymers with controlled molecular weights and terminal carboxylates. The terminal carboxylates can be further used for the block copolymerization of lactones to enable the direct synthesis of vinyl polymer-polyester block copolymers.

papers.title: Probing the spin state and a putative Ru-Ru bond in a dinuclear Ru(II) complex with X-ray quantum crystallography
papers.abstract: Determining the spin state of the metal complexes is central to understanding the electronic structure and the magnetic properties of materials. Inferring spin states from conventional crystallography is often ambiguous because it is largely limited to detecting geometric variations associated with different spin states. In this study, X-ray quantum crystallography (QCr) is employed to determine the spin state of a dinuclear ruthenium (II) complex by comparatively analyzing restricted and unrestricted wavefunctions fitted to high-resolution X-ray diffraction data. QCr models obtained from Hirshfeld Atom Refinement (HAR) and X-ray constrained wavefunction (XCW) fitting at different spin multiplicities indicate that the ruthenium centers adopt a low-spin state consistent with the electronic configuration of Ru(II), which is further corroborated by NMR spectroscopy. Additionally, electron density and bond-order analyses of the putative Ru–Ru bond based on the X-ray-derived wavefunction reveal the absence of bonding features between the Ru centers, in contrast to the single bond expected from conventional electron-counting methods.

papers.title: Modeling Xanthophyll Excited States via Cost-Effective Quantum Chemistry methods and Property-Based Diabatization
papers.abstract: Xanthophyll carotenoids play essential roles in photosynthetic light harvesting and photoprotection in biological systems, yet the accurate description of their excited states at feasible computational cost remains challenging due to their extended π-conjugation andmultireference character. Here, we compare the DFT/MRCI, FOMO-CI, and mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT (MRSF-TDDFT) descriptions of the excited states for a representative set of xanthophylls. We analyze vertical excitation energies and potential energy profiles along the bond-length alternation coordinate, adopting a multiple-property-based diabatization (MPD) scheme to consistently characterize electronic states across methods. We find a remarkably consistent description of the low-lying excited states and their potential energy curves across the methods. DFT/MRCI and the semiempirical FOMO-CI exhibit closely aligned behavior across xanthophylls, while the performance ofMRSF-TDDFT depends on the choice of exchange-correlation functional. Overall, our calculations suggest that the covalent 2A − g state lies below the ionic 1B + u at the Franck-Condon point. Our analysis provides general insight into the electronic structure of xanthophylls, including the interplay between covalent and ionic configurations induced by structural distortions and environmental effects. The MPD framework enables a direct comparison of state character, highlighting the similarities between methods and clarifying the origin of remaining differences. This work establishes a consistent framework for understanding xanthophyll photophysics, and offers practical guidance for modeling their excited states with cost-effective methods.

papers.title: Copper-Catalyzed, Photoinduced Carbonylative Cross-Coupling of Alkyl Iodides with Amines, Alcohols and Water.
papers.abstract: A general photoinduced copper-catalyzed carbonylative cross-coupling of alkyl iodides with amines for the synthesis of amides under mild conditions is reported. Using a readily accessible, inexpensive copper complex, [Cu(bcp)DPEphos]PF 6 , the reaction proceeds at room temperature and accommodates a broad range of amines, delivering the corresponding amides in good to excellent yields. Notably, the transformation can also be performed - for the first time - under ambient carbon monoxide pressure, enhancing its practicality. The procedure also extends to hydrazines, alcohols, and water, enabling an efficient and divergent access to hydrazides, esters, and carboxylic acids and providing a versatile and sustainable approach to the catalytic carbonylative functionalization of alkyl electrophiles.

papers.title: Container material and matrix effects on the adsorption and recovery of longchain perfluoroalkyl acids: a case study of PFTeA
papers.abstract: Per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) adsorb to laboratory containers, potentially causing significant under-reporting of solution concentrations. While adsorption has been examined for shorter-chain PFAS, far less attention has been given to longer-chain species, which are expected to adhere more strongly. This study focuses on the adsorption of the C14 compound perfluorotetradecanoic acid (PFTeA) on different container materials in aqueous solutions with varying salinity, evaluates both storage solvent composition (water vs. water-acetonitrile mixtures) and solvent-assisted desorption (acetonitrile vs. methanol). Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA, C8) is included for comparison. Adsorption losses were quantified by electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI-MS), with an internal standard added post-sampling to assess instrument response. PFTeA showed the greatest adsorption to plastics (HDPE), followed by stainless steel, with adsorption lowest on borosilicate glass and aluminum. In saline media, PFTeA adsorption on containers was delayed within the first 24 hours. Acetonitrile was markedly more effective than methanol at recovering adsorbed PFTeA. These results highlight the elevated adsorption risk posed by long-chain PFAS, particularly in plastic containers, and provide guidance for improving PFAS quantification, degradation studies, and sample storage and handling protocols. Relative PFTeA remaining in solution after storage over 7 days (C/C₀), demonstrating strong adsorption to HDPE and less adsorption to aluminum.

papers.title: Direct Anodic Decarboxylative Alkylation Reaction to Pharmaceutically Relevant Quinones
papers.abstract: We established an electrochemical platform for the direct decarboxylative coupling of various carboxylic acids with para -quinones. This single-step approach rapidly constructs complex molecular architectures without pre-functionalization and offers a handle for accessing drug-like scaffolds. By generating radicals via direct anodic oxidation of carboxylic acids, this approach expands the synthetic toolbox for electrochemical sp 3 –sp 2 decarboxylative couplings. The method demonstrates excellent functional group tolerance across diverse carboxylic acids, including both aromatic and aliphatic substrates. Furthermore, it enables synthesis of various antimalarial scaffolds and pharmaceutical precursors for east coast fever treatment. The method was successfully scaled up 16-fold, confirming its robustness. This electrochemical approach preserves halide moieties such as bromide on the para -quinone core and therefore allows further modification of the derived product, demonstrating the formation of a platform compound. The protocol further enables transfer of fully deuterated methyl groups from acetic acid- d 4 to pharmaceutically relevant target molecules while preserving the deuterium content without the use of hazardous methyl group transfer agents. A selectively deuterated antimalarial lead structure was synthesized successfully in two electrochemical steps from readily available starting materials.

papers.title: Structure-Induced Optical Function from Molecular Organization in Imine-Based Crystals
papers.abstract: text. Molecular science has traditionally advanced optoelectronic materials through single-molecule structure–property relationships. However, in organic optoelectronics, device performance is largely governed by solid-state aggregation and molecular packing. This shift highlights the need to resolve structure–property relationships at the supramolecular scale, where material functionality emerges from intermolecular interactions, spatial organization, and aggregate geometry. Here, experimental characterization combined with computational studies is used to investigate how molecular structure controls aggregation, packing, and the resulting optical properties of (E)-N,1-bis(4-(phenylethynyl)phenyl)methanimine derivatives. While molecular substitution induces only minor changes in optical properties in dilute solution, aggregation and especially solid-state lead to pronounced differences across the derivatives, including the formation of distinct polymorphic structures with markedly different emissive responses. These results demonstrate how crystal packing modulates excitonic coupling and enables organic optical waveguiding, highlighting the potential of these materials for crystalline organic photonic architectures and underscoring the importance of aggregation and packing in the design of organic photonic materials. Such insights provide a framework for rationally engineering solid-state order to achieve predictable and tunable photonic functionality in advanced optoelectronic systems.

papers.title: The Ballad of LLM Agents: Philosophical Reasoning for Chemistry
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show remarkable potential for scientific reasoning but often produce unreliable or scientifically unactionable outputs when faced with multi-step logic, domain grounding, and interpretability challenges, especially in complex fields like chemistry and materials science.
